metadata.title: How To Build a Medical Equipment Business
metadata.author: Earn Your Leisure
metadata.shortDescription:
In this clip, Dr. Trisha Bailey joins hosts Rashad Bilal and Troy Millings to share her inspiring journey of building a successful medical equipment business. Dr. Bailey opens up about her experience transitioning from the recruiting industry to starting a second business, the challenges she faced, and the motivation behind her entrepreneurial pursuits. Her resilience and determination to make a difference in the lives of disabled individuals led her to establish a medical equipment business that focuses on providing compassionate and personalized service to patients.

As an audience, we delve into the intricate details of the medical equipment industry, understanding the process of buying, selling, and delivering essential medical items to hospitals and patients. Dr. Bailey explains the significance of her business model, which not only caters to the financial aspect but also prioritizes the well-being and comfort of the patients.

Through this informative and engaging conversation, viewers gain insights into the regulatory requirements, profit margins, and the complexities of dealing with insurance and billing processes. Dr. Bailey's emphasis on the importance of exceptional service and the impact of strong relationships with both clients and staff members sheds light on the core values that drive her business forward.

Join us in exploring the various challenges and triumphs encountered in the medical equipment industry, and learn from Dr. Trisha Bailey's remarkable journey as she established a business with a unique blend of purpose, compassion, and profitability.

#Entrepreneurship #MedicalBusiness #Empowerment #Resilience #HealthcareIndustry #BusinessJourney #EYLMedium #SuccessStory #InspiringWomen #FinancialIndependence #MedicalEquipment #ImpactfulBusiness #Motivation

As the experienced liason between the seller and the buyer, GoSouthernMD.com makes sure that the product, seller and buyer are legitimate and that the Durable Medical Equipment listed is indeed intended for the buyer and the needs of the buyer.
We make sure of this prior to completing the sell of the Used or New Durable Medical Equipment. Since we compete against Amazon, Ebay, Craigslist, etc., we understand that there is not anyone available at these companies to make sure the choice is for the right purpose and indeed the right size, etc.
GoSouthernMD.com is going to change the way that individuals and companies can list Durable Medical Equipment both used and new that they own with a reliable and experienced source. This way we guarantee that the product is intended for the right person and specifies ones needs.
Please attach your pictures and any other relevant information you wish to add along with dimensions, weight and description.
The last step is to list your price your willing to accept. We will give you access to your page to make changes as you wish once your listing goes live.
The terms and conditions are as follows:
GoSouthernMD.com will assist for free in managing your listing and will assist in questions or concerns by the potential buyer of your listing.
Your listing will be placed with our site within 48 business hours upon your approval. Your listing fee will be $25 for access to your listing along with our back office support and Search Engine Optimization and Programming by our team. This fee will be deducted from the final sale. We will charge one fee per listing and multiple listings will be free once the $25 fee is paid. If it does not sell then you do not have to pay the fee. We have a right based on our experience to give you our opinion to give you the best chance to sell your product.
As a liaison between you and the buyer, at no time is GoSouthernMD.com liable for your product if it is false listed based on the product not being what the buyer expects. The liability will solely be held between you and the buyer but we will do everything possible to rectify any complaint.
Your listing will be placed and be seen by over 1,000 unique visitors a day and our sales support team will assist in selling your product. We will not do anything under your listing price without your approval. Once your listing sells, the buyer will pay for the product with a credit card on our site and you will be notified via an email that your listing sold. You will then decide if you wish us to ship it on our UPS account with the shipping costs deducted from the total. We will send you the cost before you agree to this or you can ship it yourself and offer tracking to the buyer.

​

Recently the FDA has issued a final rule to adopt ISO 13485 into it’s quality system regulation. 
This aligns expectations of Quality Management Systems between the US and Europe.

However, for those of you interested in the European market, even with these aligned expectations, you will need to abide by ISO 13485. 

Part 1:

21 CFR Part 820 stands for Part 820 of Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations. 

Established by the FDA, these regulations set the foundation for good manufacturing practices focusing on Quality Management Systems, or QMS. Since December 1978, it's aimed to ensure that medical devices in the US market are safe, effective, and compliant. Check our article on Design History File here: https://matrixone.health/blog/design-history-file-dhf-for-medical-devices-fda-and-mdr-compliance

21 CFR Part 820 requires manufacturers to develop a structured, process-based QMS. 

This legal framework ensures that every aspect of production meets regulatory and customer requirements, from design to distribution.


21 CFR Part 820 is divided into 15 subparts, each addressing a specific aspect of the Quality System. Let's briefly go over these:

General Provisions: Defines the scope and applicability, emphasizing its relevance to manufacturers of finished devices.


Quality System Requirements: Outlines management responsibilities, audit, and training needs.


Design Controls: Focuses on procedures and controls throughout the design cycle.


Document Controls: Ensures proper document management for accessibility and security.
Purchasing Controls: Deals with supplier management and purchasing processes.


Identification and Traceability: Ensures clear product identification through all stages.


Production and Process Controls: Covers various aspects of production and process management.


Acceptance Activities: Describes testing and acceptance criteria.


Non-conforming Product: Details how to handle products that don't meet standards.


Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA): Guides the CAPA process, from documentation to effectiveness checks.


Labeling and Packaging Control: Ensures label integrity and safe packaging.


Handling, Storage, Distribution, and Installation: Aims to protect product quality post-manufacturing.


Records: Specifies record-keeping requirements for FDA review.


Servicing: Outlines requirements for product servicing.


Statistical Techniques: Describes the use of statistical methods in quality control.



ISO 13485 vs 21 CFR Part 820

While both ISO 13485 and 21 CFR Part 820 focus on Quality Management Systems, they are different animals. ISO 13485 is a global standard, it is not a region specific standard or law, such as 21 CFR Part 820 being a regulation specific to the US.

metadata.title: What is 21 CFR 820?
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
21 CFR Part 820 is the FDA Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) regulation which became effective on December 18, 1978. The regulations ensure that medical devices distributed in the US market are designed and developed with adequate procedures, people are trained, and quality records are maintained. In 1990, the FDA revised of the CGMP regulation to add the requirement for design controls (i.e., 21 CFR 820.30) authorized by the Safe Medical Devices Act. The revised regulation was released in 1996, and it is referred to as the Quality System Regulations (i.e., QSR). Title 21 is the section of the Code of Federal Regulations (i.e., CFR) reserved for the Food and Drug Administration (i.e., FDA) regulations.

metadata.title: QSR to QMSR: What Changes Before Feb 2, 2026 (FDA Medical Devices)
metadata.author: AMORIT EDUCATION
metadata.shortDescription:
The FDA is transitioning from QSR (21 CFR Part 820) to the new QMSR — and the compliance deadline is Feb 2, 2026.

In this short video, we break down what’s changing, why it matters, and what medical device teams should do now.

Key takeaways:

QMSR is a hybrid model that incorporates ISO 13485:2016 into the regulation (“incorporation by reference”).

Risk-based thinking becomes a system-wide expectation (not just design controls).

FDA inspections will shift toward system effectiveness — and FDA may request management review records and supplier audit reports.

A practical starting plan: gap analysis → SOP/document updates → risk-based internal audits → integrated risk management.

Want a simple QMSR transition checklist?

Comment “CHECKLIST” and We’ll share it.

Disclaimer: Educational content only; not legal or regulatory advice.

#QMSR #FDA #ISO13485 #MedicalDevices #QualityAssurance #RegulatoryAffairs #MedTech #Compliance #QualitySystems

This short video clip is presented to
introduce you to some basic information
on the requirements of the code of
federal
regulations, food and drug
administration 21
CFR820 quality system regulation, good
manufacturing practices for the medical
devices. Current good manufacturing
practice requirements also known as
CGMP are set forth in this regulation.
The requirements are specifically
intended to ensure that finished medical
devices will be safe and effective and
in compliance with the FDA requirements.
21 CFR820 is the United States
regulations equivalent to the European
standard
ISO 13485 2003 in that they are both
written specifically to dictate or set
forth the requirements by which a
medical device is designed, developed,
manufactured and monitored. And by
monitor I mean how complaints are
handled. The sections of 21 CFR 820 are
as follows. Subp part A general
provisions which doesn't contain any
requirements but includes the
scope
definitions and a brief description of
what a quality system is.
Subp part B quality system requirements
which includes management responsibility
such as the requirement for a documented
quality management system and management
review quality audits or the
requirements for internal
audits and personnel requirements which
includes having competent employees and
documenting their training needs.
Subp part C design control. Each
manufacturer of any class two or three
device and some class one devices must
maintain procedures to control the
design of the device. There are quite a
few requirements in this section that
must be complied with 10 to be exact or
the FDA could potentially write the
business a warning letter or cause a
plant shutdown.
Subp part D contains the requirements
for document control or how your
documents are created, revised and
managed. Subp part E contains the
requirements for purchasing controls
which includes supplier
evaluation. Subp part F contains the
requirements for identification and
traceability. Identification and
traceability for medical devices is
critical to ensure a quick and effective
recall. if
necessary. Subp part G, production and
process controls. This is also a quite
detailed section and includes
requirements for control of production
and process changes, environmental
control if the environment can adversely
affect the product, personnel hygiene
requirements, building suitability and
maintenance of machinery.
Subar also contains requirements for
inspection, measuring and test
equipment, also known as calibration and
process
validation. Subp part H acceptance
activities which includes receiving in
process and finished device acceptance
as well as identification of acceptance
status.
Subp part I contains the requirements
for non-conforming product and how they
are
managed. Subp part J contains the
requirements for corrective and
preventive
action. Subp part K labeling and package
control. This section speaks directly to
the requirements for not only device
labeling but also device package
labeling.
Subp part L contains the requirements
for handling, storage, distribution, and
installation as
applicable. Subp part M contains
requirements for records which includes
the requirements
for all quality records and their
accessibility to regulatory
personnel, device master records and
device history records as well as
complaint files.
Subp part N contains the requirements
for servicing of a medical device if
it's
applicable. And lastly, subp part O
contains the requirements for
statistical techniques for controlling
and verifying the acceptability of
process capability and product
characteristics. We certainly hope you
enjoy this online training experience.
Please proceed to the beginning of your
Cal ISO course to receive a more
in-depth training on this FDA
regulation. If you should have any
further questions or concerns, please
see our frequently asked questions page
on our website.

Another big change involves risk management. Under the old QSR, risk was mostly explicitly required in design controls. So naturally, a lot of companies treated risk management as a design FMEA activity. You [snorts] don't risk analysis through design reviews, you document it and move on. That's all changed. Under the QMSR, risk-based decision-making is required across seven different clauses like purchasing and Kappa. It has to run through your entire quality system. So if you have risk files sitting only in your design controls and nowhere else, that's a gap an auditor's going to find. For most businesses, this means risk-based thinking needs to be embedded into every major procedure. This can be fixed with a few changes, though for many, it'll change their entire quality structure. The last change is supplier controls. Before you could get by with only approved supplier lists and incoming inspections. That's not going to cut it anymore. The QMSR follows ISO 1345 here, which requires risk-based supplier evaluation. This means you need to assess the risk of the purchased product, what happens if the supplier fails, and how that impacts your device and your compliance. So something like an office supply vendor is a low-risk control, but a sterilization contractor is a high-risk control. And for each one, you need a documented rationale and monitoring frequency that matches the risk. For companies managing dozens or hundreds of suppliers, this is probably where QMS are hits hardest on a day-to-day basis. So, those are three of the biggest challenges in the new rule. So, the question becomes, who's most exposed? The most high-risk manufacturers are those who only complied with QSR and never pursued ISO 1345. These companies will definitely need to restructure their quality processes to meet these standards. The other high-risk group, businesses still running quality processes on paper or spreadsheets. QMS are expects an interconnected, traceable, risk-based quality system. It's really hard to demonstrate with a folder of Excel files when an inspector is sitting across from you. Speaking of software, let's talk about how QMS is affected. If you already have software, you're probably wondering, does this actually support the way the FDA inspects now? Here's what to look for. First, make sure risk management is woven in, not bolted on. That means risk decisions linked to design, purchasing, and production, and aren't siloed in stand-alone modules. Secondly, traceability needs to be across the full system. Everything from design to Kappa should all be connected and auditable in a single thread. And third, make sure it still supports CFR part 11. ISO uses the word approved, but never specifies signatures and dates. The FDA clarified that still means part 11 governs electronic records and e-signatures. It's one of the key areas where ISO compliance alone isn't enough. Several QMS platforms are built specifically for medical device manufacturers and support QMS are compliance, including Greenlight Guru and Qualio. They offer pre-validated environments and built-in workflows aligned to ISO 1345 and FDA requirements. Other general systems that still help comply with QMS are include ETQ Reliance, UniPoint, and QT9. But at the end of the day, no software is a guarantee. You'll still need to validate them for your intended use, write and follow your own procedures, and make sure your team uses them correctly. That's why at Software Connect, we work with you to find the best QMS for your exact needs. If you want expert help and save weeks of research, visit softwareconnect.com and book a free call with us. With that said, let's quickly recap. QMS R is the biggest change to device quality regulations in the past 30 years, but the underlying goal here hasn't changed. Build safe, effective devices with a quality system that proves it. Only now, you just need to be aligned with ISO 1345 while you do it. So, if you're in the market for a new QMS, check out our other video comparing the best options for medical device manufacturers. Thanks for watching. We'll see you next time.

metadata.title: Selling medical imaging data to AI: HIPAA and DICOM explained
metadata.author: Sell My Data To AI
metadata.shortDescription:
Medical imaging is one of the clearest cases of labeled data in healthcare, because every study comes with a radiologist's report. It is also protected health information, held in a format that hides identifiers in places a simple export will miss.

Gareth Hoyle, founder of Sell My Data To AI, explains what AI buyers want from imaging and diagnostics centers, what HIPAA says about selling scans, how DICOM images are de-identified across headers, burned-in text and facial features, and why the organization that holds the records has to be the one that licenses them.

This video explains what the rules say. It is not legal advice for your organization.

Read the full guide: https://sellmydatatoai.net/sell-your-data/imaging-and-diagnostics-centers

Related reading:
De-identification for AI training data: https://sellmydatatoai.net/guides/de-identification-for-ai-training-data
Image datasets: https://sellmydatatoai.net/buy-ai-training-data/image-datasets
How we vet sellers: https://sellmydatatoai.net/how-we-vet

Book a free 30-minute consultation: https://sellmydatatoai.net/book-a-consultation

This video uses an AI avatar of Gareth Hoyle, created with HeyGen. The script was written and approved by Sell My Data To AI.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:33 What imaging buyers want
1:12 What HIPAA says about selling scans
2:02 How DICOM images are de-identified
2:49 Who can sign the license
3:19 What to send us

segments.text: Medical imaging is one of the clearest
cases of labeled data in healthcare.
Every study comes with a radiologist's
report describing what the images show,
and those pairs are what imaging AI
developers train on. They are also
protected health information.
I'm Gareth Hoile, founder of Sell My
Data to AI, an independent broker for AI
training data. In this video, I'll cover
what imaging buyers want, what HIPAA
says about selling scans, how DICOM
images are deidentified, and who can
sign the license. AI companies buy
imaging data that links studies to
expert interpretation and, where
possible, to outcomes.
Unreported images are worth far less
than images with reports, measurements,
or confirmed diagnoses.
A scan linked to a later follow-up or
pathology result is rarer still because
it gives a model's answer something to
be checked against.
Protenus licenses healthcare data to AI
model builders and highlights a Siemens
Healthineers medical imaging team among
its users.
No buyer whose terms are public
publishes an imaging price range, so
volume, modality mix, report quality,
and linked outcomes decide the figure.
HIPAA does not allow an imaging center
to sell identifiable scans without
patient authorization. Under 45 CFR
a covered entity may not sell protected
health information, and section
requires an authorization for any
disclosure that is a sale. Information
deidentified to the privacy rule
standard is not individually
identifiable health information, but the
same rule says disclosing a code or
other means of reidentification counts
as disclosing protected health
information.
So keep the linkage key for follow-up
studies out of the package. State laws
can add to this. Washington's My Health
My Data Act requires a
authorization to sell consumer health
data. You de-identify DICOM images by
cleaning three layers, the header
attributes, any text burned into the
pixels, and for some scans, the anatomy
itself.
HIPAA's safe harbor method lists all
elements of dates except year, full face
photographic images and any comparable
images, and any other unique identifying
number or code.
The DICOM standards confidentiality
profiles in part 15 annex E handle
burned in text through a clean pixel
data option and define a separate option
for recognizable visual features, which
matters for head CT and MRI.
The standard itself warns that using the
profiles does not guarantee every
identifier is removed, so buyers expect
a re-identification test on a sample.

in the reports. Read the reading

title, and no buyer sees a sample until

linked, who reads your studies, and how

send any images or reports at this
stage.
Sellers pay nothing to be assessed. We

completes, agreed in writing before we
introduce you to any buyer.
We're a broker, not a law firm, so take

metadata.author: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
metadata.shortDescription:
FDA’s Office of Compliance provides an overview of the proposed rule. Comments are due by June 6, 2022. When final and effective, every U.S. wholesale distributor and third-party logistics facility will be held to these standards. Only those licensed according to the proposed national standards would be able to engage in transactions related to the sale and distribution of certain prescription drugs with other members of the supply chain. Where a state does not have a licensing program in accordance with the regulation, FDA would be the licensing authority.

to complete the inspection,
records kept at the inspection site,
or that can be immediately retrieved electronically,
must be made readily available during the inspection.
For records kept at a central location
apart from the inspection site
and not electronically retrievable,
such records must be made available for inspection
within two business days
of a request by a state or federal official,
or sooner if necessitated by the duration of the inspection.
We will not be covering third-party organizations,
approved third-party organizations, or AO,
in this presentation.
However, FDA will give more information in the future
as we implement rule.
Please see proposed sections 205.17, 205.18 and 205.19
for the processes
for the use of approved third-party organizations,
general qualifications,
and the processes and procedures for approval of AOs by FDA.
Now, this concludes our discussion
of proposed 3PL requirements.
We encourage you to provide your comments
on the proposed rule to the public docket
as we described earlier,
and following those instructions provided.
I will now turn it over to Sara Keller
for an overview of the proposed requirements
for wholesale distributors.
- [Sara] Thank you for the introduction.
We now move forward with our discussion
of wholesale distributor requirements in this proposed rule.
To implement section 503(e)(1) of the FD&C Act,
proposed section 205.20(a) codifies a requirement
that a wholesale drug distributor, or WDD for short,
be licensed by the state from which the drug is distributed
or by FDA if the state from which the drug is distributed
has not established a licensure requirement
in accordance with the standards set forth in the regulation
and by the state into which the drug is distributed
if that state requires such a license.
This requirement is consistent
with how states currently license wholesale distributors.
FDA proposes to set the licensure term
for wholesale distributors at two years.
Any license issued or renewed
pursuant to this proposed section
will expire two years after the date
on which the license was issued.
A wholesale distributor may submit a renewal application
up to 90 calendar days before the date of expiration.
The agency believes that two years
aligns with current practices,
does not place an undue burden on state or FDA resources,
and provides adequate protection to American consumers
because it ensures that renewals will be based
on current information and operations.
The DSCSA requires that wholesale distributors obtain
a surety bond to be licensed
and engage in wholesale distribution.
FDA is proposing to establish the terms of this requirement
in proposed section 205.21.
The surety bond is intended to ensure compliance with DSCSA
and that any administrative penalties levied
by the licensing authorities are paid.
As we are not reviewing the details
of this section of the proposed rule,
we encourage you to review proposed section 205.21
for the requirements for surety bonds.
Proposed section 205.22 outlines the general requirements
that must be met for a state or federal licensing authority
to issue an initial license to a wholesale distributor
or a renewal of any such license.
Under proposed section 205.22,
the person submitting the application for licensure
is the applicant.
The applicant must be at least 18 years old
and submit all required information,
including an affidavit stating that applicant's ownership
or management of,
or employment by the entity would not preclude the entity
from receiving or maintaining a license
under proposed section 205.25(a).
The applicant must also pay any applicable licensing fee
to be issued a license.
As previously mentioned,
wholesale distributors are required to obtain a surety bond
to be licensed and engage in wholesale distribution.
Proposed section 205.22 requires
that the wholesale distributor must furnish a surety bond
as described in proposed section 205.21
with this application for licensure.
See section 205.21 for more details.
Proposed section 205.22(c) outlines the information
that licensing authority will require
as part of a WDD's initial application for licensure
and renewal applications.
This information is summarized on the slide.
FDA believes this information is necessary
for the licensing authority to assess
whether the WDD is in good standing
and has the infrastructure and capabilities
to fulfill its duties and obligation
under the national standards for WDD licensure.
With respect to the disclosure of certain felonies,
the application for licensure must include details
about whether the WDD has ever been convicted of a felony
relating to prescription drug distribution,
including a conviction
under section 301(i) or (k) of the FD&C Act
or 18 USC 1365 relating to product tampering.
Additionally, FDA is proposing to require
that the WDD inform FDA
if it has received any citations
for violating requirements for licensure
or received any significant disciplinary actions
within the past seven years
that presented a threat
of serious adverse health consequences, or death to humans.
FDA believes this information is necessary
to ensure the wholesale distributor can demonstrate
that it has not engaged
in a pattern of violating the standards for licensure.
For licensure renewals,
the proposed rule would require the WDD
to certify that it continually met the requirements
of subpart C of the regulation
and informed the licensing authority
of certain changes to information
if such changes have not already been submitted
to the licensing authority.
Under proposed section 205.22(e),
a wholesale distributor's license
must be available upon request.
The WDD must maintain its license
in a readily retrievable manner,
and must permit state, or federal inspectors,
or others acting on behalf of the licensing authority
to inspect the license.
Proposed section 205.23 outlines the process
for applying for WDD licensure with FDA
in the instance that the state
in which it engages in wholesale distribution
has not established a licensure program.
While proposed section 205.23 is only applicable
to WDDs obtaining a license from FDA,
FDA recommends that states implement similar procedures
to ensure that all WDD licenses issued are consistent
with the proposed regulation pursuant
to section 503(e)(1)(b) of the FD&C Act.
We will now review the proposed process
for federal licensure of WDDs.
The federal licensure process begins
when a WDD seeking licensure for a facility
submits an application to FDA for review and consideration.
The application must be submitted electronically
and include the information set forth
in proposed sections 205.21 and 205.22,
along with the surety bond and supporting documentation
that demonstrates the applicant's ability
to comply with requirements,
intend to ensure that continued safety,
identity, strength, quality,
and purity of the prescription drugs.
Where FDA has approved one or more organizations
to conduct inspections of a WDD, as permitted by the DSCSA,
the WDD should indicate which authorized organization
it prefers to conduct its inspection.
If no organization has been approved,
FDA will conduct the inspection.
The application must be signed by the applicant,
applicant's agent, or other authorized official,
and all fees must be paid.
So as not to delay the licensure process,
when reviewing an application,
FDA intends to work with WDDs
to correct minor errors made on the application
and communicate with the WDD
about additional information the agency may need.
The FDA will determine
whether applicable requirements are met.
If an approved organization
has conducted the licensure review,
the responsibility for determining
whether the applicable requirements are met
will remain with the FDA.
Issuance of a license is covered
under proposed section 205.23(d).
When FDA determines
that the WDD meets the applicable requirements
under sections 503(e)(1) and 583 of the FD&C Act
and none of the prohibited factors listed
in proposed section 205.30(a) are present,
FDA will send the applicant an approval letter
and a licensing certificate
effective on the date that it is issued.
The license will remain valid until it expires
unless it is suspended or revoked.
For the licensing authority
to effectively carry out its responsibilities,
a WDD must keep its license information current
and report any changes on information previously submitted
to the licensing authority.
Currently, the reporting requirements
for these types of changes vary by state.
Proposed section 205.24 establishes specific timeframes
for reporting changes
and FDA believes that standardizing the timeframes
will help make reporting business-related changes
less burdensome for industry and licensing authorities.
Proposed section 205.24 would require the WDD
to submit changes to certain information
such as the information submitted with the surety bond,
or as part of an application for licensure
to the licensing authority
within 30 calendar days
of the date the change became effective.
FDA is also proposing that a change in the location
at which wholesale district distribution occurs
will require an inspection of the new facility
prior to commencing wholesale distribution at the location.
For a change to the person engaged
in wholesale distribution,
a new license will be required
prior to beginning operations.
The application for a new license
must be submitted no later than 30 calendar days
prior to the change in ownership.
A new inspection of the WDD will be performed
at a reasonable time.
Proposed section 205.25
covers the standards for the qualifications
of wholesale distributors key personnel,
such as prohibited conduct,
basic standards for key personnel working
within a wholesale distribution facility,
and grounds for denying a licensure application.
As described in proposed section 205.3(g),
FDA considers key personnel to include
any individual who has responsibility
for managing the operations of the wholesale distributor,
including any principal, owner, director,
officer of the wholesale distributor,
designated representatives,
and other individuals who are authorized
to enter areas where prescription drugs are held
and are likely to handle prescription drugs
as part of their responsibilities.
Proposed section 205.25 covers prohibited persons
and qualifications for key personnel.
Under this proposed section,
a WDD is prohibited from obtaining or maintaining licensure
if the WDD has been convicted of a felony
relating to prescription drug distribution,
including a conviction under section 301(i)
or (k) of the FD&C Act
or 18 USC 1365 relating to product tampering,
or if the WDD has been cited for certain repeated violations
related to the FD&C Act
that presents threat of serious adverse health consequences
or death to humans.
Under proposed section 205.25,
key personnel working
within a wholesale distribution facility
must have the appropriate education,
background training, and experience necessary
to carry out their assigned functions within the operation.
No one within the facility
should carry out responsibilities of key personnel
without the proper training and experience.
Also under proposed section 205.25(c),
licensure may be denied if a wholesale distributor
or any of their key personnel delayed or impeded inspection,
omitted material information,
or furnished falsed or fraudulent information
in an application,
or is subject to licensure suspension or revocation
for currently or previously held license
for manufacturer or distribution of any drugs.
Proposed section 205.25(d)
states that a WDD must maintain a list of officers,
directors, facility managers, designated representatives,
and other key personnel in charge of wholesale distribution,
including storage and handling,
and include a description of their duties
and a summary of their qualification.
Proposed section 205.25(e) describes
how a WDD must also establish
and implement written policies and procedure
designed to ensure
that their key personnel meet the necessary qualifications.
These policies and procedures must identify the personnel
at the WDD's facility
who are responsible for implementing
and maintaining facility personnel requirements,
complying with all licensure reporting requirements,
and ensuring key personnel receive initial
and regular training.
Proposed section 205.25(f) limits a facility manager,
or designated representative,
to hold that position at one facility at a time.
This is to ensure that the facility manager
or designated representative is actively engaged
in managing the daily operations of the facility
and that they remain aware
of any non-compliance issues that may arise.
Section 583(b)(4) of the FD&C Act,
as added by DSCSA,
requires fingerprinting
and background checks of facility managers
and designated representative of wholesale distributors.
The background check when completed
must demonstrate that the facility manager or representative
has no history of criminal convictions
pursuant to proposed section 205.25(a)
and outlined in slide number 84.
Proposed section 205.26 establishes basic standards
for the storage and handling of prescription drugs
by wholesale distributors,
including facility requirements.
Although the FD&C Act permits an entity
to be more than one type of trading partner
so long as it complies
with all applicable DSCSA requirements,
FDA believes that the processes
and functions of each type of entity
need to be kept separate
for the licensing authority to ensure the entities complying
with all applicable requirements.
Therefore, under proposed section 205.26(a),
any wholesale distributor's facility
that is also licensed or registered
as another trading partner, such as a 3PL,
and operating from the same address
must have separate systems and processes in place
for their separate functions.
Proposed section 205.26(b)(1)
describes how the facility must be of a suitable size,
configuration and design
to ensure proper storage, maintenance, and cleanliness.
The facility must also be equipped
with clearly defined areas
that separate drugs that are unfit for distribution
from those that are saleable
to avoid potential mistakes
when distributing the prescription drugs.
Under proposed section 205.26(b)(2),
facilities must be sufficiently secure
to protect the prescription drugs in the supply chain
from possible theft or diversion.
Facilities must protect against unauthorized entry
and ensure that the premises are well lit
and not vulnerable to intrusion.
Entry and access to areas
where prescription drugs are held within the facility
must be limited to those who have the appropriate experience
and training needed to conduct wholesale distribution.
Proposed section 205.26(b)(3)
outlines how a WDD has a responsibility
of ensuring that prescription drugs are stored
under proper conditions to maintain the safety
and effectiveness of the drugs it distributes.
A facility must have equipment
that ensures prescription drugs are properly stored,
such as cold storage, refrigerators,
temperature and humidity devices, and air handling units.
Also it equipment must be maintained in good repair
and must be suitable for distribution of prescription drugs.
Facility assessments must be regularly conducted
and documented.
Accordingly, a WDD's facility
must maintain appropriate equipment and good working order
to ensure that prescription drugs are properly stored
in the facility.
To this end,
FDA is proposing that WDDs establish written procedures
to ensure that equipment is installed, maintained
and repaired by qualified individuals
following written procedures.
Equipment should be calibrated and validated
at regular intervals.
He further proposed
that WDDs use manual, electro-mechanical,
or electronic temperature and humidity recording equipment,
or logs,
to document proper storage.
Monitoring equipment must immediately alert
of any deviations from required storage conditions.
FDA expects that as crucial part
of the creation of quality system,
wholesale distributors will establish, maintain,
and follow written policies and procedures
regarding the safeguarding
of the prescription drugs within their control.
Proposed section 205.26(c) outlines several requirements
for maintaining written policies and procedures
to ensure that the requirements
are carried out properly and consistently.
The requirements listed on this slide
include the requirement to do business
with other authorized trading partners,
the requirement to properly maintain equipment
in good working order,
and the requirement to inspect shipping containers
for suspect or illegitimate products among others.
Please refer to proposed section 205.26(c)
for a complete list.
Wholesale distributors are not limited
to establishing written policies and procedures
for the stated functions in proposed section 205.26(c).
A wholesale distributor may wish to establish
written policies and procedures
pertaining to other aspects of wholesale distribution
and staffing of their facilities.
The purpose of requiring written policies and procedures
is to assist staff and management
at a wholesale distribution facility
to determine the processes required to ensure safe storage
and distribution of prescription drugs.
Wholesale distributors are responsible
for contractor compliance.
A WDD must ensure that the contractor abides
by applicable written policies and procedures.
Furthermore, written policies and procedures
must clearly describe responsibilities of the WDD
and any contractors used to fulfill the WDDs duties.
Proper record keeping is essential
to the timely identification, recording and reporting
of issues arising within the supply chain.
Section 583(b)(2) of the FD&C Act,
as added by the DSCSA,
requires FDA to create national standards
for establishing and maintaining records
pertaining to the distribution of prescription drugs.
Proposed section 205.27 covers those standards on records.
FDA is proposing in section 205.27(a)
that these records include documentation
pertaining to the storage, handling, security,
inventory, shipping, of prescription drugs.
This will include records related to the sale, purchase,
trade, delivery and receipt,
as well as policies, procedures, instructions,
contracts, data, inspection reports,
and any other documentation related
to compliance with this part.
This section also includes records related
to the distribution of prescription drugs
such as invoices, purchase orders,
packing slips, and shipping records.
These records could be stored and maintained electronically.
These records maintenance requirements will allow
for greater confidence
in the information preserved at the facility.
It will also potentially allow for greater confidence
in the information disseminated to other trading partners.
All records must be securely stored,
and any alteration made to records must be signed and dated
while preserving the original information contained
in the record.
See proposed section 205.27(b).
This is intended to ensure that all records related
to the distribution of prescription drugs
provide transparency and accurately reflect the activities
of the wholesale distributor.
FDA also believes that reliability of the records
is contingent on having processes and procedures
in place that restrict access
to protect the integrity of the data.
To this end,
FDA is proposing to require in section 205.27(c)
that wholesale distributors implement written policies
and procedures to protect the integrity of their records.
Under proposed section 205.27(d),
all records will be retained for a period of three years
except records related to suspect and illegitimate products,
prescription drug quality complaints,
and destroyed, returned and recalled prescription drugs,
which would need to be retained for a period of six years.
Such record retention is necessary
to ensure compliance and consistent enforcement
of the various record keeping requirements of the DSCSA.
Proposed section 205.28
provides for mandatory initial
and periodic inspections of WDDs
to ensure compliance with the national standards
as required by DSCSA.
As described in proposed section 205.28 for inspections,
at initial licensure,
the facility to be used in wholesale distribution
must undergo a physical inspection
prior to the issuance of the WDD's license.
FDA believes that it is imperative
for the mandatory physical inspection to take place
prior to issuing an initial license to a WDD
to ensure that only those WDDs
who have the ability to properly store, handle,
and distribute prescription drugs
in accordance with the national standards are licensed.
Where the state is the licensing authority,
the state in which the facility is located
may conduct the inspection,
or may accept an inspection by a third-party accreditation
or inspection service approved
by the state licensing the WDD.
If the facility is out of state,
the state issuing the license may conduct the inspection
or may accept an inspection
by the state in which the facility is located,
or by a third party.
Where the FDA is the licensing authority,
the FDA may conduct the inspection
or may accept an inspection conducted
by an organization approved by FDA
as described in proposed section 205.32.
Under the proposed regulations,
WDDs are expected to cooperate with the state
or federal licensing authority,
or the approved organization conducting the inspection
at reasonable times, within reasonable limits,
and in a reasonable manner
to achieve the objective of the inspection.
WDDs will also be required to undergo a routine inspection
once every three years.
FDA believes routine inspections are an essential tool
to ensure that the wholesale distributors continue to comply
with the national standards
after obtaining their initial wholesale distributor license
and move to renew that license.
Such routine inspections will be conducted
by the licensing authority,
or third-party approved organization,
or inspection service approved by the FDA,
or the state licensing the WDD.
Proposed section 205.28(b)
specifically addresses the availability of records.
To facilitate the licensing authority's ability
to complete the inspection,
records kept at the inspection site,
or that can be immediately retrieved electronically,
must be made readily available during the inspection.
For records kept at a central location
apart from the inspection site
and not electronically retrievable,
such records must be made available for inspection
within two business days of a request by a state
or federal official,
or sooner if necessitated by the duration of the inspection.
Proposed section 205.29 covers the requirements
for initial and annual reporting to FDA.
Under DSCSA, WDDs must report certain information to FDA
to be considered an authorized trading partner.
The annual reporting requirements for wholesale distributors
went into effect on January 1st, 2015.
Proposed section 205.29
clarifies the statutorily prescribed
annual reporting requirements.
FDA is proposing to require
that WDDs use an electronic system provided by FDA
to increase efficiency by providing uniformity
in the content and format of reports,
thereby making the information easier to process.
Reporting information for each WDD
in FDA's electronic system during the reporting period
is integral to FDA's ability to provide oversight,
as WDDs are prohibited
from distributing product without a license.
In accordance with reporting requirements for WDDs
set forth in DSCSA,
proposed section 205.29(c)
requires a WDD to electronically report to FDA,
the state by which the WDD is licensed,
and the corresponding license number.
FDA is also proposing to require WDDs
report the date each license expires.
FDA believes this information is paramount
to FDA's ability to establish
and maintain a public database,
identifying each authorized wholesale distributor
as required by section 503(e)(2)(b) of the FD&C Act.
If a WDD's license expires,
it is no longer an authorized trading partner
and FDA will remove it from the public database
until the license is renewed or a new license is issued.
In addition, all trade names or business names,
and significant disciplinary actions taken
against a WDD license would be reported.
A WDD's initial report must be submitted
within 30 calendar days of obtaining its initial license.
Annual reporting must be completed each year
between January 1st and March 31st.
In addition to providing required reporting information
upon initial licensure, and annually,
it is important for other trading partners and FDA
to know whether a WDD has had a license revoked
or suspended,
or whether the WDD has had any other
significant disciplinary action taken against them
that limits the ability of a facility
to conduct drug-related business.
As such,
the proposed rule includes section 205.29(d) and (e)
where WDDs must report significant disciplinary actions
as defined in proposed section 205.3(l) to FDA.
Significant disciplinary actions
must be submitted at licensure
and for subsequent significant disciplinary actions
within 30 calendar days of a final action
taken by a state or federal licensing authority.
A WDD will also be expected to report to FDA
within 30 calendar days
that it ceased operations as a WDD
or voluntarily withdrawn a wholesale distributor's license
from a state.
FDA believes that requiring a wholesale distributor
to report this information about the status of its license
is essential for FDA to comply with the requirements
under section 503(e)(2)(b) of the FD&C Act
and to ensure that the database is accurate and helpful
for the states and trading partners.
Proposed section 205.30 outlines the standards and processes
for WDD licensed denials, suspensions,
reinstatement, revocation, and voluntary termination.
Proposed section 205.30(a)(1) describes 10 circumstances
under which the licensing authority would be required
to deny a WDD's request for licensure or license renewal.
These circumstances are summarized on the slide
and include, for example,
an adequate facilities and controls
to facilitate safe operations,
failure to meet or comply with requirements
for good storage practices,
and failure to provide adequate opportunity
for inspections of facilities, controls,
or applicable records.
FDA believes that this list will help WDDs focus
on good storage practices outlined by FDA
that are necessary to protect the integrity of the products
in the pharmaceutical distribution supply chain.
To avoid denial or delays of their applications,
WDDs should ensure
that they address the reasons for denial of a license,
outlined in proposed section 205.30(a)(1)
when they file for licensure.
Under proposed section 205.30(b) and (C),
the suspension of a WDD's license
may be initiated by the licensing authority
upon reasonable belief
that the licensee has failed to comply
with any of the standards for receiving
and maintaining licensure.
The proposed standards for suspending a WDD license
are based on the risk posed to public health.
For example, if the licensing authority
has a reasonable belief
that the WDD is not in compliance
with licensure requirements,
and such non-compliance threatens the quality of the product
or threatens public safety,
the licensing authority is required
to notify the WDD in writing
of the intent to suspend its license
and provide the WDD notice of opportunity for a hearing
before suspending its license.
However, if the WDD's non-compliance
poses an imminent threat to public safety
such as a WDD continuing to ship illegitimate product
after being made aware of the product's illegitimate status,
the agency may suspend the license immediately
while giving the WDD an opportunity to request a hearing
after a license is suspended.
Under proposed section 205.30(d),
a WDD suspended license may be reinstated
if the WDD can demonstrate to the licensing authority
that it is in compliance with regulation requirements.
The standards for revoking a WDD license are set forth
in proposed section 205.30(e).
The licensing authority will revoke a license
if it finds that a WDD whose license has been suspended,
or is unable,
or refuses to comply with the licensing requirements.
In addition to describing the circumstances
under which a license may be denied, suspended or revoked,
proposed section 205.30
outlines the processes for these actions.
In general, the procedures for the denial
of an application for licensure
and for the suspension or revocation of a license
involve written notice by the licensing authority,
an opportunity for the WDD to respond,
and the opportunity for a WDD to request a hearing.
As previously mentioned, however,
where there is an imminent threat to public safety,
the agency may suspend a license immediately
without an opportunity to respond to the suspension notice.
In this scenario,
the WDD is given opportunity to request a hearing
after the license is suspended.
Under the proposed rule,
the procedures in 21 CFR parts 10 through 16,
apply with respect to hearings and appeals
of denied, suspended, or revoked WDD licenses.
FDA believes that this proposed approach
is consistent with current practice
and suggests that states develop comparable processes.
Proposed section 205.30
also sets forth conditions for licensure nonrenewals
and voluntary terminations.
Where a WDD fails to submit an application for renewal
by the date of the license's expiration,
the license will be considered expired.
The WDD may not engage in wholesale distribution
with an expired license,
and must submit a new application for licensure.
A WDD requesting
that the licensing authority terminates its license
must include in its request
a notice of the WDD's intent
to discontinue prescription drug wholesale distribution
and waiver of an opportunity for a hearing.
The WDD will be required to apply for a new license
should it decide to resume wholesale distribution.
Proposed section 205.31, 205.32 and 205.33
cover the process for the use
of approved third-party organizations,
general qualification, and approval by FDA respectively.
However, like AOs, for 3PLs,
we will not be covering approved organizations for WDDs
in this presentation.
We will follow up in the future
with more information on approved organizations
as we move forward in the implementation process.
This concludes our review
of the proposed regulations for national standards
for licensure of wholesale distributor
and third-party logistics providers.
I now turn it over back to Aaron.
- [Aaron] All right.
Thank you very much, Sara.
So, please see our webpage for a link to the proposed rule
and instructions for how to submit comments
to the public docket on the proposal.
On this slide,
we're also providing some other FDA resources for you
where you can find the latest updates
regarding the DSCSA implementation,
as well as other useful information,
including DSCSA regulatory documents
such as relevant FDA guidances and regulations,
public meetings, and webinars.
In conclusion, I'd like to thank you all for your attention
and for watching this webinar,
outlining the national standards for licensure
for wholesale drug distributors
and third-party logistics providers.
We hope you found it informative.
We'd like to remind you that you can submit comments
on the proposed regulation at regulations.gov
by June 6th, 2022,
to allow for FDA to consider your comments.
Specific thank yous to Elizabeth Pepinski
and Sara Kim Keller for joining me
by presenting at this webinar.
Thank you to Ray and the staff at the SBIA,
and my colleagues from CDER's Office of Compliance
and across the agency
for making this webinar possible.

videos.full_text: - [Ray] Good day, everyone, and welcome. This is Ray Ford with FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Small Business & Industry Assistance program, also known as CDER SBIA. Thank you for joining us today for our presentation on overview of proposed 21 CFR 205, national standards for the licensure of wholesale drug distributors and third-party logistics providers. FDA will provide an overview of the proposed rule regarding licensure processes and standards for third-party logistics providers and wholesale distributors of prescription drugs. In issuing this rule, FDA is proposing to replace the current regulations in 21 CFR part 205 with this new part 205 that will implement the licensure requirements of the drug supply chain security act and govern licensure of third-party logistics provider and wholesale distributors. When finalized, this rule will be replacing existing 21 CFR part 205 and its entirety. Our speakers today include, first, Aaron Weisbuch, senior regulatory advisor, division of Supply Chain Integrity, Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response, Office of Compliance, CDER FDA. Aaron Weisbuch is a senior regulatory advisor in division of Supply Chain Integrity within CDER's Office of Drug Security, Integrity and Response, where he focuses on policy and compliance issues related to prescription drugs and implementation of the drug supply chain security act. Following Mr. Weisbuch, we welcome Elizabeth Pepinsky, regulatory counsel, supply chain security branch, division of Supply Chain Integrity, Office of Drug Security, Integrity and Response. Elizabeth Pepinksy is a regulatory counsel in the Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response within CDER's Office of Compliance. Prior to joining ODSIR, she served as a health science policy analyst in CDER's office of prescription drug promotion, where she primarily focused on guidance and policy development. Our final speaker will be Sara Kim Keller, regulatory council, supply chain security branch, division of Supply Chain Integrity, Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response, Office of Compliance, CDER FDA. Sara Keller is a regulatory council in division of Supply Chain Integrity within the Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response. Prior to joining ODSIR, she worked in the Office of Compliance and Enforcement in the FDA Center for Tobacco Products. Please join me in welcoming our first presenter, Mr. Weisbuch. - [Aaron] All right. Thank you, Ray, for that introduction. We'll get right into our agenda for the presentation. So, first we're going to begin with a brief overview of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act, which is commonly referred to and will be referred to as DSCSA.
