Routine inspections will occur every three years. Where the state is the licensing authority, the state may conduct the inspection or may accept an inspection by a third-party accreditation or inspection service approved by the state licensing authority. If the facility is out of state, the state may conduct the inspection or may accept an inspection by the state in which the facility is located. Where the FDA is the licensing authority, the FDA may conduct the inspection or may accept an inspection by an organization approved by the FDA under proposed section 205.18. To facilitate the licensing authority's ability to complete the inspection, records kept at the inspection site, or that can be immediately retrieved electronically, must be made readily available during the inspection. For records kept at a central location apart from the inspection site and not electronically retrievable, such records must be made available for inspection within two business days of a request by a state or federal official, or sooner if necessitated by the duration of the inspection. We will not be covering third-party organizations, approved third-party organizations, or AO, in this presentation. However, FDA will give more information in the future as we implement rule. Please see proposed sections 205.17, 205.18 and 205.19 for the processes for the use of approved third-party organizations, general qualifications, and the processes and procedures for approval of AOs by FDA. Now, this concludes our discussion of proposed 3PL requirements. We encourage you to provide your comments on the proposed rule to the public docket as we described earlier, and following those instructions provided. I will now turn it over to Sara Keller for an overview of the proposed requirements for wholesale distributors. - [Sara] Thank you for the introduction. We now move forward with our discussion of wholesale distributor requirements in this proposed rule. To implement section 503(e)(1) of the FD&C Act, proposed section 205.20(a) codifies a requirement that a wholesale drug distributor, or WDD for short, be licensed by the state from which the drug is distributed or by FDA if the state from which the drug is distributed has not established a licensure requirement in accordance with the standards set forth in the regulation and by the state into which the drug is distributed if that state requires such a license. This requirement is consistent with how states currently license wholesale distributors. FDA proposes to set the licensure term for wholesale distributors at two years. Any license issued or renewed pursuant to this proposed section will expire two years after the date on which the license was issued. A wholesale distributor may submit a renewal application up to 90 calendar days before the date of expiration. The agency believes that two years aligns with current practices, does not place an undue burden on state or FDA resources, and provides adequate protection to American consumers because it ensures that renewals will be based on current information and operations. The DSCSA requires that wholesale distributors obtain a surety bond to be licensed and engage in wholesale distribution. FDA is proposing to establish the terms of this requirement in proposed section 205.21. The surety bond is intended to ensure compliance with DSCSA and that any administrative penalties levied by the licensing authorities are paid. As we are not reviewing the details of this section of the proposed rule, we encourage you to review proposed section 205.21 for the requirements for surety bonds. Proposed section 205.22 outlines the general requirements that must be met for a state or federal licensing authority to issue an initial license to a wholesale distributor or a renewal of any such license. Under proposed section 205.22, the person submitting the application for licensure is the applicant. The applicant must be at least 18 years old and submit all required information, including an affidavit stating that applicant's ownership or management of, or employment by the entity would not preclude the entity from receiving or maintaining a license under proposed section 205.25(a). The applicant must also pay any applicable licensing fee to be issued a license. As previously mentioned, wholesale distributors are required to obtain a surety bond to be licensed and engage in wholesale distribution. Proposed section 205.22 requires that the wholesale distributor must furnish a surety bond as described in proposed section 205.21 with this application for licensure. See section 205.21 for more details. Proposed section 205.22(c) outlines the information that licensing authority will require as part of a WDD's initial application for licensure and renewal applications. This information is summarized on the slide. FDA believes this information is necessary for the licensing authority to assess whether the WDD is in good standing and has the infrastructure and capabilities to fulfill its duties and obligation under the national standards for WDD licensure. With respect to the disclosure of certain felonies, the application for licensure must include details about whether the WDD has ever been convicted of a felony relating to prescription drug distribution, including a conviction under section 301(i) or (k) of the FD&C Act or 18 USC 1365 relating to product tampering. Additionally, FDA is proposing to require that the WDD inform FDA if it has received any citations for violating requirements for licensure or received any significant disciplinary actions within the past seven years that presented a threat of serious adverse health consequences, or death to humans. FDA believes this information is necessary to ensure the wholesale distributor can demonstrate that it has not engaged in a pattern of violating the standards for licensure. For licensure renewals, the proposed rule would require the WDD to certify that it continually met the requirements of subpart C of the regulation and informed the licensing authority of certain changes to information if such changes have not already been submitted to the licensing authority. Under proposed section 205.22(e), a wholesale distributor's license must be available upon request. The WDD must maintain its license in a readily retrievable manner, and must permit state, or federal inspectors, or others acting on behalf of the licensing authority to inspect the license. Proposed section 205.23 outlines the process for applying for WDD licensure with FDA in the instance that the state in which it engages in wholesale distribution has not established a licensure program. While proposed section 205.23 is only applicable to WDDs obtaining a license from FDA, FDA recommends that states implement similar procedures to ensure that all WDD licenses issued are consistent with the proposed regulation pursuant to section 503(e)(1)(b) of the FD&C Act. We will now review the proposed process for federal licensure of WDDs. The federal licensure process begins when a WDD seeking licensure for a facility submits an application to FDA for review and consideration. The application must be submitted electronically and include the information set forth in proposed sections 205.21 and 205.22, along with the surety bond and supporting documentation that demonstrates the applicant's ability to comply with requirements, intend to ensure that continued safety, identity, strength, quality, and purity of the prescription drugs. Where FDA has approved one or more organizations to conduct inspections of a WDD, as permitted by the DSCSA, the WDD should indicate which authorized organization it prefers to conduct its inspection. If no organization has been approved, FDA will conduct the inspection. The application must be signed by the applicant, applicant's agent, or other authorized official, and all fees must be paid. So as not to delay the licensure process, when reviewing an application, FDA intends to work with WDDs to correct minor errors made on the application and communicate with the WDD about additional information the agency may need. The FDA will determine whether applicable requirements are met. If an approved organization has conducted the licensure review, the responsibility for determining whether the applicable requirements are met will remain with the FDA. Issuance of a license is covered under proposed section 205.23(d). When FDA determines that the WDD meets the applicable requirements under sections 503(e)(1) and 583 of the FD&C Act and none of the prohibited factors listed in proposed section 205.30(a) are present, FDA will send the applicant an approval letter and a licensing certificate effective on the date that it is issued. The license will remain valid until it expires unless it is suspended or revoked. For the licensing authority to effectively carry out its responsibilities, a WDD must keep its license information current and report any changes on information previously submitted to the licensing authority. Currently, the reporting requirements for these types of changes vary by state. Proposed section 205.24 establishes specific timeframes for reporting changes and FDA believes that standardizing the timeframes will help make reporting business-related changes less burdensome for industry and licensing authorities. Proposed section 205.24 would require the WDD to submit changes to certain information such as the information submitted with the surety bond, or as part of an application for licensure to the licensing authority within 30 calendar days of the date the change became effective. FDA is also proposing that a change in the location at which wholesale district distribution occurs will require an inspection of the new facility prior to commencing wholesale distribution at the location. For a change to the person engaged in wholesale distribution, a new license will be required prior to beginning operations. The application for a new license must be submitted no later than 30 calendar days prior to the change in ownership. A new inspection of the WDD will be performed at a reasonable time. Proposed section 205.25 covers the standards for the qualifications of wholesale distributors key personnel, such as prohibited conduct, basic standards for key personnel working within a wholesale distribution facility, and grounds for denying a licensure application. As described in proposed section 205.3(g), FDA considers key personnel to include any individual who has responsibility for managing the operations of the wholesale distributor, including any principal, owner, director, officer of the wholesale distributor, designated representatives, and other individuals who are authorized to enter areas where prescription drugs are held and are likely to handle prescription drugs as part of their responsibilities. Proposed section 205.25 covers prohibited persons and qualifications for key personnel. Under this proposed section, a WDD is prohibited from obtaining or maintaining licensure if the WDD has been convicted of a felony relating to prescription drug distribution, including a conviction under section 301(i) or (k) of the FD&C Act or 18 USC 1365 relating to product tampering, or if the WDD has been cited for certain repeated violations related to the FD&C Act that presents threat of serious adverse health consequences or death to humans. Under proposed section 205.25, key personnel working within a wholesale distribution facility must have the appropriate education, background training, and experience necessary to carry out their assigned functions within the operation. No one within the facility should carry out responsibilities of key personnel without the proper training and experience. Also under proposed section 205.25(c), licensure may be denied if a wholesale distributor or any of their key personnel delayed or impeded inspection, omitted material information, or furnished falsed or fraudulent information in an application, or is subject to licensure suspension or revocation for currently or previously held license for manufacturer or distribution of any drugs. Proposed section 205.25(d) states that a WDD must maintain a list of officers, directors, facility managers, designated representatives, and other key personnel in charge of wholesale distribution, including storage and handling, and include a description of their duties and a summary of their qualification. Proposed section 205.25(e) describes how a WDD must also establish and implement written policies and procedure designed to ensure that their key personnel meet the necessary qualifications. These policies and procedures must identify the personnel at the WDD's facility who are responsible for implementing and maintaining facility personnel requirements, complying with all licensure reporting requirements, and ensuring key personnel receive initial and regular training. Proposed section 205.25(f) limits a facility manager, or designated representative, to hold that position at one facility at a time. This is to ensure that the facility manager or designated representative is actively engaged in managing the daily operations of the facility and that they remain aware of any non-compliance issues that may arise. Section 583(b)(4) of the FD&C Act, as added by DSCSA, requires fingerprinting and background checks of facility managers and designated representative of wholesale distributors. The background check when completed must demonstrate that the facility manager or representative has no history of criminal convictions pursuant to proposed section 205.25(a) and outlined in slide number 84. Proposed section 205.26 establishes basic standards for the storage and handling of prescription drugs by wholesale distributors, including facility requirements. Although the FD&C Act permits an entity to be more than one type of trading partner so long as it complies with all applicable DSCSA requirements, FDA believes that the processes and functions of each type of entity need to be kept separate for the licensing authority to ensure the entities complying with all applicable requirements. Therefore, under proposed section 205.26(a), any wholesale distributor's facility that is also licensed or registered as another trading partner, such as a 3PL, and operating from the same address must have separate systems and processes in place for their separate functions. Proposed section 205.26(b)(1) describes how the facility must be of a suitable size, configuration and design to ensure proper storage, maintenance, and cleanliness. The facility must also be equipped with clearly defined areas that separate drugs that are unfit for distribution from those that are saleable to avoid potential mistakes when distributing the prescription drugs. Under proposed section 205.26(b)(2), facilities must be sufficiently secure to protect the prescription drugs in the supply chain from possible theft or diversion. Facilities must protect against unauthorized entry and ensure that the premises are well lit and not vulnerable to intrusion. Entry and access to areas where prescription drugs are held within the facility must be limited to those who have the appropriate experience and training needed to conduct wholesale distribution. Proposed section 205.26(b)(3) outlines how a WDD has a responsibility of ensuring that prescription drugs are stored under proper conditions to maintain the safety and effectiveness of the drugs it distributes. A facility must have equipment that ensures prescription drugs are properly stored, such as cold storage, refrigerators, temperature and humidity devices, and air handling units. Also it equipment must be maintained in good repair and must be suitable for distribution of prescription drugs. Facility assessments must be regularly conducted and documented. Accordingly, a WDD's facility must maintain appropriate equipment and good working order to ensure that prescription drugs are properly stored in the facility. To this end, FDA is proposing that WDDs establish written procedures to ensure that equipment is installed, maintained and repaired by qualified individuals following written procedures. Equipment should be calibrated and validated at regular intervals. He further proposed that WDDs use manual, electro-mechanical, or electronic temperature and humidity recording equipment, or logs, to document proper storage. Monitoring equipment must immediately alert of any deviations from required storage conditions. FDA expects that as crucial part of the creation of quality system, wholesale distributors will establish, maintain, and follow written policies and procedures regarding the safeguarding of the prescription drugs within their control. Proposed section 205.26(c) outlines several requirements for maintaining written policies and procedures to ensure that the requirements are carried out properly and consistently. The requirements listed on this slide include the requirement to do business with other authorized trading partners, the requirement to properly maintain equipment in good working order, and the requirement to inspect shipping containers for suspect or illegitimate products among others. Please refer to proposed section 205.26(c) for a complete list. Wholesale distributors are not limited to establishing written policies and procedures for the stated functions in proposed section 205.26(c). A wholesale distributor may wish to establish written policies and procedures pertaining to other aspects of wholesale distribution and staffing of their facilities. The purpose of requiring written policies and procedures is to assist staff and management at a wholesale distribution facility to determine the processes required to ensure safe storage and distribution of prescription drugs. Wholesale distributors are responsible for contractor compliance. A WDD must ensure that the contractor abides by applicable written policies and procedures. Furthermore, written policies and procedures must clearly describe responsibilities of the WDD and any contractors used to fulfill the WDDs duties. Proper record keeping is essential to the timely identification, recording and reporting of issues arising within the supply chain. Section 583(b)(2) of the FD&C Act, as added by the DSCSA, requires FDA to create national standards for establishing and maintaining records pertaining to the distribution of prescription drugs. Proposed section 205.27 covers those standards on records. FDA is proposing in section 205.27(a) that these records include documentation pertaining to the storage, handling, security, inventory, shipping, of prescription drugs. This will include records related to the sale, purchase, trade, delivery and receipt, as well as policies, procedures, instructions, contracts, data, inspection reports, and any other documentation related to compliance with this part. This section also includes records related to the distribution of prescription drugs such as invoices, purchase orders, packing slips, and shipping records. These records could be stored and maintained electronically. These records maintenance requirements will allow for greater confidence in the information preserved at the facility. It will also potentially allow for greater confidence in the information disseminated to other trading partners. All records must be securely stored, and any alteration made to records must be signed and dated while preserving the original information contained in the record. See proposed section 205.27(b). This is intended to ensure that all records related to the distribution of prescription drugs provide transparency and accurately reflect the activities of the wholesale distributor. FDA also believes that reliability of the records is contingent on having processes and procedures in place that restrict access to protect the integrity of the data. To this end, FDA is proposing to require in section 205.27(c) that wholesale distributors implement written policies and procedures to protect the integrity of their records. Under proposed section 205.27(d), all records will be retained for a period of three years except records related to suspect and illegitimate products, prescription drug quality complaints, and destroyed, returned and recalled prescription drugs, which would need to be retained for a period of six years. Such record retention is necessary to ensure compliance and consistent enforcement of the various record keeping requirements of the DSCSA. Proposed section 205.28 provides for mandatory initial and periodic inspections of WDDs to ensure compliance with the national standards as required by DSCSA. As described in proposed section 205.28 for inspections, at initial licensure, the facility to be used in wholesale distribution must undergo a physical inspection prior to the issuance of the WDD's license. FDA believes that it is imperative for the mandatory physical inspection to take place prior to issuing an initial license to a WDD to ensure that only those WDDs who have the ability to properly store, handle, and distribute prescription drugs in accordance with the national standards are licensed. Where the state is the licensing authority, the state in which the facility is located may conduct the inspection, or may accept an inspection by a third-party accreditation or inspection service approved by the state licensing the WDD. If the facility is out of state, the state issuing the license may conduct the inspection or may accept an inspection by the state in which the facility is located, or by a third party. Where the FDA is the licensing authority, the FDA may conduct the inspection or may accept an inspection conducted by an organization approved by FDA as described in proposed section 205.32. Under the proposed regulations, WDDs are expected to cooperate with the state or federal licensing authority, or the approved organization conducting the inspection at reasonable times, within reasonable limits, and in a reasonable manner to achieve the objective of the inspection. WDDs will also be required to undergo a routine inspection once every three years. FDA believes routine inspections are an essential tool to ensure that the wholesale distributors continue to comply with the national standards after obtaining their initial wholesale distributor license and move to renew that license. Such routine inspections will be conducted by the licensing authority, or third-party approved organization, or inspection service approved by the FDA, or the state licensing the WDD. Proposed section 205.28(b) specifically addresses the availability of records. To facilitate the licensing authority's ability to complete the inspection, records kept at the inspection site, or that can be immediately retrieved electronically, must be made readily available during the inspection. For records kept at a central location apart from the inspection site and not electronically retrievable, such records must be made available for inspection within two business days of a request by a state or federal official, or sooner if necessitated by the duration of the inspection. Proposed section 205.29 covers the requirements for initial and annual reporting to FDA. Under DSCSA, WDDs must report certain information to FDA to be considered an authorized trading partner. The annual reporting requirements for wholesale distributors went into effect on January 1st, 2015. Proposed section 205.29 clarifies the statutorily prescribed annual reporting requirements. FDA is proposing to require that WDDs use an electronic system provided by FDA to increase efficiency by providing uniformity in the content and format of reports, thereby making the information easier to process. Reporting information for each WDD in FDA's electronic system during the reporting period is integral to FDA's ability to provide oversight, as WDDs are prohibited from distributing product without a license. In accordance with reporting requirements for WDDs set forth in DSCSA, proposed section 205.29(c) requires a WDD to electronically report to FDA, the state by which the WDD is licensed, and the corresponding license number. FDA is also proposing to require WDDs report the date each license expires. FDA believes this information is paramount to FDA's ability to establish and maintain a public database, identifying each authorized wholesale distributor as required by section 503(e)(2)(b) of the FD&C Act. If a WDD's license expires, it is no longer an authorized trading partner and FDA will remove it from the public database until the license is renewed or a new license is issued. In addition, all trade names or business names, and significant disciplinary actions taken against a WDD license would be reported. A WDD's initial report must be submitted within 30 calendar days of obtaining its initial license. Annual reporting must be completed each year between January 1st and March 31st. In addition to providing required reporting information upon initial licensure, and annually, it is important for other trading partners and FDA to know whether a WDD has had a license revoked or suspended, or whether the WDD has had any other significant disciplinary action taken against them that limits the ability of a facility to conduct drug-related business. As such, the proposed rule includes section 205.29(d) and (e) where WDDs must report significant disciplinary actions as defined in proposed section 205.3(l) to FDA. Significant disciplinary actions must be submitted at licensure and for subsequent significant disciplinary actions within 30 calendar days of a final action taken by a state or federal licensing authority. A WDD will also be expected to report to FDA within 30 calendar days that it ceased operations as a WDD or voluntarily withdrawn a wholesale distributor's license from a state. FDA believes that requiring a wholesale distributor to report this information about the status of its license is essential for FDA to comply with the requirements under section 503(e)(2)(b) of the FD&C Act and to ensure that the database is accurate and helpful for the states and trading partners. Proposed section 205.30 outlines the standards and processes for WDD licensed denials, suspensions, reinstatement, revocation, and voluntary termination. Proposed section 205.30(a)(1) describes 10 circumstances under which the licensing authority would be required to deny a WDD's request for licensure or license renewal. These circumstances are summarized on the slide and include, for example, an adequate facilities and controls to facilitate safe operations, failure to meet or comply with requirements for good storage practices, and failure to provide adequate opportunity for inspections of facilities, controls, or applicable records. FDA believes that this list will help WDDs focus on good storage practices outlined by FDA that are necessary to protect the integrity of the products in the pharmaceutical distribution supply chain. To avoid denial or delays of their applications, WDDs should ensure that they address the reasons for denial of a license, outlined in proposed section 205.30(a)(1) when they file for licensure. Under proposed section 205.30(b) and (C), the suspension of a WDD's license may be initiated by the licensing authority upon reasonable belief that the licensee has failed to comply with any of the standards for receiving and maintaining licensure. The proposed standards for suspending a WDD license are based on the risk posed to public health. For example, if the licensing authority has a reasonable belief that the WDD is not in compliance with licensure requirements, and such non-compliance threatens the quality of the product or threatens public safety, the licensing authority is required to notify the WDD in writing of the intent to suspend its license and provide the WDD notice of opportunity for a hearing before suspending its license. However, if the WDD's non-compliance poses an imminent threat to public safety such as a WDD continuing to ship illegitimate product after being made aware of the product's illegitimate status, the agency may suspend the license immediately while giving the WDD an opportunity to request a hearing after a license is suspended. Under proposed section 205.30(d), a WDD suspended license may be reinstated if the WDD can demonstrate to the licensing authority that it is in compliance with regulation requirements. The standards for revoking a WDD license are set forth in proposed section 205.30(e). The licensing authority will revoke a license if it finds that a WDD whose license has been suspended, or is unable, or refuses to comply with the licensing requirements. In addition to describing the circumstances under which a license may be denied, suspended or revoked, proposed section 205.30 outlines the processes for these actions. In general, the procedures for the denial of an application for licensure and for the suspension or revocation of a license involve written notice by the licensing authority, an opportunity for the WDD to respond, and the opportunity for a WDD to request a hearing. As previously mentioned, however, where there is an imminent threat to public safety, the agency may suspend a license immediately without an opportunity to respond to the suspension notice. In this scenario, the WDD is given opportunity to request a hearing after the license is suspended. Under the proposed rule, the procedures in 21 CFR parts 10 through 16, apply with respect to hearings and appeals of denied, suspended, or revoked WDD licenses. FDA believes that this proposed approach is consistent with current practice and suggests that states develop comparable processes. Proposed section 205.30 also sets forth conditions for licensure nonrenewals and voluntary terminations. Where a WDD fails to submit an application for renewal by the date of the license's expiration, the license will be considered expired. The WDD may not engage in wholesale distribution with an expired license, and must submit a new application for licensure. A WDD requesting that the licensing authority terminates its license must include in its request a notice of the WDD's intent to discontinue prescription drug wholesale distribution and waiver of an opportunity for a hearing. The WDD will be required to apply for a new license should it decide to resume wholesale distribution. Proposed section 205.31, 205.32 and 205.33 cover the process for the use of approved third-party organizations, general qualification, and approval by FDA respectively. However, like AOs, for 3PLs, we will not be covering approved organizations for WDDs in this presentation. We will follow up in the future with more information on approved organizations as we move forward in the implementation process. This concludes our review of the proposed regulations for national standards for licensure of wholesale distributor and third-party logistics providers. I now turn it over back to Aaron. - [Aaron] All right. Thank you very much, Sara. So, please see our webpage for a link to the proposed rule and instructions for how to submit comments to the public docket on the proposal. On this slide, we're also providing some other FDA resources for you where you can find the latest updates regarding the DSCSA implementation, as well as other useful information, including DSCSA regulatory documents such as relevant FDA guidances and regulations, public meetings, and webinars. In conclusion, I'd like to thank you all for your attention and for watching this webinar, outlining the national standards for licensure for wholesale drug distributors and third-party logistics providers. We hope you found it informative. We'd like to remind you that you can submit comments on the proposed regulation at regulations.gov by June 6th, 2022, to allow for FDA to consider your comments. Specific thank yous to Elizabeth Pepinski and Sara Kim Keller for joining me by presenting at this webinar. Thank you to Ray and the staff at the SBIA, and my colleagues from CDER's Office of Compliance and across the agency for making this webinar possible.

🇺🇸 USFDA Medical Device Submission – Introduction | 40-Minute Guide

Want to understand how medical devices enter the US market? This 40-minute video provides a practical introduction to the USFDA medical device regulatory pathway.

📌 Topics Covered

✅ USFDA Medical Device Regulatory Framework
✅ Device Classification – Class I, II & III
✅ 510(k), De Novo & PMA pathways
✅ Substantial Equivalence
✅ FDA Registration & Device Listing
✅ UDI & Q-Submission (Q-Sub) basics
✅ Key submission requirements
✅ Common FDA submission mistakes

🎯 Who Should Watch?
RA/QA professionals, medical device manufacturers, MedTech startups, consultants, engineers, and anyone interested in USFDA Regulatory Affairs.

📌 Subscribe for practical content on USFDA, EU MDR, ISO 13485, CDSCO & Medical Device Regulatory Affairs.

💬 Comment: Which USFDA topic should I cover next?

#usfda #medicaldevice #fda #510k #regulatoryaffairs #medtech #fda510k #medicaldeviceregulation

metadata.title: FDA Medical Device Market Entry: 510(k), De Novo, and PMA Explained for Life Sciences Leaders
metadata.author: NSF
metadata.shortDescription:
This video is designed for medical device, IVD, and life sciences professionals seeking to enter the US market and navigate FDA regulatory pathways. Learn how to select the right approval route, align quality systems, and avoid common compliance pitfalls.

Entering the US medical device market presents both significant commercial opportunity and regulatory complexity. In this NSF keynote, senior consultant Aimen Ghanemi provides a structured, practical overview of FDA market entry requirements, focusing on classification, regulatory pathways, and lifecycle compliance.

The session begins by framing the strategic importance of the US as the world’s largest medical device market, contrasting FDA’s pathway-driven model with the EU’s quality-system-first approach. Understanding FDA classification (Class I, II, and III) is critical, as it directly determines the data requirements, regulatory burden, and time to market for medical devices and IVD products.

The discussion then explores the three primary FDA premarket pathways:

510(k): The most common route based on substantial equivalence to a predicate device
De Novo: Designed for novel, low-to-moderate risk technologies without a predicate
PMA (Premarket Approval): Required for high-risk devices with robust clinical evidence

Beyond submissions, the video emphasises the importance of regulatory strategy, including selecting predicates, defining intended use, and leveraging FDA Q-submission programmes to de-risk development and approval decisions. These interactions are especially valuable for emerging technologies involving AI, software as a medical device (SaMD), and cybersecurity considerations.

The keynote also addresses current FDA priorities shaping the life sciences sector in 2026, including:
AI-enabled devices and lifecycle management strategies such as Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCP)
Cybersecurity requirements and increasing scrutiny on software transparency and risk management
Alignment of the new Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) with ISO 13485
The growing role of real-world evidence in regulatory submissions and post-market activities

Operational readiness is a key theme, with practical guidance on US-specific requirements such as Unique Device Identification (UDI), FDA registration and listing, labelling differences from EU MDR, and inspection preparedness. The session also highlights common compliance risks observed during FDA inspections, including CAPA deficiencies, complaint handling issues, and supplier control gaps.

Finally, the video explores post-market obligations, including Medical Device Reporting (MDR), recalls, and the reputational and commercial impact of FDA warning letters. These elements are critical for maintaining patient safety, product performance, and regulatory compliance across the full product lifecycle.

This keynote is highly relevant for senior professionals in pharma, biotech, and medical devices who are responsible for regulatory strategy, quality systems, clinical operations, and global commercialisation.

 We Looked at the Following Issues

How can medical device companies determine the most appropriate FDA pathway for US market entry?
What are the key differences between 510(k), De Novo, and PMA approvals?
How is the FDA evolving its expectations around AI, cybersecurity, and digital health technologies?
What changes does the new QMSR introduce for quality and compliance systems?
How should companies prepare for FDA inspections and post-market responsibilities?

Suggested Video Chapters
00:00 Introduction to FDA Market Entry
02:10 US vs EU Regulatory Landscape
04:20 FDA Device Classification Explained
07:30 510(k) Pathway and Predicate Strategy
12:15 De Novo and PMA Overview
16:30 FDA Q-Submission Programs
20:10 Breakthrough Devices and HDE Pathways
23:40 FDA Priorities: AI and Software Regulation
28:10 Cybersecurity and Compliance Expectations
32:00 QMSR and Quality System Transformation
36:45 Practical Market Entry Requirements
41:20 FDA Inspections and Common Findings
45:30 Post-Market Obligations and MDR
49:00 Key Takeaways for Regulatory Strategy

Join Registrar Corp’s experts as they dive deep into the fundamentals of medical device regulation in the United States. This comprehensive session will cover everything from device classification and 510(k) requirements to the crucial aspects of registration, labeling, and UDI (Unique Device Identification) compliance. Whether you're a medical device company looking to enter the U.S. market or aiming to expand your footprint, this session provides essential insights to navigate the complex regulatory landscape. Learn the ins and outs of compliance, ensuring your products meet FDA standards. Remember, #ExemptIsNotUnregulated—understanding these requirements is critical for success in the U.S. market!

metadata.title: How to Prepare a Medical Device 510k Submission for FDA
metadata.author: Matrix One
metadata.shortDescription:
There are several entry points for launching a medical device to market in the US. There are 3 main entry points, the first being de novo entry - Which is an entry without a predicate device. Then there is the PMA, which is the Pre Market Authorisation entry model, which is mainly for high risk (Class 3) devices, and finally there is the 510(k) process which is the most commonly used. This video will focus solely on the 510(k) process for launching a Medical Device in the US.

Chapters:
0:00 The three routes to the US market
0:49 What the 510(k) is
1:59 Device classes I, II and III
4:43 The 510(k) process, step by step
6:50 FDA review, substantial equivalence and NSE letters
8:53 Five tips for preparing a 510(k)
​

What is the 510(K)? Learn more here: https://matrixone.health/blog/navigating-the-fda-510k-submission-complete-guide

The 510(k) is a premarket submission made to the FDA to demonstrate that the device to be marketed is at least as safe and effective.

This process is named after Section 510(k) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The purpose of the 510(k) submission is to ensure that medical devices are safe and effective for their intended use before they are marketed.

What sort of classifications are there?
Learn more about classifications here: https://matrixone.health/blog/fda-eu-medical-device-classification

Medical devices in the U.S. are classified into three categories based on the level of control necessary to assure the safety and effectiveness of the device.
Class I devices are deemed to be low risk and are therefore subject to the least regulatory control. 

Class I devices are subject to General Controls, and most are exempt from the premarket notification 510(k) requirements. 

Class II devices are higher risk than Class I and require greater regulatory controls to provide reasonable assurance of the device's safety and effectiveness. 

Most Class II devices are required to submit a 510(k) premarket notification to the FDA before being marketed. 

Class II devices are subject to General Controls and Special Controls, which may include special labeling requirements, mandatory performance standards, and postmarket surveillance. 

Class III devices are considered the highest risk devices and generally require a PreMarket Approval (PMA), which is a more rigorous process than the 510(k) notification, I’ll dive into the PreMarket Approval (PMA) in our next video. 

Class III devices are those that support or sustain human life, are of substantial importance in preventing impairment of human health, or present a potential, unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Examples include implantable pacemakers and breast implants. 

The 510(k) process is primarily associated with Class II devices, but it can also apply to certain Class I and Class III devices, depending on specific circumstances related to their intended use and the level of risk they pose.

Learn more about Matrix One QMS here: https://matrixone.health/products/qms
and the ALM here: https://matrixone.health/products/matrix-requirements

The Process for obtaining a 510(k) clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) involves several steps, designed to demonstrate that the new device is as safe and effective as a legally marketed device that is not subject to premarket approval (PMA). 

Tips and Tricks 

Preparing for the 510(k) process is time consuming and requires careful planning, thorough documentation, and a strategic approach to demonstrate that your medical device is equivalent to a legally marketed predicate device. 

Here are some tips and tricks to help prepare for the 510(k) process:

Utilize a Pre-Submission meeting to gain valuable insights and feedback on your submission strategy and study designs. This early engagement can clarify expectations and help tailor your approach to meet FDA requirements effectively.

Choose a predicate device that closely aligns with yours in terms of technology, intended use, and performance is crucial. A well-chosen predicate simplifies the demonstration of substantial equivalence. Estar info here: https://matrixone.health/blog/unlocking-fda-estar-streamlining-medical-device-approvals-with-the-electronic-submission-template

Ensure your 510(k) submission is comprehensive, well-organized, and adheres to the FDA's recommended format. 

Back your claims of substantial equivalence with solid scientific evidence, including bench testing, clinical data, and any applicable standards compliance. Detailed documentation of your methodologies and results is essential.

Keep up to date with the latest FDA guidance, regulations, and standards relevant to your device. Compliance with these and readiness for post-market surveillance and reporting are key to not only obtaining clearance but maintaining it. By focusing on these core strategies, you can effectively navigate the 510(k) process, addressing the FDA's requirements and paving the way for a successful device market entry.

metadata.shortDescription: Almost half of all medical devices marketed in the United States must pass through the 510(k) process. Yet many businesses are getting it wrong: successful applications are falling, and 30% of 2021 applications weren’t even accepted for initial review. All Class II medical devices, and other devices in certain cases, need a robust, right-first-time 510(k) plan. This webinar gives you everything you need for success.

► Webpage: https://podcast.easymedicaldevice.com/43

The challenge for Medical Device companies is to understand the different pathways to register their products in a certain region. On this episode, we will focus on the US FDA regulation for Medical devices.

To help us, I invited Michelle Lott from LeanRAQA. She will let you know what are the different steps to consider when you are trying to register a Medical Device in the USA.

We will talk about the product classification, the different registration procedures (510k, deNovo, PMA) and also about the Quality Management System acceptable by the FDA.

After listening to this episode, you will have a minimum understanding to place your product to the US market. But anyway if you need support you can contact Michelle or me to answer your questions.

► Who is Michelle Lott

Michelle Lott is founder and principal of leanRAQA, which has supported 100+ companies with regulatory strategy, regulatory submissions, quality systems compliance, FDA audits, due diligence, technical support services – (and grief counseling, because dealing with regulators can be emotionally draining!).

She has served on the FDA Device Good Manufacturing Practices Advisory Committee and is a vocal advocate of EU MDR readiness. Michelle serves the medical device, dietary supplements, biologics, pharmaceutical, cosmetics, and food industries. She has a weakness for tequila and anything barbecued.

metadata.title: How to prepare an FDA eSTAR 510(k) submission
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
In 2020, the FDA launched the new eSTAR pilot program. eSTAR is a PDF eSubmission that is an alternative to the eSubmitter software that the FDA has been developing over the years, and an alternative to the current FDA eCopy that is the primary method companies use to prepare a 510(k) premarket notification. The eSTAR template was created by reviewers and is actually easy to use (if you understand the basics of preparing a 510(k) in the first place).

The implementation plan for eSTAR was set back by the Covid-19 pandemic, but the FDA is accepting eSTAR submissions for 510(k) premarket notifications. This video provides an introduction to the templates and explains how Medical Device Academy is adapting its normal 510(k) workflow to use the templates. The templates are designed to ensure that the submitter includes everything that is required for a 510(k) submission and eliminates the need for RTA screening by the FDA. The process also eliminates the need to format 510(k) submissions for an FDA eCopy. We are able to use all of our existing templates for a 510(k) submission, the need for some of the templates is eliminated, and only our 510(k) cover letter template was modified specifically for use with eSTAR submissions.

Particular highlights associated with the eSTAR template include: 1) built-in workflows for creating a summary of the testing provided for sterilization validation and biocompatibility and sterilization, 2) a built-in checklist for software and firmware verification and validation documentation, 3) hyperlinks to the most recent FDA guidance documents for each section of the 510(k) submission, 4) the ability to attach non-PDF files up to 1GB in size; and 5) automatic verification that each section of the 510(k) is complete.

The FDA has not released formal guidance to accompany the eSTAR templates, but help features embedded into the template largely eliminate the need for instructions or guidance. One of the most interesting observations we had was related to the three big yellow caution statements which warn the user not to enter confidential information into the PDF form. It appears that there is the potential for FOIA requests to be fulfilled in a semi-automated way by exporting the XML content of an eSTAR submission. The attachments are not exported. Therefore, an FOI could consist of the content provided by the XML export rather than manually creating a redacted 510(k) submission of much larger file size (no more 2-year waits for an FOIA?).

If you have any personal experience with eSTAR submissions, questions, or related updates, please comment on our video below.

metadata.title: What's an RFD and when do I need one for a FDA 510(k)?
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
In the FDA eSTAR, near the beginning in the device description section, the FDA asks if there has been an RFD or "request for designation." This usually is required when you device contains a drug as an component (e.g., pre-filled syringe) or the device itself resembles a drug (e.g., a liquid formulation).

Usually companies are submitting an RFD to convince the FDA that a drug-like product should be regulated as a device, because it works mechanically and locally (e.g., lubrication) instead of systemically.

To learn more, please visit our blog: https://medicaldeviceacademy.com/request-for-designation/

The following link is for pre-RFD guidance - https://medicaldeviceacademy.com/wp-content/uploads/How-to-Prepare-a-Pre-Request-for-Designation.pdf

The following link is for guidance on how to write an RFD - https://medicaldeviceacademy.com/wp-content/uploads/Guidance-for-Industry-and-FDA-Staff-How-to-Write-a-Request-for-Designation-RFD.pdf

metadata.title: Medical Device Design Controls: Complete FDA 510(k) Guide with ISO 13485 Compliance
metadata.author: Dave Saunders
metadata.shortDescription:
Medical Device Design Control Process: Complete Guide to FDA Clearance and ISO 13485 Compliance

Learn the complete design control process for medical devices from initial requirements through FDA 510(k) clearance. This comprehensive walkthrough covers ISO 13485 quality management systems, design history file documentation, verification and validation protocols, and traceability matrix management for Class II medical devices.

🎯 What You'll Learn:
- Design control lifecycle from user needs to FDA submission
- Requirements decomposition: Top level requirements to design inputs
- Design outputs and engineering documentation requirements
- Verification vs validation: Understanding the difference and when to use each
- Design history file (DHF) structure and management
- Traceability matrix creation and maintenance
- Risk management integration per ISO 14971
- Design review process and accountability
- Change control and impact assessment procedures
- FDA inspection readiness and audit preparation

📋 Perfect For:
- Medical device engineers (mechanical, electrical, software)
- Quality engineers and regulatory affairs professionals
- Product managers and systems engineers
- Manufacturing and clinical specialists
- Anyone working in regulated medical device development
- Teams preparing for FDA 510(k) submissions
- Companies implementing ISO 13485 quality systems

🔑 Key Topics Covered:
✓ 21 CFR Part 820 Quality System Regulation compliance
✓ ISO 13485:2016 medical device quality management
✓ Design input and design output documentation
✓ Verification protocols and test reports
✓ Validation studies and clinical evidence
✓ Document control and revision management
✓ Design review board responsibilities
✓ Biocompatibility, sterilization, and EMC validation
✓ Predicate device comparison for 510(k) pathway
✓ Risk analysis and hazard mitigation strategies

🎓 Who Should Watch:
This presentation is designed for the entire medical device organization, from CEOs to individual contributors. Whether you're new to medical device development or experienced in regulated industries, you'll gain practical insights into how design controls protect patients and ensure regulatory compliance.

📚 Related Standards and Regulations:
- FDA 21 CFR Part 820 (Quality System Regulation)
- ISO 13485:2016 (Medical Device Quality Management)
- ISO 14971 (Risk Management for Medical Devices)
- IEC 62304 (Medical Device Software Lifecycle)
- ISO 10993 (Biocompatibility Testing)
- IEC 60601 (Medical Electrical Equipment Safety)

💡 Practical Implementation:
Learn actionable next steps including document numbering schemes, traceability matrix templates, design review gate definitions, and document management system requirements. Understand common pitfalls and how to avoid them during FDA inspections.

🏥 Device Classes Covered:
While the example focuses on Class II devices requiring 510(k) clearance, the design control principles apply to Class I, II, and III medical devices under FDA jurisdiction as well as international markets requiring CE marking and other regulatory approvals.

#MedicalDevices #FDA #DesignControl #ISO13485 #QualityManagement #RegulatoryAffairs #MedicalDeviceEngineering #510k #DeviceValidation #DesignVerification #MedicalDeviceRegulation #QualityAssurance #MedTech #HealthcareCompliance #FDAApproval #DesignHistoryFile #Traceability #RiskManagement #ISO14971 #MedicalDeviceTesting

⏱️ Timestamps:
00:00 Introduction and Design Control Overview
03:45 Class II Device Example
06:30 The V Model Explained
09:15 User Needs to Requirements
12:00 Design Input Decomposition
15:30 Engineering Design Outputs
19:00 Role and Responsibility Matrix
22:45 Design Output Requirements
26:00 Verification Process and Examples
32:15 Validation Activities
38:00 Traceability Matrix Management
41:30 Design History File Structure
45:00 Document Control Requirements
48:15 Design Review Process
51:45 Real World Implementation Timeline
55:30 Common Pitfalls to Avoid
58:00 Change Control Process
01:01:15 Risk Management Integration
01:04:30 FDA 510(k) Submission
01:07:45 FDA Inspection Readiness
01:11:00 Individual Roles and Accountability
01:14:30 Key Takeaways
01:17:00 Next Steps and Implementation
01:20:30 Resources and Q&A



⚠️ Disclaimer: This presentation provides educational information about medical device design controls and regulatory processes. It does not constitute legal or regulatory advice. Always consult with qualified regulatory professionals and legal counsel for specific guidance on your medical device development programs.

metadata.shortDescription:
November 2014 Industry Basics Workshop IDE 510k de novo CAPA eMDR

Webinar: CDRH Industry Basics Workshop
Summary: This workshop (presented by webinar) provided information on the fundamental concepts of medical device regulations.

The workshop featured five sessions, each of which consisted of a presentation followed by a question and answer (Q&A) session with a panel of experts. Participants were able to email or call us with questions during each session.

Slides: 
Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) Program: http://bit.ly/IDEBasics
510(k) Program: http://bit.ly/510kBasic
de novo: http://bit.ly/DenovoBasics
Corrective and Preventive Actions (CAPA): http://bit.ly/CAPABasics
Electronic Medical Device Reporting (eMDR): http://bit.ly/eMDRBasics

Target Audience: Medical Device Industry, Medical Device Developers, Medical Device Industry Associations

https://MedicalDevicesGroup.net/Webinar/Rob-Packard-FDA for the slides. 

The Medical Devices Group presents Medical Device Academy founder Robert Packard. In an hour-and-a-half workshop, Rob covered Changes to RTA process, Human Factors Guidance, Changes to eCopy process, Small Business Qualification Changes, Interoperability Guidance, eSubmitter software status, Device Modification Guidances, Quik 510(k) Pilot, Impact of De Novo & Fee Changes, Cybersecurity Policies, UDI Requirements, New ISO 10993-1:2018 Standard.

metadata.shortDescription:
Should your medical device enter the U.S. or Canada first? The answer depends on more than just market size — it comes down to submission structure, quality system requirements, and your regulatory readiness.

In this video, we break down the key differences between FDA and Health Canada's medical device frameworks so you can make a smarter market entry decision.

Whether you're preparing your first North American submission or evaluating market entry options, understanding these differences early can save significant cost and regulatory friction.

segments.text: When companies develop a medical device
and look to enter North America, one of
the first strategic questions is should
we go to the United States first or to
Canada first? While both countries have
mature riskbased regulatory systems,
there are important structural and
procedural differences that
manufacturers need to understand. Let's
break it down.
In the United States, medical devices
are regulated by the US Food and Drug
Administration, known as the FDA,
specifically the Center for Devices and
Radiological Health under the US FDA. In
Canada, devices are regulated by the
medical devices directorate, MDD, under
Health Canada.
Both agencies use a riskbased
classification system, but the
terminology differs slightly. In the US,
devices fall into class 1, 2, or three.
Class one is low risk, class 2, moderate
risk, class 3, high risk. In Canada,
devices are classified as class one, 2,
three, or four. Class one is the lowest
risk. Class 4 is the highest risk. Now,
generally speaking, US class 3 devices
often align with Canadian class 4
devices, though classification must
always be assessed carefully. In the
United States, most moderate risk
devices require a 510K submission
demonstrating substantial equivalence to
a predicate device. High-risk devices
require pre-market approval or PMA,
which involves extensive clinical data
and a much more rigorous and robust
review.
In Canada, class 2, 3, and four devices
require a medical device license, MDL
for short. One key difference here is
that in the US 510K pathway relies
heavily on comparison to a legally
marketed predicate. Whereas in Canada,
there is no predicate equivalence model
in the same way as it is in the US.
Instead, it evaluates safety and
effectiveness based on the submitted
evidence package. In the US,
manufacturers must comply with 21 CFR
part 820. This is known as the quality
system regulation. However, the FDA is
transitioning to align more closely with
ISO ISO 13485 under the quality
management system regulation framework.
In Canada, ISO 13485 certification is
mandatory for class 2, 3, and four
devices. Certification must be obtained
through a recognized registar under the
medical device single audit program
known as MDSAP. medical device single
audit program. This is the MDSAP is a
major strategic difference. So again in
Canada ISO 13485 and MDSAP is required
before licensing. In the United States
FDA inspection typically occurs
postmarket
unless you have MDSAP
timelines and strategy between these two
cases. So in many cases, Canada
offers a more predictable licensing
pathway, especially for moderate risk
devices. In the US market, uh it is
significantly larger and may require
more complex predicate analysis or
clinical justification.
Some companies pursue Canada first to
gain North America regulatory experience
and postmarket data before entering the
US. Now, that's of course if they have
MDSP. That's often a big hurdle. Now,
others prioritize the US due to market
size and reimbursement potential. Both
countries require
complaint handling, adverse event
reaction reporting, recalls, and
corrective actions. However, reporting
timelines and definitions differ
slightly,
and manufacturers must ensure procedures
reflect the jurisdictional nuances. At a
high level, both Canada and the United
States use riskbased frameworks focused
on safety effectiveness
and quality systems. The real
differences
lies in submission, the the structure of
the submission, the quality system
certification requirements, predicate
reliance, strategic market access
considerations.
Choosing the right pathway isn't just a
regulatory decision. It's a commercial
one. Understanding these differences
early can save significant cost and
regulatory friction.

segments.text: How much liquid helium does an MRI Use?
The Niobium-Titanium core inside an MRI uses liquid helium to supercool the magnet to around
4 Kelvin, which is about -269 degrees Celsius or -452 degrees Fahrenheit. With liquid helium prices
nearly doubling in recent years, the high cost of liquid helium has become a significant factor
in the rising cost of medical imaging procedures. So, How Much Liquid Helium Does an MRI Use under
normal scan conditions and how often are they refilled? First, let’s start with the main
liquid helium vessel. The average 1.5T MRI and 3T MRI magnet hold between 1200 and 1500 liters
of liquid helium. So, that’s about $60,000 USD in liquid helium for the initial fill. However,
liquid helium boils and evaporates away at room temperature, even in well insulated systems,
Older systems have a higher boil-off rate as high as 5 to 10 liters per day. That’s up to
$500 a day in liquid helium costs alone. Newer systems are designed to be much more efficient
and significantly reduce boil-off rates to less than 1 liters of liquid helium boil-off per day.
Older MRI systems with higher liquid helium boil-off rates require refills of about 1000
liters every 9 to 14 month. More efficient systems require liquid helium fills every 24 to 48 months,
or more. These numbers are based on normal operating conditions,

The average 1.5T MRI and 3T MRI magnet hold between 1200 and 1500 liters of liquid helium. So, that’s about $60,000 USD in liquid helium for the initial fill. However, liquid helium boils and evaporates away at room temperature, even in well insulated systems, Older systems have a higher boil-off rate as high as 5 to 10 liters per day. metadata.title: The Market Outlook for Medical Equipment in Latin America
metadata.author: Global Health Intelligence
metadata.shortDescription: In this webinar conducted by GHI, Guillaume Corpart (CEO) and Christophe Leroy (Project Manager) discuss key highlights from Medical Equipment Market Report Latin America 2021. This comprehensive report features more than 1,500 data points about hospital infrastructure in Latin America that are designed to help medical equipment/medical device manufacturers understand the market and explore new opportunities. The webinar features a range of data from the report, including COVID recovery in Latin America (projected dates for reaching herd immunity in different countries),  totals and year-on-year change in Latin America of basic equipment (EKG machines, ventilators, etc.) and specialized equipment (MRI machines, CT scanners, etc.). It also highlights the medical equipment categories that grew the most in 2020 in Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Central America, Chile, Colombia and Peru, while sharing a list of hospitals in each country that are the technology adoption leaders. Beyond the wealth of data shared, the webinar also looks at how the medical equipment market is recovering in Latin America and when it will reach pre-pandemic levels. To find out more about the report discussed in the webinar and download a sample, please visit: https://medical-equipment-market-report-latin-america.com/

metadata.title: 2022 Latin America Medical Equipment Market
metadata.author: Global Health Intelligence
metadata.shortDescription: This webinar focused on strategic data for sales and marketing teams of medical equipment manufacturers operating in Latin America. After offering the broad view of the LatAm marketplace, it offered specific data for the medical equipment markets of Brazil, Argentina, México, Colombia, Chile, Peru and Central America, all derived from GHI's 2022 Medical Equipment Market Report Latin America, a 72-page report designed to help with sales and marketing planning for 2023 and beyond.

metadata.author: Global Health Intelligence
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Guillaume Corpart—CEO and Founder of Global Health Intelligence—explains how medical equipment/device sales professionals focused on Latin America can quickly find prospects among the 19,000 hospitals in Latin America.

The key to finding targeted prospects at lightning-fast speeds is HospiScope. This database contains medical equipment/devices and other strategic data for more than 90% of Latin America’s hospitals.

Are you selling MRI machines in Mexico?
Are you selling robotic surgery equipment in Brazil?
Are you selling EKG machines in Argentina?
Are you selling linear accelerators in Colombia?
Are you selling ventilators in the Dominican Republic?
Are you selling patient monitors in Chile?

Regardless, all of these equipment types—in all these hospital markets—are in HospiScope.

GHI created HospiScope in 2014 and has continued to expand it since then. These days, for 19,000 Latin American hospitals in 15 countries, HospiScope features equipment counts for base installed equipment in dozens of categories, whether it’s basic equipment like monitors or high-tech equipment like DaVinci surgical robots or C-arms.

You’ll see how quickly HospiScope can find hospitals with the size and other features that match the buyer profile for your product and quickly deliver prospects for your outreach.

In just 90 seconds of your time, you’ll see how easy it is to expand your sales pipeline for medical equipment/devices in Latin America.

--

If you want to learn more about GHI, go to https://globalhealthintelligence.com/

Optometry’s scope of practice has changed several times over the past 50 years to ensure ODs can provide the best care for their patients. Senate Bill 36, the Primary Eye Care Modernization Bill, was created for this same purpose. 
 
As Ohio’s population ages and the demand for eye care continues to rise, adjusting optometry’s scope will ensure that patients can get timely, quality care close to home. 
 
Learn more about scope modernization and Senate Bill 36: www.trustedeyecareohio.com/

metadata.title: Laser Safe - The Biomed’s Path to LSO Certification
metadata.author: TechNation TV
metadata.shortDescription:
Presenters: Vangie Dennis, MSN, RN, CNOR, CMLSO, FAORN, FAAN, Perioperative Consultants, LLC and Patti Owens, MHA, BSN, RN, CMLSO, CNOR
AestheticMed Consulting International, LLC

This educational webinar highlights the importance of training and certifying Biomedical Engineers to serve as Medical Laser Safety Officers (MLSO) in your facility. 

Biomedical engineers should be Laser Safety Officers (LSOs) because their technical expertise with medical devices, understanding of safety protocols, and familiarity with equipment maintenance and calibration make them ideal for managing complex laser systems and ensuring patient, staff, and public safety in healthcare environments. Their technical background directly aligns with the need for precise risk assessment, implementation of control measures, and adherence to strict  ANSI standards. 

Over 50% of laser-based hospitals and outpatient surgical centers are considered deficient because they lack an MLSO, which puts patients and staff at risk. Without proper credentialing, classified laser systems, updated standard operating procedures, or appropriate protective eyewear, serious injuries can happen. Incidents can quickly lead to costly penalties, regulatory actions, and litigation. Ensuring compliance with national regulations, state laws, laser standards, and practice guidelines is essential for fostering a culture of safety. 

Course objectives will include the duties of the MLSO, a specially trained professional responsible for ensuring the safe use of lasers in medical settings such as hospitals, surgical centers, vision clinics, or dermatology offices. This webinar will review the MLSO role as defined and guided by ANSI Z136.3, the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard for the Safe Use of Lasers in Healthcare. In addition, the webinar will discuss the benefits of having Biomedical Engineers assume this regulatory role within the facility-based laser program.

Ofstead’s CE webinars are now available via the Healthcare Sterile Process Association (HSPA) (eLearning.myhspa.org). See below for more information.”

In September 2025, Ofstead & Associates entered into a partnership with the Healthcare Sterile Processing Association (HSPA) to provide access to high-quality sterile processing education. The full catalog of Ofstead’s webinars—addressing essential topics such as sterile processing, endoscope processing, quality management, and leveraging scientific evidence—is now available as part of the HSPA eLearning library. Healthcare professionals can access these webinars at eLearning.myhspa.org to stay current, earn CE credits, and maintain their CE transcript. To explore the complete webinar catalog, visit eLearning.myhspa.org, go to the “On-Demand Webinars,” and search for Ofstead under the Category menu.

The FDA MAUDE database contains reports of adverse events associated with medical devices, including malfunctions, injuries, and outbreaks. In this video, Abby Smart, MPH, provides a how-to on using the MAUDE database to support purchasing and decision-making. 

Please like and subscribe to our channel so you don’t miss any videos!

And check out the other resources listed in this video, including:
Peer-reviewed literature: 
o Ofstead et al. Reprocessing effectiveness for flexible ureteroscopes: A critical look at the evidence. Urology. 2022;164:25-32.

o Ofosu et al. Analysis of reported adverse events related to single-use duodenoscopes and duodenoscopes with detachable endcaps. Gastrointest Endosc. 2022;96(1):67-72.
https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0016-5107(22)00118-3

metadata.title: Who's Maude Anyway? Two FDA Databases Get Updates
metadata.author: in2being
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you find out what's gone wrong with devices like yours? Consider spending some time with these databases. MAUDE and openFDA... 

CONTAINS NEITHER LEGAL NOR MEDICAL ADVICE

segments.text: Gene Parunak (00:05): MAUDE is basically a searchable database
that contains the last 10 years of MedDevice report data. It doesn't include data based on
certain exemptions, variances or alternative reporting requirements, and this has been
the subject of some amount of debate because there are other databases that FDA maintains
which are maybe less obvious. And there has been some pushback that
not every adverse event makes it to MAUDE, into one central repository.
(00:43): There are downloadable data files that
consist of voluntary reports back to June 1993. There's actually data that goes before that. There
are zip files all over the MAUDE database. You can pull these zip files. Let's talk about openFDA.
All sorts of data about recalls. They got drugs, they got devices, they got everything in here,
but they also have APIs that allow you to access the data. MAUDE and openFDA two amazing resources.
(01:16): But I know we use it into being.
Why study what went wrong? Before we tell you what's changed at these two databases. Why should
you study what went wrong? That may seem like an obvious answer. We want to make it better, right?
But beyond that, here's the word, risk. Can I have two words? Okay. Risk management.
This is heart and soul of medical device, and in general, medical product development,
including drugs and everything else under the sun that treats people.
We need to manage risk and there are standards out there for how you manage risk. In fact,
there's often requirements to consider what has gone wrong in previous generations of devices.
Understanding what has gone wrong in a device class that you may be interested in
is really important. This is something we do in our company all the time. We'll go to MAUDE and
other reports to be able to look and see, how have similar devices fared in the marketplace?
What kinds of errors do they have? What you find is very interesting and it could be surprising.
(02:25): Okay, so what got added to MAUDE and to openFDA?
Really it's just this, unique device identifiers. These are, for lack of a better word,
the barcodes that now allow you to track things like the lot number and the production
date and things like that. The manufacturer's location. For every medical device in the US.
Requirements were rolling out over the past 10 years, they're now fully established,
and UDIs have now been added to the database, so that problems can be tracked down.
You'll now have specific lot, manufacturer and other info, which we think is pretty cool.
But if you want to think about the device that you're developing, I encourage you
to look at device failures. MAUDE is a publicly accessible database, openFDA, publicly accessible.
Even if you're not a data scientist and want to dig in deeply, a cursory
look through based on some keywords for similar devices is well worth your time.

metadata.title: EPISODE 2: Product Recalls, Including Removals and Corrections
metadata.author: Mr. Regulatory
metadata.shortDescription:
#medicaldevice #regulatory #FDA #recalls

What steps do medical device manufacturers need to take if they have to notify FDA and consignees about a product recall, and what specific information is used to evaluate the recall?

In this episode of "FDA Guidance Review," medical device regulatory affairs expert and former FDA staffer David Pudwill discusses these topics, and provides helpful hints based on his years of experience, in a review of the March 2020 Guidance Document: “Product Recalls, Including Removals and Corrections.” Note that as a broad Guidance, it covers products including medical device, drugs, biologics, and others, and thus impacts a number of centers within FDA.

Here are 3 Key Takeaways that David would like viewers to understand from this video:

1.  What recall information is submitted to FDA?
2.  What recall information is sent to consignees/end-users?
3.  What information is used to evaluate the recall?

Guidance Document on the FDA website: https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/product-recalls-including-removals-and-corrections 

Guidance Document PDF: https://www.fda.gov/media/136987/download 

David’s easy-to-follow Guidance review provides clarity and context to those currently working in regulatory affairs, those aspiring to enter this important field, and anyone across healthcare with an interest in the device regulatory process.

With each episode in David Pudwill’s "FDA Guidance Review" video series, stay on top of FDA's evolving policies, and learn how to engage effectively with the agency - both being critical to the success of your medical device regulatory strategy.

MAKE SURE TO SUBSCRIBE to receive updates on when new "FDA Guidance Review" episodes are posted. We also look forward to your feedback, comments, and suggestions for topics that you would like David to cover in future episodes, so that this channel provides maximum benefit to you and your team!

Visit our website at https://mrregulatory.com/, where you can read more about David Pudwill and sign up to receive our monthly e-newsletter with updates on new video releases, his upcoming speaking engagements in the medtech regulatory affairs space, and more!

Follow @RegMastery on Twitter: https://twitter.com/RegMastery

Follow David Pudwill on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/david-pudwill/

E-mail: david@mrregulatory.com

DISCLAIMER: The views and opinions expressed on this channel and in all videos are those of the authors, speakers, and guests, and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of any company, FDA, or any other entity.

metadata.title: FDA Recall vs Warning Letter vs Safety Communication: Know the Difference
metadata.author: Treomark
metadata.shortDescription:
An FDA warning headline can describe very different things: a product recall, a warning letter to a company, or a safety communication. Those records do different jobs. Before deciding what the news means for a treatment, identify the document type, the exact product in scope, and the latest update.

Read the complete source-linked guide:
https://treomark.com/articles/fda-recall-vs-warning-letter-vs-safety-communication/

Subscribe to Treomark for clear explanations of aesthetic treatments and health measurements.

General education; individual clinical assessment matters. This explanation does not replace individualized medical advice.

Chapters
00:00 An FDA headline needs a document type
00:17 A recall can mean correction or removal
00:36 Match the product identifiers
00:54 A warning letter opens a correction process
01:12 A close-out has a limited meaning
01:29 A safety communication gives risk guidance
01:48 Risk class and status answer different questions
02:06 Follow the current instructions
02:26 Name the action before drawing the conclusion

Primary sources
FDA: Product recalls:
https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/fda-101-product-recalls

FDA: Enforcement report definitions:
https://www.fda.gov/safety/enforcement-reports/enforcement-report-information-and-definitions

FDA: Warning and close-out letters:
https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/about-warning-and-close-out-letters

FDA: Medical device safety communications:
https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/medical-device-safety/safety-communications

Treomark: FDA action records:
https://treomark.com/articles/fda-recall-vs-warning-letter-vs-safety-communication/

segments.text: An FDA warning headline can describe very
different things:
a product recall, a warning letter to
a company, or a safety communication.
Those records do different jobs.
Before deciding what the news means for
a treatment, identify the document type,
the exact product in scope,
and the latest update.
A recall addresses a product problem through
removal or correction.
It does not always mean every unit
must be returned.
Some equipment can be corrected where it
is installed.
Companies often start recalls voluntarily;
voluntary describes how the action began,
not whether the problem is minor.
Read the specific instructions.
A brand name alone may be too
broad.
Match the product, lot or serial number,
model, and relevant dates to the notice.
Our fictional record covers one identified
batch, not every product carrying the same
name.
If you already received treatment,
ask the clinic to match its records
to the actual notice.
A warning letter sets out significant violations
the FDA believes it has identified,
such as manufacturing or marketing concerns.
It gives the recipient an opportunity to
respond and address those concerns.
The letter is not itself a product
recall.
Look for the cited activity,
the requested corrections, and later agency
records.
A later close-out letter can mean the
FDA evaluated and verified corrective actions
for the violations in the warning letter.
It is not blanket approval of every
product or claim from that company.
Read the two records together,
with their dates, so an old headline
does not substitute for the current record.
A medical-device safety communication explains
the FDA’s analysis of an issue and
recommendations for patients or professionals.
Read the named products,
uses, affected people, and suggested actions.
It may be updated as information develops.
Its title alone does not tell you
that a device has been recalled or
lost clearance.
In a recall record,
classification describes the relative health
hazard.
Status describes the progress of the recall.
A terminated recall means the FDA determined
the removal or correction process met its
criteria.
It does not erase the original problem
or create a new product approval.
Keep those fields separate.
Open the current agency page instead of
relying on a cropped screenshot.
Check dates and linked updates,
then match the product and treatment record.
Ask the clinic what the notice means
for your care and who owns follow-up.
Follow the notice’s specific instructions and
clinical guidance rather than inventing a
broader stop-or-continue rule.
Recall, warning letter, and safety communication
are different starting points.
Identify the type, match the scope,
and read the update before sharing a
conclusion or changing a plan.
Read the FDA action-records guide at Treomark
dot com for linked definitions and a
practical verification checklist.
