metadata.title: Don’t Ship Medical Equipment Like Regular Freight—Here’s Why
metadata.author: Ntwdequiptrans
metadata.shortDescription:
Medical equipment freight is not standard freight. If you’re moving CT scanners, imaging systems, surgical devices, hospital beds, or any high-value medical machinery, you cannot afford to treat it like a normal pallet shipment. In this video, we break down why medical freight requires specialized equipment, trained carriers, tighter planning, and far more attention to detail than most people realize.

With decades of experience in heavy equipment transport, high-value machinery moves, oversized loads, sensitive freight, and nationwide logistics, we’ve seen the consequences of improper medical equipment handling—delays, damage, calibration issues, rejected deliveries, and costly losses that could have been avoided with the right partner.

You’ll learn why medical devices require air-ride trailers, precise securement, and experienced carriers, why healthcare delivery sites require strict coordination, why insurance coverage must match the freight’s value, and why timing isn’t just about efficiency—it impacts patient care, installation schedules, and clinical operations. Medical freight doesn’t allow shortcuts. It demands precision, communication, and risk management at every step.

Nationwide Equipment Transportation works only with vetted, trained carriers who understand the sensitivity of medical equipment. We plan delivery sites, verify insurance, coordinate with healthcare staff, confirm access requirements, and manage every detail from pickup to delivery.

If you’re shipping medical equipment or preparing for future moves, and you need it handled with accuracy—not assumptions—reach out. This freight deserves the highest level of care, and that’s exactly how we move it.

metadata.title: Medical Equipment Training | Biomedical Equipment Technology
metadata.author: Centura College
metadata.shortDescription:
Train to Fix Medical Equipment | Biomedical Equipment Technology

Biomedical Technicians are often overlooked in the healthcare field. As Regina says, someone needs to make sure that medical equipment not only works, but functions at its peak performance. 

At Centura College, the Biomedical Equipment Technology program introduces students to a wide variety of skills including the install, testing and calibrating of medical equipment, repairing and replacing parts associated with medical equipment, and performing preventive maintenance and servicing medical equipment.

Coursework includes foundations in electronics, basic networking, biomedical instrumentation, basic anatomy and physiology, and biomedical troubleshooting and repair.

Centura College | Allied Health & Trades 

For more information, visit us on http://centuracollege.edu/
or give us a call at (877) 523-9528

Make sure to follow us on
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/centura.edu/
Twitter: https://twitter.com/CenturaCollege
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/centuracollege/

Centura College adapts to needs of their students and offers temporary online classes for their educational training.

metadata.title: Medinas Health: Building a Medical Equipment Marketplace | Berkeley Haas Case Series
metadata.author: Berkeley Haas Case Series
metadata.shortDescription:
This case centers on the startup Medinas Health, a technology company based in Berkeley, California that aimed to increase the efficiency of the medical equipment market in the U.S. Chloe Alpert, Medinas Health’s CEO, envisioned a more sustainable healthcare industry and aimed to reduce waste and improve the financial bottom-line of hospitals. These goals led her to create a digital marketplace to help hospitals manage the sale and acquisition of used medical equipment. An active secondary market would reduce waste by putting used equipment to use and keeping it out of waste dumps. It could also improve a hospital’s financial bottom-line by enabling them to recover money by selling their used equipment. If Medinas Health could match surplus equipment to customer demand, they would simultaneously provide cost savings for all parties and reduce the volume of medical equipment entering the waste stream. Their challenge was to make it easy and convenient for medical facilities to promote reuse of medical equipment and to sell their surplus to other medical entities.


Based on the case study "Medinas Health: Building a Medical Equipment Marketplace" by Don Moore, Marieshka Barton, and Robert Girling
https://cases.haas.berkeley.edu/2020/08/medinas/




For more information, please visit our website:
https://cases.haas.berkeley.edu

segments.text: Hello everybody! This is Jordan with Block Imaging, and today I'm going to share with you seven questions
that you should ask any company you're considering for medical imaging equipment refurbishment.
These seven questions can help you make sure you're getting the best quality and also the best experience
as a buyer out of any company that you're going to work with. We’ve compiled these questions into one helpful
checklist that you can download below.
Question one: Is your refurbishment process ISO-certified? ISO certification is an auditing process many companies
undergo as a way to standardize their processes and demonstrate tangibly their commitment to quality assurance. For refurbishment,
this is a great way to understand the level of quality you can expect from the equipment you're about to purchase.
Question two: Can you send me documentation of your refurbishment process? For a company that's ISO-certified, this should be very easy.
It can be a document. It can be a video or a blog; anything that details, step-by-step, what's going to be done to the equipment to make sure it's
in great shape when it arrives at your facility.
Question three: Does your refurbishment process include a HIPAA compliance step? HIPAA is a federal requirement that says all patient information needs
to be removed from the system before it leaves one facility to go to another. Making sure that your refurbishment has this step in their process can help you
avoid being fined for having information you're not supposed to.
Question four: Does your refurbishment process include internal decontamination of every system? Systems, over the course of general use, can get dusty, dirty.
Blood, contrast dye, and other bodily fluids can accumulate on the outside, and it's relatively easy to clean these off, but is the same level of care taken on
the inside of each system, where accumulated dust and debris can clog fans, overheat components, or just be a general biohazard for future users?
Making sure your refurbisher cleans the inside as well can help you from taking on any ‘hangers-on’ that you didn't bargain for.
Question five: Can you provide video confirmation of functionality before the system leaves your facility? Now this could be as simple as an iPhone video, or as high-tech
as a professional-grade camera. The important thing is a seamless, without edits clip, front-to-back, of the system going through all its movements and taking a scan.
It provides an additional layer of credibility and protection for you, the buyer.
While we are on the subject of credibility and protection for the buyer, that leads us to question six, which is: Can I have access to QA results before the system ships?
This could be anything from a PDF report, to a short video clip, or maybe even a screen capture of a successful QA screen. This is proof to you that the system is functioning
within specifications set by the original manufacturer.
Our final question doesn't have much to do with equipment, but it has an awful lot to do with the experience you'll have as a buyer.
A refurbishment provider who also offers project management assistance gives you a common touch point for communication from start-to-finish on your refurbished equipment project.
So that's it, everybody! Thank you for sticking around for all seven questions. Don't forget we have those below as a downloadable checklist for your reference.
You can ask these to any vendor to know that they're going to give you a quality refurbished product.
And, if you’d like to know more, please do subscribe to Medical Imaging Equipment Channel on YouTube. Thanks again, and have a great day!

metadata.title: FDA Reprocessing Medical Devices: Validation Methods and Labeling.#MedicalDeviceReprocessing
metadata.author: Medical and Health Tips (MHT)
metadata.shortDescription:
FDA webinar on a final guidance for "Reprocessing Medical Devices in Health Care Settings: Validation Methods and Labeling" - March 24, 2015.The FDA webinar on a final guidance for "Reprocessing Medical Devices in Health Care Settings: Validation Methods and Labeling," held on March 24, 2015, aimed to inform healthcare professionals and manufacturers about the critical aspects of reprocessing medical devices safely and effectively. This guidance emphasized the importance of validation methods that ensure devices are adequately cleaned, disinfected, and sterilized for reuse, thus protecting patient safety and promoting public health.

During the webinar, attendees were introduced to the essential components of the reprocessing lifecycle, including the need for comprehensive written protocols that outline the specific steps required for each type of device. The FDA officials highlighted the significance of using scientific evidence to support claims made on device labels regarding the intended use and reprocessing instructions. 

Moreover, the session addressed common challenges faced by healthcare facilities in implementing reprocessing procedures, encouraging the adoption of best practices and rigorous training programs for staff involved in these processes. Participants were encouraged to ask questions and engage in discussions to clarify guidelines and enhance their understanding of compliance requirements.

The FDA underscored its commitment to continuing to work collaboratively with stakeholders, including manufacturers and healthcare providers, to improve the safety and effectiveness of reprocessed medical devices. The provision of the final guidance was positioned as a crucial step in ensuring that patient care remains a top priority while maximizing the benefits of device reuse in a cost-effective manner. 

Through this informative session, the FDA reiterated its ongoing efforts to facilitate greater awareness and adherence to standards that ultimately extend the lifecycle of medical devices while safeguarding the health of patients in diverse healthcare settings.

Current FDA Medical Device Reprocessing Guidance Documents are as follows:  

1. Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff: Reprocessing Medical Devices in Health Care Settings: Validation Methods and Labeling - This document outlines the expectations for manufacturers and healthcare facilities regarding the validation of reprocessing methods, ensuring that devices can be safely reused without compromising their functionality or patient safety.

2. Guidance for Industry: Medical Device User Fees: Reprocessing - This guidance provides information on the user fee structure associated with the reprocessing of medical devices, including the submission of 510(k) applications for reprocessed single-use devices.

3. Draft Guidance: Reprocessing and Reuse of Single-Use Devices - This draft guidance discusses the considerations and best practices for the reprocessing of single-use devices, emphasizing the importance of thorough risk assessments and the need for robust validation studies.

4. Guidance for Industry: Labeling Reprocessed Single-Use Devices - This document addresses the labeling requirements for reprocessed single-use devices, ensuring that the information provided to users is clear and informative, allowing for safe handling and use.

5. Guidance: Medical Device Reporting for Reprocessed Devices - This guidance highlights the reporting obligations for adverse events related to reprocessed devices, stressing the importance of monitoring and reporting to maintain patient safety.

These guidances collectively aim to ensure that reprocessed medical devices meet safety and efficacy standards, providing a framework for manufacturers and healthcare providers to follow in their reprocessing practices.

radiation.

problems.

A computed tomography scan uses x-rays

The x-ray machine rotates around the
patient taking many images.

produce detailed cross-sectional slices,
which can also be reconstructed into 3D
views.
CT scans are mainly used to detect
internal injuries, identify bleeding,
diagnose tumors, examine organs, detect
strokes,
and to plan surgery.
The advantages of a CT scan includes

normal x-ray.

uses more ionizing radiation than an
x-ray.

MRI scan.
Magnetic resonance imaging uses strong
magnets and radio waves to produce
detailed images of soft tissues inside
the body.
So, how does it work? Strong magnetic
fields and radio waves cause hydrogen
atoms in the body to produce signals.
A computer converts these signals into
highly detailed images.
MRI scans are mainly used to examine the
brain,
diagnose spinal cord injuries,
view muscles and tendons,
detect ligament damage, and identify
some tumors.
The advantages of an MRI scan
includes there's no ionizing radiation.
It produces excellent detail of soft
tissues.
It produces very clear images.

The limitations of an MRI scan include
it takes longer than X-rays or CT scans.

with metal implants or certain medical
devices.
Ultrasound scan.
An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency
sound waves to produce real-time images
of structures inside the body.
So, how does it work?
A handheld probe sends sound waves into
the body.
The sound waves bounce off organs and
tissues, and the returning echoes are
used to create an image.
Ultrasound scans are mainly used to
monitor pregnancy, examine the heart,

The advantages of an ultrasound scan

radiation, it's safe during pregnancy,

The limitations of an ultrasound scan

imaging, MRI scans are best for soft

ligaments,
ultrasounds are best for pregnancy,

metadata.title: Deep Learning for MRI Reconstruction | MRI Data Acquisition #10
metadata.author: MRI R&D Program - TACTIX Twinning Project
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Dr. Tolga Çukur explains how deep learning can be useful in MR reconstruction. The lecture reviews classical parallel imaging methods (SENSE, GRAPPA, ESPIRiT) and regularized optimization before detailing how deep learning transforms this inverse problem through data-driven, physics-guided, and generative frameworks, along with supervised, self-supervised, and scan-specific training strategies.

This video was created as part of the European Union-funded TACTIX project, with grant agreement no. 101159624.

First video on gammaSTAR Introduction:
https://youtu.be/NP_j2QnEVYA

Previous video on MRI Artefacts:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8dGILVXcDZ8&list=PLo5_MVynYkJLE3wFF3QfY-2DQrZ_KmQxm&index=14

MRI Data Acquisition Playlist:
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLo5_MVynYkJLE3wFF3QfY-2DQrZ_KmQxm&si=3hmyIpEX7DvQtP4k

Reference links:
- TACTIX - https://tactix.bogazici.edu.tr/

- BART (Berkeley Advanced Reconstruction Toolbox): Classical and physics-based MRI reconstruction framework (Interfaces: C, Python, MATLAB; TensorFlow integration).

- Deep Inverse: PyTorch-compatible library for deep learning imaging inverse problems (Plug-and-Play, Unrolled, Diffusion, Self-Supervised models).

Chapters:
00:02 -  Introduction and MRI Physics Basics
04:21 - Under-Sampling and The Inverse Problem
06:21 - Classical Parallel Imaging
16:50 - Optimization and Regularization
18:20 - Deep Learning Frameworks for MRI
25:07 - Architectural Building Blocks
28:07 - Training Paradigms
34:00 - Software Frameworks and Tools


Keywords:
#GenerativeAI
#Neuroimaging
#MRIReconstruction
#ParallelImaging

So in the first framework of data driven, basically we assume knowledge of k-space consistency encoding, so none of the physics of MRI is is involved. We just feed the alias and and poor quality images or k-space data from the left as input to the network and ask it to reconstruct high quality combined image on the right side by network based mapping. So the the nice thing about this is that you don't need to inject any specialized network blocks, for example, something like a simple as a U-Net or ResNet. We can just adopt from the computer vision literature stick it in here and train it and hope that it works. But the downside is of course knowing nothing about the physics of the the MRI acquisition, these models are poor in terms of generalization and robustness to different under sampling patterns, different consistency profiles. So because they tend to memorize also the particular coil array and and under sampling factors you train them all. But but this is the typical framework, so it's simple to implement, computationally efficient for the most part, but no mechanism to enforce fidelity to acquire data which costs them in terms of generalization. Then the answer to this is physics guided networks in which we do not no longer have only network blocks which tend to do data driven regularization of the the images, but we also have these physical blocks, I would say, or physically guided blocks that that this typically called the data consistency block. And we interleave between these two modules within the network to ensure that we both do data driven regularization through the network model, but as also shown in the second line here, we also respect the physics and acquire data in the second line. So we we project the recovered image onto the k-space and and we can do something as simple as replacing the acquired data with the with those and and the recovered network based estimates to ensure that we we remain fidel to the actual physics. So by going across these in iterations kind of like in traditional optimization algorithm, we can try to converge onto a compromise solution that achieves the best of both worlds. These are typically called or one popular framing of these is unrolled architectures. Of course, you need to iterate between multiple blocks and then you need to have multiple iterations to reach a converged solution. These can be a little bit heavier than purely data driven networks and they can still be sensitive to different under sampling patterns or rates because there is nothing in in these DC blocks that will allow the network to generalize across different under sampling patterns. And if you want to have the greatest robust and and flexibility, I should say to any under sampling pattern that you want be coil sensitive to profile, you want the network to be completely flexible. One thing you can do is you can still try to enforce the imaging operator, the physics of the process, but you do it at training time. So at training time, the model is only asked to asked to learn the distribution of high quality coil combined MR images like M hat shown here. So you ask the network just to learn to synthesize realistic looking high quality MR images. But the downside or what you need to do with generator networks is you need to combine them with physical consistency enforcing block at test time. So what you'll do, you have this generate network or synthesize a random image, then you would apply the physical operator of your under sampled acquisition at test time for that one particular subject. So you subject it to coil sensitivities, free encoding, sampling, and you ask the resulting case space data to be consistent with what you actually measured in that subject. Now this involves some kind of optimization at test time. So that's the But it allows you to completely flex be flexible to different under sampling patterns, different But as I said, you need to run this test time optimization procedure on each subject which can elevate cost of running inference on a trained model to somewhere two or three orders of magnitude higher than a typical trained network that is frozen at test time. The second bit that you need to decide on when designing these architectures. So there's this framework issue. You need to decide whether you want to use data driven, physics guided or generative. And then the second bit is the architecture with which you build each framework. And these are completely independent design choices. So there, when building the network blocks, you can choose from a number of options. You can use fully connected architectures where each pixel in the input is mapped to each other pixel in the output. So multi-layer perceptrons is a common example of this. You can use the popular convolutional mappings which take a small neighborhood of pixels in the input map and then map them to a single output pixel. So this is efficient because it uses few parameters to do the mapping. There are the attentional mappings which look at interactions between all possible pairings of pixels or patches in the image to do input adaptive mapping. So this is more powerful because it can link even distant pixels, but the and and it's used frequently in transformer architectures. But the downside, as with fully connected architectures, it's very computationally heavy. And then there are recurrent architectures that have made a comeback in recent years. So there are the regular RNNs, LSTMs, but in in recent years we see state space models and the Mamba architectures that try to achieve convolutional level efficiency while integrating long there is this of course tradeoff between your representational power and computational efficiency. So depending on your GPU compute budget you may need to decide on whether you will discard or neglect long range dependencies and go with a convolutional model or if you have if you can afford it you can use recurred or attentional architectures to better learn the dependencies between even far apart pixels in in the image. So this is the mapping for a fully connected architecture. All pixels in the input are mapped to all output pixels in a static fashion. This is the convolutional mapping. It assumes spatially invariant mapping. So the filter is applied the same way in all regions of the image and it's locally constrained. This is the attentional mapping. So the filter weights the interesting bit about this is are learned from the relationships between the data points. So they are not static. They change per image depending on its structure. And then this is the recurrent state space modeling approach where we just keep accumulating and and summarizing the relationships between pixels as we run through a trajectory in the image so that it learns long range context in an efficient manner compared to transformers. And the last bit about the the training of the model so you selected your framework and you decided on how to construct in architecture wise the individual building blocks the data driven blocks in that network. Now is the time to train it. Okay so how are you going to train these architectures? This is also an independent choice. And this depends closely on the availability and structure of your training data. Do you have a sufficient large training set? Do you actually have ground truth data derived from fully sampled acquisitions or are you working on an application where it's impossible to capture fully sampled data because of time restrictions, say trying to collect some dynamic acquisition and it's simply possible for the patient to keep their blood breath hold for that long to for you to capture fully sampled acquisition. So all you have is this under sampled data. Then depending on that, there are three main paradigms. If you can capture population level data with the ground truth derived from fully sampled acquisitions, then you would do supervised learning. If you have population level data, meaning you can capture data from hundreds of subjects or or at least tens that but you don't have fully sampled data available, only under sampled, then you would do self supervised learning. And then if you have none of these, so and then you want to just deploy the deep learning model at test time, you would do scan specific training. So we can look at these briefly. In the case of supervised learning, you have access to paired under sampled and fully sampled data sets and then you ask the network to specifically map the under sampled to the fully sampled ground truth. So this will be supervised learning. And then you deploy it at test time. Of course, because the training and test sets are going to be well aligned in the structure, it typically performs well at test time, but it it is costly in terms of collection of the paired data sets it requires. And in some cases for high spatial or temporal resolution imaging, it might not be it may not be possible to capture the ground truth as I mentioned. So for those cases, we have self supervised learning in which you only have under sampled images at the output. So what you would do is you would take the ask the network to recover still an image that looks like full sampled image, but you would enforce your data fidelity only on subset of the acquired data as opposed to ground truth. Okay, so the the this idea is known in machine learning as mask prediction is commonly used in training of self-supervised transformer models for vision and language and the adoption of that idea in the MRI domain is called SSDU. Basically, we take an undersampled dataset. We further sub split into two into two disjoint subsets. One of them is used for running predictions with the model and the other case based subset is used to see how well the the predictions are running so that we can optimize the network weights. So this idea, so basically you take the original undersampled case space, split it into two. You run predictions with one and you ask the network to recover the held out set set two at its output. So this is how we express a lot. Of course, the good thing is we can do self-supervised learning now. We don't need full sample data, but the downside is especially for higher acceleration factors as you say have an eight-fold undersample data here. You split it further. Now these become 16-fold undersampled. The quality of supervision that you can provide to the network grows weaker and weaker towards higher accelerations. But this works really well if you have if you're interested in moderate acceleration factors. Okay, and this is an example. So this is a supervised trained deep learning network whereas at R4 this is a self-supervised network. You can see that they give very comparable quality without ever needing the full sample data. But this is for mostly restricted to limited acceleration factors as I mentioned. And now finally, if you don't have any training data, this is very difficult or you have a pre-trained model, but the domain has shifted to a different anatomy, different scanner, and you're having difficulty in generalizing performance. Now you can do test-time training or or scan-specific learning. So you have some kind of network that is capable of generating an output, and then you subject this to the imaging operator for that test subject kind of like in the generative networks. You undersample it, you apply the processes to these, and then once you get the resulting k-space data, you compare it to what you measured in that subject actually. And then by trying to minimize this data consistency loss, you can optimize the parameters of your network. So you can do pure test-time training. There is a variant of this. One variant is deep image prior where the network actually maps noise to actual images. The other is a network that maps undersampled data or its least squares reconstruction to images. In the second case, this network can be actually pre-trained on some training set, and you're further boosting its generalization by doing this test-time training. The disadvantage is now at inference you need to run an optimization that probably takes hundreds or or thousands of iterations even in a GPU that will, you know, elevate your runtime costs. Now to sum up the discussions now as as subsequent to this presentation, I think you will have some tutorial where you play with some tools that allow you to implement and experiment with these networks. So part of the the difficulty is that everyone these days publishes their networks on GitHub repositories that may have been coded in libraries such as PyTorch or TensorFlow. But it's not always easy or streamlined process to implement it yourself. So there are some packages people have put together in the community over the years that are aimed at streamlining this process and trying to put together all of the tools you would need to build a deep learning reconstruction model and deploy it in one package so that you don't run into these compatibility issues. One of them is is Bart. There are many more of course, but these ones are quite popular. That's why I wanted to exemplify them. So if you don't want to do things from scratch, but you want an easy introduction, then Bart is an MRI specific package that was actually developed in the era of classical reconstruction methods, it has many of the tools and and methods that you may need if you're interested in classical techniques called sensitivity estimation, E-spirit, non-linear inversion and and so on. It has accurate MRI physics, so it has the scripts to do that and and is has interfaces to see Python and and MATLAB. So it's it's powerful in that sense. The only downside is that its deep learning interface assumes tensor flow and it's not that compatible, at least until recently with with PyTorch. And if you are a PyTorch fan, then you can adopt Deep Inverse. Now the difference in Deep Inverse is that it's not MRI specific. It's actually for many modalities including those for natural images and photography. It includes includes tools for MRI, CT, PET and so on. So it's a more general inverse imaging problem solver, but it's very heavily focused on deep learning. There are unrolled plug and play diffusion, self-supervised implementation for that, physics operator, pre-trained models that you can deploy like foundation models. And then the nice thing that I like about Deep Inverse is it's by default compatible with PyTorch. So many of the published models on on GitHub that people have attached to their their papers, you can just download and and them in Deep inverse to to run them. Uh so this is an interface and the web link for Bart. If you're interested in in the solvers and capabilities, you can check this out uh the the the website. As I said, for MRI specific and mostly classical or compressed sensing era work, this will be the go-to tool uh for deep learning stuff. It's more limited to TensorFlow uh and if you're interested in PyTorch, I think deep inverse would be an easy or more compatible ecosystem. And with that, so that that's the end of my presentation. metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about taking the CBET Exam (Certified Biomedical Equipment Technician Exam)? In this video, I share my honest opinion, what the test was like, and tips to help you get ready.  

The CBET exam covers six major areas:  
- Anatomy & Physiology  
- Public Safety in Healthcare  
- Fundamentals of Electricity & Electronics  
- Healthcare Technology & Functions  
- Problem Solving & Troubleshooting  
- Healthcare Information Technology  

I’ll walk you through what I studied, the resources I used, and my personal experience preparing for and taking the exam. If you’re a biomedical equipment technician (BMET), or just getting started in the field, this exam is a huge milestone for your career.  

📚 Helpful Resources:  
- AAMI Online Training Courses:  https://www.aami.org/training/overview

 - AAMI CBET Exam: https://www.aami.org/home/about-aci/aci-home/cbet

#CBET #CBETExam #BMET #Biomed #MedicalEquipment #Certification #ExamPrep

segments.text: hi my name is dr. Cathy Kelly and I work
at four paws Animal Hospital in
Fredericksburg Virginia today we're
going to be talking to you about how we
prepare our surgical packs for surgeries
and other sterile procedures
[Music]
depending on the type of surgical pack
that were preparing there are a
different set of instruments that should
be included in each pack for example a
spay pack is going to have a different
set of instruments than a neuter pack if
you look closely you can also see that
there is a small colored band on each
surgical instrument in order to help us
make sure that the correct instrument
goes into the correct color-coded pack
once you have collected all the
appropriate instruments then they can be
transferred into the metal tray the
instruments are loaded in a particular
fashion every time so that they're in
the same order every time when you
unwrap the pack
it is also important that the assistant
who is preparing the pack count out an
exact number of gauze sponges to place
in there it is important that we knew
exactly how many are in there in order
to assure that none are accidentally
left behind
when the surgery is completed an
indicator strip is also placed inside
the tray as this will help us determine
whether or not the pack was properly
sterilized when it's unwrapped on
the right is a strip that has not been
sterilized yet and on the left is a
strip that has been sterilized
once the tray has been filled with the
correct instruments an indicator strip
and the correct number of gauze sponges
it then needs to be wrapped in these
cloth drapes most surgical packs are
double wrapped and there's a very
specific technique that need be used in
order to wrap them properly
as the subject wrap is completed there's
a small pull tab that's left in order to
facilitate the appropriate way to open
the pack this allows a non sterile
assistant to pull on the tab to start
the unwrapping process of the pack in
surgery by doing it this way they do not
touch the inside surfaces of the pack
which remain sterile and therefore the
surgeon can still touch the inside
surfaces
finally some tape is applied to keep the
pack wrapped snugly throughout the
sterilization procedure the blue tape is
just plain old painters tape but the
most important part is applying a strip
of indicator tape just like the
indicator strips inside the pack the
indicator tape will let us know when
this pack has been sterilized properly
the assistant always writes the date
that it was prepared what the pack is as
in what kind of instruments it contains
and also their initials in case there
are any questions about the contents of
the pack
once the packs have been prepared
they're loaded into the autoclave for
the sterilization process
once the autoclave is finished the packs
are removed and you can now see that the
indicator tape on the outside has some
black stripes on it this lets us know
that the sterilization cycle was
completed properly I
hope you found this interesting
and look forward to seeing you soon
[Music]

metadata.author: Vet Candy | Veterinary Education, CE & News
metadata.shortDescription:
Thank you PRN Pharmacy for sponsoring this program!

The veterinary technician's role in surgery is a discussion about how to assist your veterinary team during surgical procedures.  From preparing the room, clipping and scrubbing the patient, to post-surgical cleaning and care of the surgical suite.  This program  is hosted by certified veterinary technician, Alyssa Mages.

Topics covered:
• Preparing for surgery
• Preparing the patient for surgery
• Care of surgical instruments
• Cleaning and follow up post-surgery 

CONTINUING EDUCATION INFORMATION: 

This program is approved by AAVSB RACE and New York State for veterinary technician CE credit (20-843781). 

To get your CE credits: 
1. Watch the show 
2. Pass this quiz: https://www.classmarker.com/online-test/start/?quiz=kac611b6627cdc0d

3. Save your certificate 

Email hello@myvetcandy.com if you have any questions or concerns. 

This program (20-843781) is approved by the AAVSB RACE and the State of New York for a total of 0.50 CE Credits, with a maximum of 0.50 CE Credits being available to any individual veterinarian. This RACE approval is for the subject matter category of medical using the delivery method of digital/anytime. This approval is valid in jurisdictions which recognize AAVSB RACE; however, participants are responsible for ascertaining each board's CE requirements. Expires August 16, 2023. https://conferencepanel.com/conference/mastering-fda-510-k-submission-process-a-practical-guide

The 510(k) submission process is one of the most critical regulatory pathways for Class II medical devices seeking FDA clearance. Understanding and navigating this process efficiently can determine a product’s success in the U.S. market.

This webinar will provide an in-depth roadmap for preparing a compliant 510(k) submission, highlighting the critical elements required by the FDA, common pitfalls that lead to delays, and best practices for ensuring a smooth approval process.

Participants will gain insights into:

The role of substantial equivalence and predicate selection – understanding what qualifies as an appropriate predicate device and how to demonstrate equivalence.
Required documentation and submission components – an overview of safety and performance testing, labeling, and software validation.
Quality system requirements – why maintaining a robust quality system is crucial, even if it’s not directly submitted in the 510(k).
FDA’s new e-Star submission process – how it simplifies and streamlines regulatory submissions.
Best strategies for avoiding rejections – a review of the most common reasons why FDA submissions are denied and how to mitigate risks.
At the end of this session, attendees will have a clear framework for preparing their 510(k) submissions efficiently, minimizing regulatory hurdles, and expediting time-to-market.

Areas Covered

Overview of the 510(k) Submission Process
Predicate Device Selection & Substantial Equivalence
Required Documentation & Testing Expectations
FDA’s e-Star Digital Submission Process
Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Rejections
Best Practices for Streamlining the Approval Process.

The 510(k) preparation and submission process is an essential regulatory requirement for medical device manufacturers seeking to market their products in the United States. It serves as a pathway to ensure that a device is substantially equivalent to an existing legally marketed device, thereby bypassing the more rigorous Premarket Approval (PMA) process. With the increasing number of regulatory changes, heightened compliance scrutiny, and evolving FDA submission formats, professionals need clear guidance to successfully navigate the process. This webinar provides essential insights and actionable strategies for achieving efficient and compliant 510(k) submissions.

Why Should You Attend

Preparing and submitting a 510(k) to the FDA can be an intimidating process filled with complexities, uncertainties, and potential rejections. Companies often struggle with predicate device selection, testing requirements, formatting submission documents, and ensuring compliance with the latest regulatory updates. Mistakes can lead to costly delays, increased submission fees, and lost market opportunities.

In this exclusive webinar, we will:

Demystify the 510(k) preparation and submission process, ensuring you understand each step clearly.
Highlight common mistakes that lead to FDA rejections and how to avoid them.
Offer a step-by-step guide on identifying an appropriate predicate device.
Provide insightful tips on FDA expectations for testing, labeling, and software validation.
Explain the latest e-Star electronic submission process and its advantages.
Equip yourself with actionable best practices to streamline your submission timeline and increase approval chances.
Whether you are a start-up, regulatory affairs professional, quality manager, or product developer, this session will empower you with the knowledge and confidence needed to successfully navigate the 510(k) submission process.

metadata.title: Behind the 510(k): The Science of Material Compatibility and FDA Clearance Ft. CS Medical Staff
metadata.author: CS Medical
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to the kNOw Risk podcast, powered by CS Medical and hosted by Jill Holdsworth, Medical Affairs Manager and Infection Preventionist.

kNOw Risk features conversations with healthcare experts focused on infection prevention, patient safety, education, and safer reprocessing practices.

In this episode, Jill is joined by members of the CS Medical leadership, engineering, and laboratory teams for a behind-the-scenes look at the FDA 510(k) clearance process and the science required to bring a medical device to market.

The conversation explores what "FDA cleared" really means, what a 6-log reduction is and why it matters, how CS Medical tests and validates its automated cleaner-disinfector devices, and how the laboratory and engineering teams work together on material compatibility testing. The guests also share common misconceptions about the FDA submission process and the questions healthcare professionals should ask manufacturers when comparing automated disinfection devices that appear similar.


Featured Guests

Kendall Ashe, Vice President/General Manager, CS Medical

John Jans, Director of Engineering, CS Medical

Dawn Pierson, Director of Laboratory Operations, CS Medical



Learn More and Connect with CS Medical

Website: https://www.csmedicalllc.com

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/cs-medical-llc

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/csmedicalllc

X: https://x.com/CSMedicalLLC



Subscribe to the kNOw Risk podcast and follow CS Medical to stay connected and receive updates about future episodes.

disinfectants or cleaner disinfectants

litany of paperwork from safety to lab
work um to user requirements to risk

through the FDA.
>> So can you use a device if it's not 510k

>> So if a device is not 510k cleared and
it is considered a class II, then no, it
should not be used at a facility here in
the US. Um the FDA looks at this very

that the devices are safe and effective
to make sure that you're not causing
harm to patients or causing harm to the
end user of the device.
>> Okay. So can you give us a little more
detail about what a class II device is?
>> So a class II device would be like I
said, maybe a disinfectant or a
disinfectant, maybe an infusion pump,
maybe a powered wheelchair, all sorts of
different devices that are considered
moderate risk.
Um once you get into like a high risk

something like a would have, you know,
sustaining for life,
um where it would actually be required

considered a class three and those have
much more higher risks associated with

a very important that the 510k matches

in a in brief summary,

throughout the process to try and reduce
any harm that could come to the patient

then there's a number of different
validation testing that we go through
the lab to check all the different
disinfection efficacy properties,
um all of the different clinical and use
testing that we do where we take our
devices actually into various clinics,
test there in a safe way to make sure
that the devices are safe and effective.
And even on the engineering side, we'll
do human factor studies where we bring a
litany of people in to test the device
in a very specific setting, like a

the device operates safely and how it's
supposed to so it's clear for the end
user on how to do basic operations and
how to do basic preventative
maintenance.
>> Wow, that sounds like a lot of I bet
that you are really thankful for these
guys,
John and John, to have them helping you
with this process.
So let's
switch it over to John and put him in
the hot seat for a minute and
let let you tell us, John, how does
engineering fit into this overall
process of the 510k clearance process?
What does your department contribute and
how do you work with Kendall and his
team to make sure that this gets
completed and
what where do you start? What's your
first steps?
>> Sure. So
um
generally we'll have a set of
requirements that we're building a
device to. So this involves regulatory
requirements,
um human factors requirements, like what
the user is going to need,
uh electrical or infrastructure
requirements.
Uh and once we have those requirements

a design, like what's
how are we going to specify the device
that we're going to build?
Once we have our specification set, then
we'll start doing design work around
that,
building our device to those
specifications.
Uh the reason this is important because
you have to essentially know what you're
building and make sure that as you're
designing it, you're going to
satisfy the needs of the user and all
the requirements that we've already
spelled out.
So as we're designing the device and

eventually get to the point where we're

If that makes sense. So you've done your

the right product?
Once we've satisfied all of those

We've we've satisfied, we've verified

needs of the user.
It's functioning well, all the
chemical validations and everything are

And it's ready for the 510k.

You want to make sure that a normal user

So
if they read through the manual, they

Yep.

it is

board. But once we get those results,

then work with Kendall for submission.
But one of the other things that we do

Unfortunately, you can't test everything

together and say, okay, we

>> I would say we've gotten feedback from

really valuable because we bring in
actual users, actual people who would

probes, and we get some of their
feedback um as to, you know, this

this fit well, how could this be

feedback and decide, okay, does this
work to incorporate this and how can we
improve the device?
>> That's really valuable.
Now Don, can you explain to us what six
log reduction means? We say that a lot.
>> Mhm.
>> I say it my webinars all the time and I
heard it as an IP all the time, but I
don't know that everybody really
understands
what that actually means. We just say it

reduction. So what does that actually

all the bacteria of a million except for

getting in your bacteria. So,
which is your six log reduction, means

million bacteria.

sounds
pretty good to me. How how significant

have one bacteria left. If you're only
doing 99% you still have 10,000 bacteria

So this involves regulatory requirements, um human factors requirements, like what the user is going to need, uh electrical or infrastructure requirements. Uh and once we have those requirements nailed down, then we'll start working on a design, like what's how are we going to specify the device that we're going to build? Once we have our specification set, then we'll start doing design work around that, building our device to those specifications. Uh the reason this is important because you have to essentially know what you're building and make sure that as you're designing it, you're going to satisfy the needs of the user and all the requirements that we've already spelled out. So as we're designing the device and developing prototypes, eventually get to the point where we're satisfied with the design and then we'll start verifying. So in the parlance that we have in medical device engineering, verification is did you build the product right? If that makes sense. So you've done your verification activities, everything is working correctly. Now you have to go back and make sure it satisfies the needs of the users, the original requirements, and that is did I build the right product? Once we've satisfied all of those conditions, it's ready to basically button up and hand over to regulatory. We've we've satisfied, we've verified everything, we've made sure it meets the needs of the user. It's functioning well, all the chemical validations and everything are done. And it's ready for the 510k. >> Now John, how do we verify those needs of the user? How does that process work? >> That's where human factors comes in. You want to make sure that a normal user can operate the machine as intended with the instruction that you provide. So if they read through the manual, they take the training that you've provided to them and they still can't operate the machine, obviously you have an issue with either your instructions or the machine isn't operating as expected. So that's how we validate that the need the user needs are met. >> And we do we do that with actual humans? We have humans try it? Okay. >> We do. Yep. >> That's pretty cool. And Don, what what part do you play in in the 510k clearance process? >> So I work heavily with Mohavi's teams, but once John's team starts building the machine, it sort of goes back and forth between engineering and the lab because we start testing it with the devices with the disinfectant to make sure that it is cleaning properly or that it's disinfecting properly or that it's rinsing all the chemicals off. So each step along the way, we work with them to make sure that we are getting the results that we want. And if we don't, we go back to the drawing board. But once we get those results, then we start verifying, doing more testing um to let John know that it worked out well. Then we sort of compile all of our reports, then work with Kendall for submission. But one of the other things that we do is once all the lab testing is done, we test all the hardest organisms and viruses you can. Unfortunately, you can't test everything in the lab. So therefore we do clinicals, which is where we go to actual clinic or site and test on site to make sure that it operates as it should. It's cleaning, it's disinfecting, it's doing what it's supposed to do in the real world setting um before it actually even goes to Kendall for submission. So >> Have you guys ever ran into a barrier where you had to kind of come back together and say, okay, we have something we need to work on or or rework before you move forward? >> I would say we've gotten feedback from human factors before, which has been really valuable because we bring in actual users, actual people who would reprocess T probes or endo cavity probes, and we get some of their feedback um as to, you know, this operated well, this didn't operate well, this fit well, how could this be improved? And then we can take that feedback and decide, okay, does this work to incorporate this and how can we improve the device? >> That's really valuable. Now Don, can you explain to us what six log reduction means? We say that a lot. >> Mhm. >> I say it my webinars all the time and I heard it as an IP all the time, but I don't know that everybody really understands what that actually means. We just say it aloud. Like we want to achieve six log reduction. So what does that actually mean? >> Yeah, that's a good question. Um we get this all the time and there's a couple ways to look at it, but it is a logarithmic scale that is looking at how much of the bacteria is reduced. So the easiest way I look at it is so the log reduction is the number of nines. So if it's a two log reduction, you have 99% kill rate. So it will kill 99% of your bacteria. If it's three logs, you have three nines, so 99.9. Um four logs is 99.99. You get all the way up to six logs, which is 99.9999% of a kill rate, which turns out to be you are killing one or all the bacteria of a million except for one. So, um it's the percent of reduction you're getting in your bacteria. So, that 99.9999, which is your six log reduction, means that there's only one left out of a million bacteria. >> How significant is that? I mean, 99% sounds pretty good to me. How how significant is all the all the extra nines? >> Uh pretty significant. If you had a million bacteria and you only killed 99% you'd still have 10,000 bacteria left on there. So, when you get to six log you have one bacteria left. If you're only doing 99% you still have 10,000 bacteria left on that device. So, um the nines don't sound like they matter, but they make a big deal at the end. >> All right. You convinced me. I think I'll I'll go with the six log. And and why is why is that what we talk about so much with high level disinfection? Why are we so concerned with six log when it comes to high level disinfection? >> Those are sort of the standards that have been set for set forward for us. Um so that's sort of the minimum that you have to do in order to be able to make uh claim with the FDA. Um they sort of picked a standard and that's what everybody sort of follows from there. >> It also relates back to the Spaulding classification from the CDC. So, our devices are considered again semi-critical devices. They're going into the body, but not into sterile areas of the body. So, that's why a six log reduction is okay and the one bacteria left on the device is okay because the area you're breathing right now, the water you're drinking, that has a little bit of bacteria in it right now, your body's used to dealing with that. If it was going into a sterile area, then you'd be looking at a critical medical device and then it wouldn't be necessarily a six log. You'd be looking for a complete kill of 100%. Um and that's where we get our semi-critical devices like our T probes or endocavity probes just need the six log reduction. >> Uh that that's great to bring up the Spaulding classifications because that's we talk about that a lot around here. What is semi-critical versus critical versus non-critical. Um so great call out there. So John, let's go back to you for a second and let's switch over to talking a little bit more about material compatibility. We talk about a that a lot here probably every day. And when we talk about material compatibility, what does that actually mean when we're talking about our our probes and what we're testing? >> Sure. So uh manufacturers will supply end of cavity probes to us um to determine if their materials are impacted by the disinfectant that we have uh created for use in our device. So um generally they want a certain number of cycles performed on their devices. Uh and because it's pretty labor intensive to just there run cycle after cycle, we have automated machines which will basically run 24/7 cycle after cycle after cycle until we've met the the required number by the manufacturer. Um so we have a suite of machines that are dedicated to running nothing but uh individual cycles on end of cavity probes for instance or T probes. Um and that saves us from having a person dedicated to a machine loading it, restarting the cycle, everything like that. >> So that's pretty cool. So now we're back to material compatibility. How does this process start? So say we have a new device and now we need to do material compatibility what with everything, right? Because we've got a new device. So how does this get started? >> So we'll we'll look at [clears throat] common materials that are used in probes across all sorts of different manufacturers and we'll test those materials. We'll also look at every single material that's in various fluid paths, whether it's the cleaner fluid path or the disinfectant fluid path inside our cleaner disinfectants or the disinfectants. And we'll test all of those in the lab with hours and hours or days and days of soaking um to check them. And then we'll also look at it in the automated machines running them many many times over and over again to look at these coupons or materials. And then finally we get to the point of after we're confident that the coupons are little uh squares and material are good and test well, then we can reach out to the manufacturers and say, hey, on this device. It's imminent for 510k or it's been cleared. We're having feedback from either your customers or we know different customers. We know we want it and then we'll work with the manufacturers to test their actual devices. And we have good working relationships with many of the ultrasound companies, so that hasn't been too much of a problem. >> Do you think there's misconceptions about the clearance process with some of our customers or how it all happens? I I know people will just kind of think it it all happens really quickly or magically. What what do you think that the customers or the end users think about how all this happens? >> So I know I've gotten some feedback from some people at different trade shows and I've kind of been shocked about what different people have said where they think that, you know, we send a device to the FDA and then the FDA does all the testing. Or the FDA has designed a device and then they send it to us to manufacture, but they've done everything with it. Um so there's definitely some confusion about how it works in the in the industry. Um but it's been it's been good to learn the whole process and go through the whole process and see it here over and over and over at CS Metals successfully. >> I think it's good that we do it all ourselves because we can see the good, the bad, everything. I mean, would you rather send it to the FDA to have them do it all ourselves? I mean, what what would you rather do? [laughter] Me to be less work, but I guess you never would really see what happens. >> Yeah. >> I I'm not sure why somebody would would think that I don't know. Again, they it just magically happens, I think, is is what our our customers think. But yeah, I think there's a lot of misconceptions about how the testing happens, how quickly it happens. I mean, like John said, it it has to run for hours and hours, sometimes weeks and weeks, right? Depending on how often we are are are how many cycles we're doing. So uh yeah, so it it it takes a while. Takes a lot of work. >> Yeah, and it's so a lot of it has to be real time. So we come out with a new disinfectant, we come out with a new cleaner. That has to go through stability studies and that's real time. Um you can't accelerate those with the US FDA. So if you want 24 months of claim stability, it's got to sit in bottles and we test it every month to see is it still stable after 24 months? And we have lots of opened, unopened bottles inside various stability chambers that we have. So a lot of this testing and new medical device development is years and years in the making. >> Yeah, I don't think anyone understands that at all. [laughter] So Don, what what would be the next step? So we get a new device or and now we have to do some probe testing on the new device. Does it come to you next or does it come to Don next or do you two work together on the next steps? >> Uh we work together on the next steps. Um it goes back and forth between us quite a bit. Um again, all the testing for FDA is not just one person, it's multiple departments. Um generally when the probe comes to us, we will write a report, um send it to the manufacturer, make sure they're on board with it. We take pictures ahead of time, we prep the probe, um John's team usually preps the machines and the disinfectants and then they all start running it, you know, and we'll test the chemistry every day or every so often just to make sure it's still running at um the right concentrations. Um once testing's done, then we, you know, start to take pictures, evaluate the probe, which John also does throughout the process. They're constantly checking the probe to make sure there's no damage. And then it goes back to the manufacturer for testing to make sure that the probe is functioning the way it's supposed to and there was no damage. And we sort of get that approval process wrapped up at that point once we make sure that we didn't damage it, they verify that. >> Don, how do you inspect the probe? >> Uh we do a visual inspection. Um if um we generally we're looking for material degradation, that's pretty obvious, or uh if the manufacturer um would say allows it, we can actually do an ingress protection test on it. So if they have a IPX rating of seven, which is waterproof to 1 m. We can actually uh replicate that testing here if the manufacturer wants that done. Uh but generally it's a visual inspection. >> Can you explain those IPX ratings? That was something new to me when when I started working here. Sorry to put you on the spot. >> Yeah, no problem. Um most medical devices that are going into a patient are going to be waterproof, so that's an IPX7. Uh IP is ingress protection. The X is generally filled with a number if you don't have a waterproof rating. So that would be that's your dust rating. So the so you could see something an IP 54 rating, which should be a five for dust and a four for water. Uh but if you're going to go waterproof, the most likely rating you'll see is an IPX seven. They don't test for dust, they'll test for water because that's a harsher condition. An IPX7 is waterproof to 1 m for half an hour. >> And what happens if during the process you start to inspect and you see something that you're not sure of? How do the three of you or the two of you work together to go back to the manufacturer and and reset or come up with something different to to go a different course? >> Like this. We'll uh we'll notify the customer, generally supply photographs like this is what we're seeing. Um ask them if they want an IPX test on it to see whether it's a compromised waterproofing or not. Um and then, you know, if if the customer or the manufacturer believes that it's not an issue, then we can continue the testing. Um but if that happens, you know, we would send it back to them if they want to perform testing. If they find it's fine, it'll come back and we'll continue the testing. But everything is upfront and as soon as we notice any damage or anything that could potentially be damaged, we'll notify them and have a conversation. >> Okay. So So lot of back and forth conversation with the manufacturers that we're working with, basically to make sure that everybody's on the same page and and we're talking a lot with them. >> Mhm. >> Okay. Now John, this question is is for you. Once we were finished, we send them their their report, they test, everything's fine. How quickly do we feel like the IFUs are are getting updated with with new approvals? Um it varies. Um sometimes it takes multiple months. Sometimes it's, you know, they're pretty quick. Smaller team, they can push it through, but a lot of times it has to go through their quality, their regulatory, and then it goes through, you know, their if it goes on their website, it takes a while for that to get uploaded. Um otherwise, if it's in, you know, manuals, by the time it goes through revisions and their quality, it can take months before we get approval or you see approval on the website or on the IFU. So a lot of times you just have to call the manufacturer to ask and they can give you that approval at that point. >> And I think this is important for end users to know because we're always saying check the IFUs. You need to see if the IFUs allow this. You need to make sure that everything's compatible, but sometimes the IFUs >> not up to >> have everything. And And that It's unfortunate, but it does mean you need to dig a little more. You need to check the IFUs, but if it's not there, maybe you do need to go to the manufacturer and ask or, you know, if it's one of our pieces of equipment, ask us cuz we may have that letter that you're talking about. So it it is important to ask a couple questions if you don't find it in the IFU, which I hate to say that because it you should just be able to look at the IFU, but I think we have learned that it doesn't happen immediately. And it definitely not immediately. [laughter] But it it will happen. Just everybody has their own timeline and their own priorities, so you do have to, you know, keep asking a little bit more. >> Yep. >> Um Kendall, back to you. If you could say one thing that you would like everybody, all end users to understand about this process that you feel like they don't know already, either 510K or material compatibility, what do you think that would be? >> Um, I would just want them to make sure they understand how much testing and validation work goes into the 510K process. not something to be taken lightly. It's not something where you hear this phrase, oh, substantially equivalent, um, and then that means it's okay, pretty much the same as anything else and yeah, it's good. Um, no, there's a lot of testing, there's a lot of validation, there's a lot of time and effort put into these devices that get cleared through the FDA. >> How about you, John? Do you feel like there's something from the engineering side that you wish people knew? >> Yeah, and it's may not be a typical engineer engineering answer, but um, we like to build to user requirements. I mean, having the user needs satisfied is what we're about. So we just don't think up something cool and do it. [clears throat] Um, if we meet the needs of the user, that's a successful product. So we're always thinking about that when we're working on the design, how is the user going to be using this particular device? Can they see the screen while they're doing something else, for instance? Uh, you know, just this is a it's not successful if the user can't use your device and use it well. >> Okay. Dawn, how about you? >> Yeah, um, I think, you know, a lot of times people think it's one or two lab tests, but it's not. There's multiple that we do. There's multiple groups we work with. We outsource a lot, but one of the biggest things that we do that is usually is we do clinicals, so we go on like into the hospital or clinics to actually test the product. So we are very thankful for our customers that we work with that let us come in and do that. So uh, it's a big help, but that's the last hurdle that we have to get through is doing testing offsite. It's not just lab testing, it's not just one group that does it. There's multiple groups that have to work together to get all the testing done. >> Now I know you gave us some things that you wish people understood about material compatibility. What do you wish people understood more about the 510K clearance process? >> Um, things to >> understand more about the 510k clearance process would just be to not think that because something is substantially equivalent to another device, it's the same as the other device. The FDA uses that as kind of a starting point and a reference point. They'll look at what testing was done and we don't necessarily know what testing was done with that other device. We have guidance documents to look at and we just have our own risk assessments and, you know, our own internal knowledge about what is safe and effective. So from there, it's really, you know, leaning on a lot of people's experience, Dawn's experience, John's experience, a lot of other people on our team who's worked with the FDA a lot to know, okay, these are the types of things we need to answer. These are the types of things that would make a device safe and effective. And then from there, going and executing. But they don't give you a exact list of everything that they want you to do. They'll give you guidance. They'll point you in directions, but you got to make sure that you've done adequate risk testing to make sure that the device is safe and effective. >> Awesome. I have one last question for everybody and with Thanksgiving coming up soon, I I hope that you guys are all very thankful with that for everything that we put into our 510k clearance process, our material compatibility. So I I want to ask each of you to give just one last kind of thought about what makes you thankful and confident on why you feel that way with our processes. What makes you feel confident when we send in something for 510k clearance or what makes you feel so confident when we say we've completed this material compatibility for our per process? What what makes you feel thankful and confident in what we do here? Dawn, I'll start with you. >> Yeah, I think because we've done the testing, we've proven it, we sought it for ourselves, we didn't send it to outside testing, so we know we saw the results. We saw it happen, but there's no, you know, human error. We automated it, so there's no human error and that the patient will be safe at the end and our product is top the line. Done? >> Uh for me, it's the entire product development process that we follow. Um FDA requires that you follow it you know a process and do what you say and say what you do. Um and we have a very robust product development process that we follow. So you know I'm thankful for that because I don't have to worry about did I miss this test? Is there something I didn't verify or not? We've done this enough times following our own processes that I'm I'm confident that when we bring a product to its conclusion that it's ready to go to the FDA. >> We'll finish with you, Kendall. >> I guess I'm most thankful for a lot of our end users and customers that have trusted us over the years. Um you know we've been in business for over 20 years at this point and they've seen us grow from just a disinfectant to now offering automated disinfectants for T probes and now automated cleaner disinfectants and automate cleaner disinfectants for endocavities and surface probes and that you place that trust in us to have a safe device for your facility. I really appreciate that so I'm very thankful for that. >> And with that we are wrapping up this episode of the No Risk podcast powered by CS Medical. Thank you so much for watching and thank you guys so much for being here. And if you'd like more information or you'd like to see some of our past episodes you can visit our website at csmedicalllc.com or wherever you stream your podcast. Thank you for watching. >> Now a message from CS Medical. >> Quick dry ultrasound drying cloth. Removing the unknown from your drying method. [music] The Centers for Disease Control, ultrasound probe manufacturers and high-level disinfectant manufacturers all recommend the thorough drying of an ultrasound probe [music] prior to high-level disinfection and at the conclusion of high-level disinfection. The purpose [music] of drying is different depending on the reprocessing step of the ultrasound probe. Drying after enzymatic cleaning and [music] rinse is recommended by reusable high-level disinfectant manufacturers to minimize the potential for dilution [music] of the chemistry that would directly affect the MRC and result in a shortened useful life. The drying method should be one that does not transfer other contaminants that would result in [music] disinfectant efficacy issues or potential damage to an automated reprocessor. Are you a medical device enthusiast, entrepreneur, or healthcare professional looking to navigate the complex world of regulatory approval? Look no further! In today's video, we're diving  into the Medical Device 510(k) process.

**🔍 What is the 510(k) Process?**

The 510(k) process is a critical step for getting your medical device approved by the FDA, ensuring it's safe and effective for patient use. Whether you're a startup founder or a seasoned professional, understanding this process is essential for bringing your innovation to market.

**🌟 Why Watch This Video?**
Whether you're a medical professional, an aspiring entrepreneur, or simply curious about the medical device industry, this video provides valuable insights. Our aim is to empower you with knowledge, ensuring you have a clear understanding of the 510(k) process and the tools to streamline your regulatory journey.

**🔔 Stay Updated and Engage!**
Don't forget to subscribe to our channel for more in-depth discussions on healthcare innovations, regulatory updates, and expert interviews. Hit the notification bell so you never miss an upload. Have questions or topics you'd like us to cover? Leave a comment below and join the conversation!

Join us on this educational journey as we unravel the complexities of the Medical Device 510(k) Process. Let's work together to make the world of healthcare innovation more accessible and understandable for everyone.

🌐 **Connect With Us:**
https://patientguard.com

If you are looking for Quality Assurance Templates to help you with your Quality Management System then head over to:

https://qmsregs.com

Thank you for tuning in! Let's revolutionize the medical device industry together. Stay tuned for more enlightening content, and until next time, stay curious and keep innovating! 🌟

metadata.title: Coffee and Q&A: When a Software Update Needs a New 510(k), FDA's Warning Letter to O.N. Diagnostics
metadata.author: Innolitics
metadata.shortDescription:
James Swink hosted Yujan Shrestha, J. David Giese and Mary Vater on LinkedIn Live on October 22, 2026, to discuss FDA's warning letter to O.N. Diagnostics, LLC (MARCS-CMS 730301). FDA issued the letter on September 1, 2026, and posted it on October 6, 2026.

In June 2024, O.N. Diagnostics shipped version 3.0.0 of its VirtuOst Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA) software without a new 510(k). The original device was cleared under K171435 on August 3, 2018, as a semi-automated tool with no machine learning. The letter names three changes in version 3.0.0 and says each one needed a new premarket notification: a new machine learning algorithm for vertebral landmarking, a move from a desktop application to a web-based architecture, and a technology platform migration. The letter also cites CAPA, supplier control and MDR procedure findings from a March 2026 inspection, and asks the company to stop distributing version 3.0.0.

The panel discusses how gaps between engineering and regulatory teams lead to unfiled changes, why adding or retraining an AI model can be a significant change, how to calibrate the 2017 software-change guidance flowchart to a company's risk tolerance, why companies avoid going back to FDA, and what a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) could have done here. Two audience questions close the session: PCCP examples for software in a medical device (SiMD), and whether a PCCP can go in a Special 510(k).

Corrections (also shown on screen as notes):
- K171435 was submitted in May 2017 and cleared on August 3, 2018. The clearance year is given as 2017 on air and on one slide.
- The cleared VirtuOst VFA used no machine learning. Version 3.0.0 added the ML algorithm.
- The letter describes a move from a desktop application to a web-based architecture. It does not use the word cloud.
- O.N. Diagnostics also holds K113725 (VirtuOst, 2012) and K220402 (VirtuOst, 2023). K171435 is its only VFA clearance.
- At 45:14, about 25 seconds of David's comment were lost in both the Zoom and the LinkedIn Live recordings, so the replay goes from his remark on FDA's new PCCP page to his point about FDA reviewers and PCCPs. The 15 seconds that follow come from the LinkedIn Live recording.

Speakers:
- Yujan Shrestha, MD: Partner and co-founder of Innolitics, physician and software engineer working on FDA strategy for AI medical devices
- J. David Giese: Partner and co-founder of Innolitics, biomedical engineer focused on FDA software rules and device cybersecurity
- Mary Vater: Director of Regulatory Affairs at Innolitics, focused on AI/ML software as a medical device
- James Swink (host): Principal Regulatory Specialist at Innolitics, 22 years at FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health

FDA warning letter to O.N. Diagnostics (CMS 730301):
https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/diagnostics-llc-730301-09012026

K171435 in the FDA 510(k) database:
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/pmn.cfm?ID=K171435

FDA's 2017 software-change guidance, annotated:
https://innolitics.com/articles/fda-guidance-deciding-when-to-submit-a-k-for-a-software-change-to-an-existing-device/

FDA Device Explorer, a free 510(k) and predicate search tool: https://fda.innolitics.com/

Innolitics newsletter: https://innolitics.com/newsletter/

Previous Coffee and Q&A, FDA's Generative AI Discussion Paper (October 8, 2026):
https://youtu.be/ADra_F3iU14

2:18 Meet the panel
4:57 Engineering and regulatory silos

11:19 O.N. Diagnostics and the VirtuOst VFA

metadata.title: How to Pick a Predicate Device for Your 510(k): Intended Use, Split Predicates & FDA Best Practices
metadata.author: Cleared 인허가 노트
metadata.shortDescription:
Every 510(k) is built on one comparison: your device, next to a legally marketed device called the predicate. This video walks through how to pick one, using the rule text and FDA's own guidance.

✅ FREE 510(k) Submission Checklist (5 pages, 44 checks)
https://clearedra.gumroad.com/l/510k-submission-checklist

📘 Field guide: FDA Registration & 510(k) Without a Consultant (155 pages)
https://clearedra.gumroad.com/l/fda-510k-without-a-consultant
📕 Also on Kindle: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HRVXR8S6

In this video: the three kinds of legally marketed devices that can serve as a predicate (21 CFR 807.92(a)(3)), the substantial equivalence test (21 CFR 807.100(b)), intended use vs. indications for use, why FDA's 2014 guidance calls a “split predicate” inconsistent with the 510(k) regulatory standard, when multiple predicates and reference devices are used, where to search for candidates, and the four best practices in FDA's 2023 draft guidance (a draft, not for implementation).

How did you pick your last predicate? Tell us in the comments.

🎙 AI narration · script written and checked by a human regulatory professional

Chapters
00:00 Intro
00:52 What counts as a predicate (21 CFR 807.92(a)(3))
01:24 The test FDA uses (21 CFR 807.100(b))
02:03 Intended use vs. indications for use
02:33 Split predicates, multiple predicates, reference devices
03:28 Where to find candidates
04:01 FDA's draft best practices (2023)
04:52 Checklist
05:17 Free checklist & field guide

Sources (checked 11/14/2026)
· 21 CFR 807.92, Content and format of a 510(k) summary (eCFR, current) — ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-807.92
· 21 CFR 807.100, FDA action on a premarket notification (eCFR, current) — ecfr.gov/current/title-21/section-807.100
· FDA guidance (final, July 2014), The 510(k) Program: Evaluating Substantial Equivalence in Premarket Notifications [510(k)] — fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/510k-program-evaluating-substantial-equivalence-premarket-notifications-510k
· FDA DRAFT guidance (September 2023, not for implementation), Best Practices for Selecting a Predicate Device to Support a Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submission — fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/best-practices-selecting-predicate-device-support-premarket-notification-510k-submission
· FDA 510(k) Premarket Notification database — accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfpmn/pmn.cfm
※ Rules and guidance change, and a draft guidance can change before it is finalized. Always check the current eCFR text and FDA's current guidance before you act. FDA decides substantial equivalence for each submission.

General information only, not regulatory or legal advice for your device.
