metadata.title: S2 E8 – MRI Quench Pipes: Engineering Challenges and Safety Solutions
metadata.author: FGI
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, Toby Gilk returns to discuss the intriguing and complex world of MRI technology. Learn about the role of superconductivity in MRI machines, the potential hazards of quench pipes, and the importance of proper design to prevent catastrophic failures. Toby explains how superconductivity allows MRI machines to operate efficiently without continuous power but also introduces risks if not managed correctly. Hear about real-world examples of quench pipe failures and the engineering solutions that mitigate these dangers, and gain insights into the latest advancements in MRI technology and how they impact safety protocols in healthcare facilities.
 

 
 

Sponsored by: 
 

American Society for Health Care Engineering (ASHE): (https://www.ashe.org/)  Optimizing health care facilities 
 

 
 

 
 

Link to show notes: https://fgiguidelines.org/podcast/s2-e8-mri-quench-pipes-engineering-challenges-and-safety-solutions (https://fgiguidelines.org/?post_type=podcast&p=15827) 
 

Learn more about AIA self-reporting LUs: https://fgiguidelines.org/aia-self-reporting-lus/ 
 

Connect with us on LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/company/facility-guidelines-institute-inc)

metadata.title: Software License Trap: Audits, Fees, Control
metadata.author: Hidden Industries
metadata.shortDescription:
Inside corporate software licensing: audits, shadow fees, and the lock-in machinery that controls critical systems. Real cases, hard numbers, and the hidden playbook vendors use.

#TechSecrets #CorporateMonopolies #HiddenIndustries

Disclaimer: All visual elements used in this video are legally sourced and heavily edited to create original, transformative educational content under Fair Use.

segments.text: 2:00 a.m. Midwest hospital gets an
Oracle audit email.
Support access flagged, 30 days to prove
licenses or pay seven figures.
ICU dashboards blink, the night shift
freezes.
a theory.
Real patients, [music] live systems, a
countdown.
A single clause in a license,
virtualization misapplied.
One checkbox during a rushed [music]
install triggered the threat.
The CIO calls legal, finance, vendor
relations.
Server racks hum, database logs scroll,
and a whiteboard fills with versions,
cores, [music]
and user counts they never track
precisely.
This is the hidden world of software
licensing.
Contracts that [music] decide who works,
who waits, and who pays when your
critical system breathes through someone
else's terms. [music]
Hospitals, courts, airlines, every
sector runs on paid permissions.
Miss one audit clause, and your day
becomes invoices, screenshots, and
overnight patches to [music] avoid
service denial.
Hidden lever is ambiguity.
Per core, per user, per [music] device,
per processor, each priced differently,
each audited differently, and each
changed quietly across product versions.
A hospital case ends without shutdown.
A negotiated settlement, maintenance
locked for three years, and a migration
[music] plan they did not want, but
cheaper than court.
Multiply that across thousands of firms.
That's the revenue engine nobody
advertises.
The audit pipeline feeds sales targets
quarter after quarter.
Chapter one resets.
Let's decode the license maze that fuels
this machine.
How the terms are written and why they
are hard to count.
Per core licensing sounds simple.
Count CPU cores, pay per core.
Then virtualization arrives.
Now count virtual sockets, capped cores,
cluster nodes, failover pairs, if
permitted.
Per user model split further.
Named user, concurrent user, active
user, external user.
One misclassified contractor and your
compliance delta explodes during [music]
audit season.
Thin device-based.
Thin clients multiply counts.
Shared kiosks blur identities.
VDI farms shift sessions across hosts
while the contract insists every
endpoint be licensed.
Cloud credits promise flexibility.
Real [music] bills track vCPU, RAM
hours, IOPS, data egress, region
uplifts, and enterprise [music]
agreements bundle cloudy workloads with
on-prem terms.
Hot terms to know: soft partitioning
bands, subcapacity, secondary use
rights, indirect access, multiplexing.
Each a switch that turns normal usage
into billable exposure.
Audits ignite from three sparks: support
tickets, partner tips, [music]
telemetry.
An odd spike in users, an integration
discovered, or a sales slump triggers an
informal review.
Once started, the calendar tightens.
10 business days for data, 30 for
remediation, then a true-up invoice.
Discounts vanish, penalties do not.
Now the audit playbook.
Real tactics vendors use [music] and the
negotiation patterns that shape
outcomes, often before your IT team even
joins the call.
Tactic one: scope creep.
Start with two products, end with the
entire stack.
A friendly data clarification email adds
components [music] you never meant to
discuss.
Tactic two: tool bias.
Approved discovery tools [music] scan
endpoints, miss offline hosts, and
guesstimate users high.
Vendors insist their tool is
authoritative.
Yours is informational.
Tactic three: indirect access.
A portal, bot, or API touches licensed
data.
Now every person behind that system is
counted as a user, even without direct
login.
Tactic four: time pressure.
Quarter-end threats, expiring discounts,
escalations to regional VPs.
The discount grows if sign now, and the
penalty grows if you do not.
Negotiation reality, audits rarely end
at list price.
They end with bundles, maintenance
lock-ins, [music] and migration credits
that steer your roadmap toward one
platform.
Legal edge, most contracts allow
self-audit rights, cure periods, and
dispute windows.
If you control data release order, you
control the narrative and the invoice.
Next, the shelfware trap and the
reseller triangle,
where seats are sold and used and
endlessly renewed [music]
without anyone raising a flag until
budget screen.
Shelfware lives in spreadsheets.
10,000 seats bought during a merger.
4,000 deployed.
6,000 renew each year because the

Back-end rebates [music] reward certain
bundles.
The free add-on increases maintenance by
20% [music]
for 3 years.
The bill hides in fine print.
SAM tools promise clarity.
Some report risks accurately.
Others over-report to drive services.
Question their assumptions, sources, and
coverage before they become your audit
evidence.
Support leverage gets sharp.
Miss maintenance, lose patches.
Lose patches, fail audits.
Fail audits, face back maintenance plus
penalties.
If you ran that factory, would you risk
it?
Security risk rides along.
Unlicensed components skip updates.
A known CVE stays open.
A breach follows.
The forensic bill dwarfs the license fee
you argued over.
Meanwhile, finance seeks predictability.
[music]
Vendors offer unlimited agreements.
Sounds easy.
Reality, a grace period ends, counts
freeze high, and the renewal locks the
peak forever.
Operational impact is concrete.
A port delay deploying scanners for 3
weeks during an audit freeze.
Containers stacked, drivers waited, and
fines hit the schedule.
Now the counterplay.
Tactical steps companies used to cut
exposure, cut shelf ware, and turn
audits into controlled events instead of
budget disasters.
Inventory is step one.
Hardware, VMs, users, [music]
contractors.
Tag systems by environment and business
unit.
Tie every install to a [music] purchase
order and a named owner.
Contract hygiene next.
Ban soft partitioning clauses where
possible.
Add audit notice limits, capped
penalties, [music] and vendor tool
approval.
Put cure periods in bold.
Architect for compliance.
Segment virtual clusters.
Pin licensed workloads to hosts.
Use license affinity rules.
Log admin changes that could inflate
counts accidentally.
Create a red team for audits.
Legal, procurement, ITM, security.
One intake email.
A script for data release.
A calendar that buys time without
hostility.
Pull shelf ware fast.
Reharvest named users quarterly.
Disable dormant [music] accounts.
Retire duplicate tools.
Redirect spend into buyout clauses that
remove risky [music] bundles.
One manufacturer fought an SAP claim
down by 80%.
They proved indirect access was cached,
not stored.
Logs, architecture diagrams, and sworn
admin notes won the day.
Another firm prepaid cloud credits
[music] wisely.
They fenced workloads, tracked egress by
team, and cut untagged resources [music]
weekly.
Renewal time arrived. Their usage graph
dropped, not spiked.
Factory avoided a midnight shutdown by
isolating backup nodes.
Failover rights were limited, but
documented drills proved compliance.
Vendor backed down after council
reviewed logs.
Final check.
When a license [music] decides who works
tomorrow, do you want price or control?
If it were your payroll, your port, your
ICU, how would you defend it?

metadata.title: Secondary Use: Can Your Clinic License Its Data?
metadata.author: AI Training Data Broker
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to know what your clinic's data is worth? Try our data value calculator: an estimate, not a final offer. https://AITrainingDataBroker.com/tools/data-value-calculator/

An AI lab asks a clinic for a sample of its de-identified visit notes, and then asks one question: which contract lets you use this data for AI training? When nobody knows, the deal stops. This video explains secondary use, where the limits sit, and what to bring to the first call.

Q: What is primary use and what is secondary use?
Caring for patients is the primary use: treatment, payment and running the practice (HIPAA Privacy Rule, 45 CFR 164.506). Research, quality studies and training an AI model are secondary uses. A secondary use clause is the line in a contract that says which of those uses are allowed, and who may do them.

Q: Where can a limit sit?
In your EHR or practice software contract, in the business associate agreements you signed, in your patient forms, privacy notice and study consent forms, in your hospital network, lab and insurer contracts, and in HIPAA and your state's rules.

Q: I run a clinic. Where do I start?
With the data rights section of your software contract: who controls the data, what the vendor may do with it, and whether you can export all of it. What clinic data AI labs look for: https://AITrainingDataBroker.com/sell/healthcare-practices/

Q: I run a health software company. Can I license my customers' data?
Only as each business associate agreement allows (45 CFR 164.502(a)(3)). How this works for health software: https://AITrainingDataBroker.com/sell/health-tech-companies/

Q: How is patient data made safe to license?

segments.text: An AI lab likes a clinic's de-identified visit notes and asks for a sample.
Then its lawyer asks for one question, which contract lets you use this
data for AI training? Nobody at the clinic knows, so the deal stops right
there. Most clinic owners think HIPAA, the federal health privacy law
from 1996, is the hard part of a health data deal.
But often the deal waits on the contract the clinic signed years ago,
such as the one with its software vendor.
That contract has a clause about secondary use, and it is easy to miss.
While nobody can answer, the AI lab will not move, and the weeks go by.
So let us start with what secondary use means.
First, your clinic collects patient data to care for patients, and that
is the primary use. According to the HIPAA Privacy Rule section 164.506,
a clinic may use that data for its own treatment, payment, and day-to
-day operations. Anything else is a secondary use, such as research, a
quality study, or training an AI model.
A secondary use clause is a line in a contract that says which of those
uses are allowed, and that line can sit in more than one place.
So, there are five places to look. First, come to your software contract,
the agreement you signed with a vendor that handles patient data, and the
forms your patients signed. Then, come to your network and insurer contracts,
and the privacy laws, both federal and the state.
Any one of them can say no, so an AI lab will usually ask about each one
before it signs. The first one is the contract for your electronic health
record, the software that holds your charts.
In September 2016, the US health IT office, ONC, published a guide to these
contracts. It warned that many standard contracts give vendors a very broad
right to use and make money from your data.
Its sample clause goes to the other way, the vendor may use your data only
to do the work in the contract. So, check who controls the data and whether
you can export all of it. Now, flip it around, because some of you run
a health software company, not a clinic.
If you handle patient data for clinics, HIPAA calls you a business associate,
and you sign an agreement with each clinic.
The same federal rule in section 164.502 says a business associate may
use that data only as its agreement allows.
So, the data your clinic sends you is not yours to license, unless each
agreement says so. Next, look at the forms your patients signed, and at
your privacy notice. Those papers can promise more than the law asks,
such as never sharing your data for research.
Patients will hold you to a promise like that, even when the data is de
-identified. And, if some patients join the study, its consent form limits
that data to the study. Then, come to the contract with your hospital network,
your lab partners, and the insurers that pay you.
Many keep their terms private, and data you get through a shared network
often comes with its own use rules. So, this will not fit every clinic.
If your clinic runs inside a hospital system, the data may not be yours
to license at all. And the last comes the privacy laws.
Another line of section 164.502 lets a clinic de-identify
its own patient data, or have a business associate to do it for that purpose.
We de-identify your data, which means we strip out the names, birth dates,
addresses, and the chart numbers before anything leaves the clinic.
Some states add their own rules on top, so your state matters too.
The patient names are never licensed to an AI lab, and the rest is handled
within the privacy rules that apply to it.
So, why do so many health data deals stall?
Because the questions come one at a time.
After the AI lab is interested, each one waits for someone to find a contract.
A deal will not move fast unless the clinic has the answer before the first
call. When it does, the AI lab can go straight to the data.
Before you talk to any AI lab, bring four documents to the first call.
Bring your software contract with a line about how data may be used, marked,
and every business associate agreement you have signed.
Then add your patient forms, your privacy notice, and any study consent
forms, plus your network and insurer contracts.
A health lawyer should read these clauses with you because one word can
change what is allowed. You may be wondering what part of your data an
AI lab could license once those documents say yes.
Often, it is the work around care: de-identified visit notes, referral
letters, care plans, and the steps the front desk follows to book and bill.
Patient names, contact details, and anything a contract forbids cannot
be licensed, and they stay private. So, which clause does your clinic have,
and what would they allow? That is where I come in.
I'm Jimmy. I have worked in data at Fortune 500 companies as a data analyst,
a data engineer, and a software engineer.
And I am trained in data science. I am also a Canadian military veteran
specializing in data analysis and reporting.
As your broker, I help you create relationships with AI labs and bring
back their offers so you can compare the price and terms before you decide.
As your technical advisor, I guide your team through what to export, the
format, the de-identification, and compliance.
I work on commission only, paid by the AI labs.
If you are buying data for an AI lab, I find the right data for you and
see it through to delivery so you can focus on AI research.
In health data, the contract decides before the AI lab does, so find your
secondary use clauses first. More on licensing health data at AITrainingDataBroker.com.
Thank you for watching, and I'll see you next time.

metadata.title: The FDA MAUDE Database.  Who is reporting and how good are the reports.
metadata.author: Health Watch USA
metadata.shortDescription:
Lindsay Calderon describes the reporting requirements for the MAUDE Database and who is making the reports.  Over 96% of reports are filed directly to the FDA by the manufacturer.  Physicians file very few reports directly to the FDA, less than nurses and patients.  Over all the reports were unstructured and a small minority of reports contained truly clinically useful data.   Health Watch USA(sm) Conference Presentation Oct. 17, 2019.
View Article:  https://www.dovepress.com/articles.php?article_id=46767

metadata.title: Case Study: How is My Medical Device Classified?
metadata.author: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
metadata.shortDescription: This CDRH Learn module provides an illustrative example of how you can determine the class of an FDA regulated medical device. Determining how a medical device is classified is instrumental in understanding and identifying the appropriate regulatory requirements for a device.  To view more medical device educational resources please visit https://www.fda.gov/training-and-continuing-education/cdrh-learn
keywords: Center for Devices and Radiological Health

segments.text: Hello, my name is Commander Kimberly
Piermatteo of the United States Public Health
Service and I am a Consumer Safety Officer
within the Center for Devices and Radiological
Health's Division of Industry and Consumer
Education at FDA.
Welcome to CDRH learn, CDRH's resource for
multimedia industry education.
Within this CDRH Learn module I will provide you
will an illustrative example of how you can
determine the class of a medical device using three
different determination methods.
Determining how a medical device is classified is
instrumental in understanding and
identifying with the appropriate regulatory
requirements for a device.
This module is a companion module to the CDRH Learn
module titled “How is my medical device
classified?”
If you have not done so already, please review
this module first before proceeding to watch this
case study module.
Before I begin the case study, I'd like to review
a few points made in the companion module.
First, medical devices are classified based on risk.
Medical devices may be classified as class I,
class II or class III.
Second, the risk of the device determines the
extent of regulatory controls.
And lastly, there may be an applicable premarket
submission type for a device unless exempt.
The table displayed on this slide was discussed
in detail within the companion module, and I
have provided it again here as it provides an
overview of the medical device classes and their
applicable regulatory requirements.
The following learning objectives will be
addressed within this case study.
I will describe three different classification
determination methods.
The methods are, one, search for an appropriate
product classification, two, search for a similar
device by clearance or approval and three, search
for a similar device by device listing.
For this case study I'm going to use a traction
device as my example.
The intended use of this traction device is to
treat low back pain through intermittent and
static traction.
As I mentioned when determining a device's
product classification, there are three methods
that I recommend.
The first is to directly search for the appropriate
product classification.
I'll refer to this as method 1 and this is the
most common method used.
A second method, or method 2, is to search for a
similar device by its clearance or approval.
And lastly, method 3 is to search for a similar
device by device listing.
I'm going to walk through how to conduct each of
these search methods over the next several slides.
First, we will look at method 1.
To search for an applicable product
classification, I will be searching the FDA's public
product classification database.
A screen shot of the product classification
database is provided on this slide.
You may search the various fields provided; however,
I recommend you go to the quick search feature which
is circled in red on this slide.
From the quick search you can search using a key
word.
For this example, I'm going to search using the
key word traction.
I would enter the key word in the search field and
select search.
I could conduct multiple searches using other
words, but I feel this one most appropriately
describes the example device.
When searching the product classification database,
remember to conduct multiple searches using a
variety of key terms so that you ensure you
capture as many potentially related
product classifications which you can then narrow
down.
Keep in mind spelling matters and I suggest you
avoid plurals and don't be too specific as this will
limit your results.
On this slide, you will see a screen shot of my
quick search results using the key word traction.
Circled in red at the top left of the screen shot
shows that I am displaying 1 of 11 results.
The default display setting for this database
is 10 results, so if you wish to expand the number
of results displayed per page, you can select the
drop down circled in blue at the top right of the
screen shot to change the number of results
displayed per page.
For this example, I have chosen to display 100
results.
There are 11 results, which is not too many, so
I could review each product classification to
determine if it applies to my traction device, or I
could further define the intended use of the
traction device so that I can narrow down the
results even faster.
For this example, I'm going to clarify the
intended use of the traction device to
indicate that it is a powered traction device.
Now looking at the results, I see there is a
product classification for a non-powered traction
apparatus, highlighted in yellow on the slide, but
then there is a more applicable powered
traction equipment highlighted in green
below.
Therefore, the ITH product code looks to be more
applicable to my powered traction device.
I'm going to take a further look at this
product code to confirm whether the ITH product
code appropriately describes my device.
This next slide displays a screen shot of the product
classification information for the ITH product code.
At this point, I want to ensure this product code
and the associated regulation number, 21 CFR
or code of federal regulations, 890.5900,
appropriately describes my powered traction device.
Therefore, I'm going to select the hyperlink for
the regulation number to further review the
description.
I have highlighted the regulation number I'm
going to select in the black box and orange arrow
on this slide.
The regulation description states - “Powered traction
equipment consists of powered devices intended
for medical purposes for use in conjunction with
traction accessories, such as belts and harnesses, to
exert therapeutic pulling forces on the patient's
body.” Based on this regulation description, I
believe this would be the most appropriate
regulation for the traction device in my
example, as well as the ITH product code seems to
be the most appropriate.
Going back to the screen shot for the ITH product
code in the public Product Classification database, I
can then determine what regulatory requirements
apply to this powered traction device.
I can see on the screen that the submission type
for a powered traction equipment device is
510(k), which is highlighted in yellow on
this slide.
This means I would need to obtain 510(k) clearance
prior to marketing this device.
Additionally, this device type is considered to be
class two, which means general controls apply as
well.
If there were any special controls for this device
type I would have been able to review them as
part of the regulation description.
Next, I'm going to discuss method 2, which is to
search for a similar device by its clearance or
approval.
Using method 2, I will demonstrate that I will
come to the same conclusion as Method 1 by
determining that the ITH product code is the most
appropriate for a powered traction device.
Using method 2, I can search for a similar
device by 510(k) clearance or PMA approval.
For this method it is important to note, I would
only be able to search for devices which have
received FDA 510(k) clearance or PMA approval.
Since most class I devices are exempt from 510(k), I
would not be able to find them by using this method.
One note I'd like to make is regarding De Novo
applications.
The De Novo pathway provides a possible route
to classify novel devices of low to moderate risk.
If you think a similar device to your own was the
first new, novel device type, then this first
marketing authorization would not be found in the
510(k) clearance database.
You would need to search the De Novo database to
find this first classified device under the newly
created regulation.
To find a 510(k) cleared or PMA approved device you
can search the respective public databases using the
hyperlinks provided on this slide.
The powered traction device, in this example,
is not life supporting or life sustaining, so I can
presume that it is likely not considered high risk,
so I wouldn't need to search the PMA database
for a similar device.
Additionally, I do not believe powered traction
devices are new or novel, therefore, I'm not going
to search the De Novo database either.
I'm going to proceed and search the 510(k)
clearance database to see if I can find the similar
device I'm looking for.
On this slide, I've provided a screen shot of
the public 510(k) clearance database.
The Advanced Search is the default, but there is also
a Quick Search available which is circled in red at
the bottom of the screen shot.
Within the Advanced Search, there are many
fields you may search, but I find the Quick Search to
be more helpful in identifying a wide range
of results which I can then narrow down myself.
In order to steer this example even further, I'm
going to state that I'm looking for a similar
device called the Digit-trac 930.
So, let's take a closer look and see if this
similar device has a 510(k) clearance which I
can review, and then determine how it has been
classified to ultimately determine if the same
classification applies to my traction device.
Within the Quick Search of the 510(k) clearance
database, which is pictured on this slide, I
still want to keep my search broad to capture as
many results as possible, so I'm going to enter the
word “traction” in the search box.
The screen shot provided on this slide shows that
by searching the key word “traction”, I obtained 93
results, which I've circled in red at the top
left and the first 14 results are displayed.
Note, I conducted this search in July of 2019,
therefore, if you were to conduct a similar search
after this date, you may obtain different results
if a more recent device received 510(k) clearance.
For this example, I said I'm looking for the
similar device called the Digit-trac 930.
After reviewing the first few results I can see, as
I've highlighted in green on the screen, I was able
to find a device called the “traction system,
digit-trac 930.”
In order to review more information about this
510(k) clearance, I could either select the device
name hyperlink or the 510(k) number hyperlink.
I'm going to select the 510(k) number K052453 as
identified by the green arrow on this slide.
This slide shows detailed information about the
510(k) that I selected for the Digit-trac 930.
I can see this type of device was cleared under
the regulation number 21 CFR 890.5900 and product
code ITH, as highlighted in red on this slide.
If I want, I can review more information about the
regulation and product code by selecting the
respective hyperlinks which will take me to the
product classification database results that I
viewed previously under method 1.
After reviewing this information, I could then
determine if this regulation and product
code appropriately describe my traction
device.
And then I could determine what the regulatory
requirements are, such as for the ITH product code a
510(k) clearance is required.
I could also review the 510(k) summary for the
digit-trac 930 to obtain more information on this
device's intended use, to ensure this is the similar
device I am was originally searching for.
A hyperlink to the 510(k) summary is highlighted in
green on this slide.
The last method I recommend for determining
the appropriate product classification for a
device is method 3, which is to search for a similar
device by device listing.
This method is useful because establishment
registration and device listing are a general
control, which means all medical device
manufacturers currently marketing a device in the
U.S.
must be registered and their devices listed.
So, if I know of a similar device currently being
marketed, I can search for it by its listing and see
if the same product classification then
applies to my example device.
A screen shot of the FDA's public Establishment
Registration and Device Listing database is
provided on this slide.
Again, the default is the Advanced Search which
allows me to search by establishment or trade
name, or I could search by key word, again using the
Quick Search.
I'm going to use the Quick Search.
This slide shows the Quick Search for the
Establishment Registration and Device Listing
database.
The Quick Search for this database is very similar
to the Quick Searches in the other public databases
I used for the previous methods.
I'm going to also search using the key word
“traction”, as circled in red on this slide, to see
what device listings I can find.
By searching using the key word “traction”, I
obtained 22 results, as circled in blue on this
slide.
Remember, I'm looking for the similar device called
the digit-trac 930, so if I review my results, I
eventually see that there is a digit-trac 930
powered traction equipment listed by the company Ever

highlighted in red.
If I select the establishment name, this

videos.full_text: Hello, my name is Commander Kimberly Piermatteo of the United States Public Health Service and I am a Consumer Safety Officer within the Center for Devices and Radiological Health's Division of Industry and Consumer Education at FDA. Welcome to CDRH learn, CDRH's resource for multimedia industry education. Within this CDRH Learn module I will provide you will an illustrative example of how you can determine the class of a medical device using three different determination methods. Determining how a medical device is classified is instrumental in understanding and identifying with the appropriate regulatory requirements for a device. This module is a companion module to the CDRH Learn module titled “How is my medical device classified?” If you have not done so already, please review this module first before proceeding to watch this case study module. Before I begin the case study, I'd like to review a few points made in the companion module. First, medical devices are classified based on risk. Medical devices may be classified as class I, class II or class III. Second, the risk of the device determines the extent of regulatory controls. And lastly, there may be an applicable premarket submission type for a device unless exempt. The table displayed on this slide was discussed in detail within the companion module, and I have provided it again here as it provides an overview of the medical device classes and their applicable regulatory requirements. The following learning objectives will be addressed within this case study. I will describe three different classification determination methods. The methods are, one, search for an appropriate product classification, two, search for a similar device by clearance or approval and three, search for a similar device by device listing. For this case study I'm going to use a traction device as my example. The intended use of this traction device is to treat low back pain through intermittent and static traction. As I mentioned when determining a device's product classification, there are three methods that I recommend. The first is to directly search for the appropriate product classification. I'll refer to this as method 1 and this is the most common method used. A second method, or method 2, is to search for a similar device by its clearance or approval. And lastly, method 3 is to search for a similar device by device listing. I'm going to walk through how to conduct each of these search methods over the next several slides. First, we will look at method 1. To search for an applicable product classification, I will be searching the FDA's public product classification database. A screen shot of the product classification database is provided on this slide. You may search the various fields provided; however, I recommend you go to the quick search feature which is circled in red on this slide. From the quick search you can search using a key word. For this example, I'm going to search using the key word traction. I would enter the key word in the search field and select search. I could conduct multiple searches using other words, but I feel this one most appropriately describes the example device. When searching the product classification database, remember to conduct multiple searches using a variety of key terms so that you ensure you capture as many potentially related product classifications which you can then narrow down. Keep in mind spelling matters and I suggest you avoid plurals and don't be too specific as this will limit your results. On this slide, you will see a screen shot of my quick search results using the key word traction. Circled in red at the top left of the screen shot shows that I am displaying 1 of 11 results. The default display setting for this database is 10 results, so if you wish to expand the number of results displayed per page, you can select the drop down circled in blue at the top right of the screen shot to change the number of results displayed per page. For this example, I have chosen to display 100 results. There are 11 results, which is not too many, so I could review each product classification to determine if it applies to my traction device, or I could further define the intended use of the traction device so that I can narrow down the results even faster. For this example, I'm going to clarify the intended use of the traction device to indicate that it is a powered traction device. Now looking at the results, I see there is a product classification for a non-powered traction apparatus, highlighted in yellow on the slide, but then there is a more applicable powered traction equipment highlighted in green below. Therefore, the ITH product code looks to be more applicable to my powered traction device. I'm going to take a further look at this product code to confirm whether the ITH product code appropriately describes my device. This next slide displays a screen shot of the product classification information for the ITH product code. At this point, I want to ensure this product code and the associated regulation number, 21 CFR or code of federal regulations, 890.5900, appropriately describes my powered traction device. Therefore, I'm going to select the hyperlink for the regulation number to further review the description. I have highlighted the regulation number I'm going to select in the black box and orange arrow on this slide. The regulation description states - “Powered traction equipment consists of powered devices intended for medical purposes for use in conjunction with traction accessories, such as belts and harnesses, to exert therapeutic pulling forces on the patient's body.” Based on this regulation description, I believe this would be the most appropriate regulation for the traction device in my example, as well as the ITH product code seems to be the most appropriate. Going back to the screen shot for the ITH product code in the public Product Classification database, I can then determine what regulatory requirements apply to this powered traction device. I can see on the screen that the submission type for a powered traction equipment device is 510(k), which is highlighted in yellow on this slide. This means I would need to obtain 510(k) clearance prior to marketing this device. Additionally, this device type is considered to be class two, which means general controls apply as well. If there were any special controls for this device type I would have been able to review them as part of the regulation description. Next, I'm going to discuss method 2, which is to search for a similar device by its clearance or approval. Using method 2, I will demonstrate that I will come to the same conclusion as Method 1 by determining that the ITH product code is the most appropriate for a powered traction device. Using method 2, I can search for a similar device by 510(k) clearance or PMA approval. For this method it is important to note, I would only be able to search for devices which have received FDA 510(k) clearance or PMA approval. Since most class I devices are exempt from 510(k), I would not be able to find them by using this method. One note I'd like to make is regarding De Novo applications. The De Novo pathway provides a possible route to classify novel devices of low to moderate risk. If you think a similar device to your own was the first new, novel device type, then this first marketing authorization would not be found in the 510(k) clearance database. You would need to search the De Novo database to find this first classified device under the newly created regulation. To find a 510(k) cleared or PMA approved device you can search the respective public databases using the hyperlinks provided on this slide. The powered traction device, in this example, is not life supporting or life sustaining, so I can presume that it is likely not considered high risk, so I wouldn't need to search the PMA database for a similar device. Additionally, I do not believe powered traction devices are new or novel, therefore, I'm not going to search the De Novo database either. I'm going to proceed and search the 510(k) clearance database to see if I can find the similar device I'm looking for. On this slide, I've provided a screen shot of the public 510(k) clearance database. The Advanced Search is the default, but there is also a Quick Search available which is circled in red at the bottom of the screen shot. Within the Advanced Search, there are many fields you may search, but I find the Quick Search to be more helpful in identifying a wide range of results which I can then narrow down myself. In order to steer this example even further, I'm going to state that I'm looking for a similar device called the Digit-trac 930. So, let's take a closer look and see if this similar device has a 510(k) clearance which I can review, and then determine how it has been classified to ultimately determine if the same classification applies to my traction device. Within the Quick Search of the 510(k) clearance database, which is pictured on this slide, I still want to keep my search broad to capture as many results as possible, so I'm going to enter the word “traction” in the search box. The screen shot provided on this slide shows that by searching the key word “traction”, I obtained 93 results, which I've circled in red at the top left and the first 14 results are displayed. Note, I conducted this search in July of 2019, therefore, if you were to conduct a similar search after this date, you may obtain different results if a more recent device received 510(k) clearance. For this example, I said I'm looking for the similar device called the Digit-trac 930. After reviewing the first few results I can see, as I've highlighted in green on the screen, I was able to find a device called the “traction system, digit-trac 930.” In order to review more information about this 510(k) clearance, I could either select the device name hyperlink or the 510(k) number hyperlink. I'm going to select the 510(k) number K052453 as identified by the green arrow on this slide. This slide shows detailed information about the 510(k) that I selected for the Digit-trac 930. I can see this type of device was cleared under the regulation number 21 CFR 890.5900 and product code ITH, as highlighted in red on this slide. If I want, I can review more information about the regulation and product code by selecting the respective hyperlinks which will take me to the product classification database results that I viewed previously under method 1. After reviewing this information, I could then determine if this regulation and product code appropriately describe my traction device. And then I could determine what the regulatory requirements are, such as for the ITH product code a 510(k) clearance is required. I could also review the 510(k) summary for the digit-trac 930 to obtain more information on this device's intended use, to ensure this is the similar device I am was originally searching for. A hyperlink to the 510(k) summary is highlighted in green on this slide. The last method I recommend for determining the appropriate product classification for a device is method 3, which is to search for a similar device by device listing. This method is useful because establishment registration and device listing are a general control, which means all medical device manufacturers currently marketing a device in the U.S. must be registered and their devices listed. So, if I know of a similar device currently being marketed, I can search for it by its listing and see if the same product classification then applies to my example device. A screen shot of the FDA's public Establishment Registration and Device Listing database is provided on this slide. Again, the default is the Advanced Search which allows me to search by establishment or trade name, or I could search by key word, again using the Quick Search. I'm going to use the Quick Search. This slide shows the Quick Search for the Establishment Registration and Device Listing database. The Quick Search for this database is very similar to the Quick Searches in the other public databases I used for the previous methods. I'm going to also search using the key word “traction”, as circled in red on this slide, to see what device listings I can find. By searching using the key word “traction”, I obtained 22 results, as circled in blue on this slide. Remember, I'm looking for the similar device called the digit-trac 930, so if I review my results, I eventually see that there is a digit-trac 930 powered traction equipment listed by the company Ever Prosperous instrument, incorporated, which I've highlighted in red. If I select the establishment name, this will take me to information about the establishment's registration. But I want to know more about the device and see how it is classified, so I'm going to select the product name, as indicated by the green arrow on this slide. Under this device listing, I can review information about how this device has been classified to determine if the same classification applies to my device example. Highlighted in red, I can see the digit-trac 930 falls under the product code ITH, it is class two, and the applicable regulation is 21 CFR 890.5900. This is the same classification information I was able to find by searching the two previous methods. If I want to review more details about this device type and classification I could, again, select the hyperlink to the ITH product code or hyperlink to the regulation number. I could also select the 510(k) number, which is highlighted in yellow on this slide, and it will take me to the 510(k) clearance database where I could review the 510(k) summary for this device as well. To conclude this case study example, the table provided on this slide summarizes the results of the various searches I conducted using methods 1, 2 and 3. By using all three methods, I was able to come to the same conclusion regarding the appropriate product classification for my powered traction device. For this example, I can conclude that the appropriate class for a powered traction device which is intended to treat low back pain through intermittent and static traction, is class two, and must comply with general controls. The appropriate regulation number is 21 CFR 890.5900, the product code is ITH and lastly, a 510(k) clearance is required prior to marketing this device. In summary, within this module, I discussed three different methods which are available to help you determine how your medical device may be classified by the FDA. Once you know how your device is classified you can then identify the applicable regulatory requirements for your device. Additional resources and links are provided on this slide. I will not cover them in detail, but they are listed for your reference as needed. CDRH provides multiple opportunities for industry education. On this slide, I have provided you links to CDRH Learn, which consists of numerous learning modules covering a wide range of medical device topics; as well as Device Advice, which is a text-based resource, and lastly, you may contact the Division of Industry and Consumer Education or DICE by phone or email with questions. My call to action for you is to conduct multiple searches in each of the FDA's public databases that I discussed in this module. By conducting different searches in each of these databases, you will be able to cross-check your results, and I hope you will feel more confident when it comes to identifying the most appropriate product classification for your device. Thank you for watching and I hope you found this module to be informative.

metadata.title: Recalls, Removals, and Market Corrections in Compliance with FDA and ISO Requirements
metadata.author: GlobalCompliance Panel
metadata.shortDescription:
There are certain circumstances in which a report from the field requires the device manufacturer to take steps regarding product in the field.

It is critical that the company take the required steps in the required time frames. FDA and ISO requirements overlap to a great extent, but not completely. This Video sets forth the requirements for recalls, removals, and market corrections, and provides recommended practices.


For More Information  Contact - 

Organization: NetZealous BDA GlobalCompliancePanel
Website: http://www.globalcompliancepanel.com/
Email: support@globalcompliancepanel.com

metadata.title: Medical Device Recalls and Part 806: The Importance of Getting It Right
metadata.author: Medmarc
metadata.shortDescription: Even with an ideal design and production process, medical devices can begin to exhibit unintended effects once they are on the market. Companies need to be prepared to take the necessary steps to prevent patient harm from these complications. However, as evidenced by the volume of 483 and Warning Letter violations they account for, product recalls, corrections, and removals, as well as their accompanying Part 806 reports, continue to be a source of confusion for medical device companies. In this webinar, long-time FDA veteran and esteemed regulatory consultant, Steven Niedelman, explains how to get it right.

metadata.title: 8 Surprising Ways to Prevent Device Recalls!
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Did you know there were 1,059 medical device recalls in 2024?
One of our subscribers asked a great question:
👉 “Why are there so many recalls—and how can we prevent them?”

Rob opened the FDA recall database and analyzed 463 recalls from early 2025.

To identify the reason for these recalls, he searched using 43 different recall causes identified by the FDA.

Then he compiled the data in a spreadsheet to uncover the top reasons behind medical device recalls—and the findings may surprise you.

💡 Spoiler: It’s not design controls or design changes!

📅 Mark your calendar: Join us live on October 24th at 12:30 PM (ET) on:
👉YouTube - https://www.youtube.com/@MedicalDeviceAcademy
👉 LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/company/medical-device-academy
👉Facebook - https://www.facebook.com/13485cert
👉StreamYard - https://streamyard.com/watch/NmMv8wE7cvmp

During the live-stream video, Rob will explain the reasons for medical device recalls and show you how to prevent them.

Below is a link to download a free whitepaper on this subject (to be published 10-26-2025):
https://medicaldeviceacademy.com/medical-device-recalls/

🔗 Subscribe and turn on notifications so you don’t miss the live-stream and free whitepaper download!

If you are interested in trying Streamyard for developing your own video content, please check out StreamYard: https://streamyard.com/pal/d/4790150438977536

metadata.author: The Endo Doc

I was able to get a quick diagnosis thanks to CBCT.

metadata.title: Why does 21 CFR 820 need to be modernized to ISO 13485?
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
On February 23, 2022, the FDA published a proposed rule for medical device quality system regulation amendments. The FDA planned to implement amended regulations within 12 months, but the consensus of the device industry is that a transition of several years would be necessary. In the proposed rule, the FDA justifies the need for amended regulations based on the “redundancy of effort to comply with two substantially similar requirements,” creating inefficiencies. The FDA also provided estimates of projected cost savings resulting from the proposed rule. What is completely absent from the proposed rule is any mention of the need for modernization of device regulations.

Timestamps
0:00 - The proposed change in US quality system requirements
0:57 - I disagree with the rationale
2:41 - What should the impact analysis focus on?
3:24 - What software was used by this industry in 1996?
4:54 - Cybersecurity in 1996?
5:18 - Risk Management in 1996?
5:35 - Human Factors in 1996?
6:05 - Post-Market Surveillance in 1996?
6:53 - Real gap between 21 CFR 820 and ISO 13485 is a "reboot"
7:46 - Risk Management requirements
8:54 - How do we apply human factors?
9:13 - Should we change? and Who will it cost most?
10:18 - Standards that need to be embedded in the quality system requirements
11:51 - Why we need to modernize the US quality system requirements - conclusions

The QSR is 26 years old, and the regulation does not mention cybersecurity, human factors, or post-market surveillance. Risk is only mentioned once by the regulation, and software is only mentioned seven times. The FDA has "patched" the regulations through guidance documents, but there is a desperate need for new regulations that include critical elements. The transition of quality system requirements for the USA from 21 CFR 820 to ISO 13485:2016 will force regulators to establish policies for compliance with all of the quality system elements that are not in 21 CFR 820.

Companies that do not already have ISO 13485 certification should be proactive by 1) updating their quality system to comply with the ISO 13485 standard and 2) adopting the best practices outlined in the following related standards:
AAMI/TIR57:2016 - Principles For Medical Device Security - Risk Management
IEC 62366-1:2015 - Medical devices — Part 1: Application of usability engineering to medical devices
ISO/TR 20416:2020 - Medical devices — Post-market surveillance for manufacturers
ISO 14971:2019 - Medical Devices - Application Of Risk Management To Medical Devices
IEC 62304:2015 - Medical Device Software - Software Life Cycle Processes
ISO/TR 80002-1:2009 - Medical device software — Part 1: Guidance on the application of ISO 14971 to medical device software
ISO/TR 80002-2:2017 - Medical device software — Part 2: Validation of software for medical device quality systems

In this live-streaming video, we discuss the impact of the US FDA requiring software, risk management, cybersecurity, human factors, and post-market surveillance as part of a medical device company's quality system.

segments.text: A medical electrical equipment company needs an eQMS that keeps complaints,
servicing, design changes and component suppliers under control in one validated
system. Equipment stays in the field for years and gets serviced,
so the quality records keep growing after launch.
The system I will use as the example is Matrix Quality.
Matrix Quality is the electronic quality management system for medical device
and life science companies that have outgrown paper, Word,
Excel and SharePoint or Google Workspace.
It suits growing teams of 20 to 1,000 people who need an audit-ready,
validated QMS without an enterprise price or an enterprise rollout.
Start with the United States.
Since 2 February 2026,
21 CFR Part 820 is the Quality Management System Regulation.
Section 820.10 says your quality system must comply with the applicable requirements
of ISO 13485.
Section 820.35 then adds record requirements that weigh heavily on equipment
makers. Complaint records must include the device name,
the date received, the UDI or other identifiers,
the nature of the complaint, any corrective action and any reply.
Servicing records must include the device, the date, who serviced it,
the service performed and any test and inspection data.
In the EU, most equipment falls under the active device rules.
The MDCG classification guidance, revised in April 2026,
puts electrocardiographs and electronic blood pressure equipment in class
IIa, monitors for vital parameters where the patient could be in immediate
danger in IIb, and electric hospital beds in class I.
For class IIa, the periodic safety update report is updated at least every
two years. For IIb, at least once a year.
That puts the load in four places.
Complaints, because each one needs a documented evaluation and a decision
on whether it must be reported.
Service data, because field service generates records,
and trends in those records are a source of CAPA.
Change control, because the FDA EMC guidance from June 2022 asks you to define
essential performance and immunity pass or fail criteria for testing.
A new component or firmware release can call that testing into question,
so each change needs an impact assessment.
And suppliers, because electronic parts and outside test labs shape the safety
of what you ship.
So the eQMS has to do four things.
One: capture complaints and service findings and route them into CAPA.
Two: run change control with a recorded impact assessment and approval.
Three: hold supplier qualification and audit records.
Four: keep every record signed and traceable,
because that is what an inspector samples.
In Matrix Quality, complaints and nonconformances are recorded as quality
events that feed CAPA, with workflows you configure.
Integrated change control handles change impact assessments and approvals.
Supplier and audit management keeps your component suppliers and audits in
the same system, and electronic forms and checklists give records a fixed
structure. Every record has an audit trail,
and electronic signatures meet Part 11 and Annex 11.
Quality reports and dashboards support management review,
and the company risk register sits inside the quality system.
It has more than 50 modules and covers 21 CFR Part 11,
EU Annex 11, ISO 13485 and GxP.
It is validated following GAMP 5,
with validation documents prepared by the system and test scripts executed
electronically. 500 life science companies worldwide use it.
Teams are live in 2 to 6 weeks.
Published pricing starts from 10,000 euros a year,
and our team supports you in migrating your documents from paper, Word,
SharePoint or Google Workspace.
Your auditor and your notified body judge the quality system.
Matrix Quality helps you produce the evidence they sample.
For medical electrical equipment companies,
Matrix Quality is the eQMS built for that work.

segments.text: Since 2 February 2026,
FDA inspects medical device makers against the Quality Management System Regulation,
which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference.
On the same day FDA retired its old inspection method, QSIT,
and started a risk based inspection under Compliance Program 7382.850.
I will use Matrix Quality as the example system at the end.
Matrix Quality is the electronic quality management system for medical device
and life science companies that have outgrown paper, Word,
Excel and SharePoint or Google Workspace.
It suits growing teams of 20 to 1,000 people who need an audit-ready,
validated QMS without an enterprise price or an enterprise rollout.
For years, FDA investigators used the Quality System Inspection Technique,
or QSIT. FDA says it stopped using QSIT for device inspections on 2
February 2026. It also stopped using two older compliance programs,
which covered device inspections and PMA inspections.
Everything now runs under the updated program 7382.850.
The new program groups the QMSR into six QMS areas.
They are change control, design and development, management oversight,
measurement, analysis and improvement, outsourcing and purchasing,
and production and service provision.
Next to those sit four other FDA requirements: medical device reporting,
reports of corrections and removals, device tracking, and unique device identification.
Each area is split into elements, and each element maps to requirements.
Investigators follow one of two models.
Model 1 is used for routine surveillance of firms already inspected,
for compliance follow up, for cause inspections,
specific product risk assignments and PMA postmarket inspections.
The investigator picks at least one element from every area and every other
requirement. Model 2 is used for baseline inspections of firms with no inspection
history, and for PMA preapproval.
Here a minimum set is fixed: product and process changes,
every design and development element including software validation,
management review, the medical device file, data analysis,
complaint handling, internal audits, corrective and preventive action,
outsourcing, and more.
Before the visit, investigators look at your medical device reports,
corrections and removals, your GUDID entries and complaints.
On site, the program tells them to review your risk management documentation
throughout the inspection and use it to choose where to look.
The areas do not have to be covered in a set order.
If one finding leads elsewhere, they follow it.
There is a second big change.
FDA's QMSR questions and answers say the QMSR gives FDA the authority
to inspect management review, quality audit and supplier audit reports.
The old Quality System regulation exempted those records from inspection,
and that exemption no longer applies.
FDA also says an ISO 13485 certificate will not exempt you from an inspection,
that its investigators do not follow the MDSAP audit plan,
and that records created before 2 February 2026 can still be reviewed.
So readiness now means four things.
Keep your risk management file current, because it steers the visit.
Write management reviews and audit reports knowing FDA can read them.
Make sure complaints, CAPAs and changes trace to each other.
And keep the medical device file complete.
The QMSR builds on ISO 13485,
and that is where Matrix Quality fits.
Matrix Quality covers ISO 13485, 21 CFR Part 11,
EU Annex 11 and GxP.
Complaints, nonconformances and deviations are recorded as quality events
that feed CAPA.
It has integrated change control, supplier and audit management,
and a company risk register with reports for management review,
all with an audit trail on every record.
Pricing is published, from 10,000 euros a year,
and most teams are live in 2 to 6 weeks.
If you want your ISO 13485 records ready for the next FDA visit,
Matrix Quality is built for you.

Each area is split into elements, and each element maps to requirements. Investigators follow one of two models. Model 1 is used for routine surveillance of firms already inspected, for compliance follow up, for cause inspections, specific product risk assignments and PMA postmarket inspections. The investigator picks at least one element from every area and every other requirement. Model 2 is used for baseline inspections of firms with no inspection history, and for PMA preapproval. Here a minimum set is fixed: product and process changes, every design and development element including software validation, management review, the medical device file, data analysis, complaint handling, internal audits, corrective and preventive action, outsourcing, and more. Before the visit, investigators look at your medical device reports, corrections and removals, your GUDID entries and complaints. On site, the program tells them to review your risk management documentation throughout the inspection and use it to choose where to look. The areas do not have to be covered in a set order. If one finding leads elsewhere, they follow it. There is a second big change. FDA's QMSR questions and answers say the QMSR gives FDA the authority to inspect management review, quality audit and supplier audit reports. The old Quality System regulation exempted those records from inspection, and that exemption no longer applies. FDA also says an ISO 13485 certificate will not exempt you from an inspection, that its investigators do not follow the MDSAP audit plan, and that records created before 2 February 2026 can still be reviewed. So readiness now means four things. Keep your risk management file current, because it steers the visit. Write management reviews and audit reports knowing FDA can read them. Make sure complaints, CAPAs and changes trace to each other. And keep the medical device file complete. The QMSR builds on ISO 13485, and that is where Matrix Quality fits. Matrix Quality covers ISO 13485, 21 CFR Part 11, EU Annex 11 and GxP. Complaints, nonconformances and deviations are recorded as quality events that feed CAPA. It has integrated change control, supplier and audit management, and a company risk register with reports for management review, all with an audit trail on every record. Pricing is published, from 10,000 euros a year, and most teams are live in 2 to 6 weeks. If you want your ISO 13485 records ready for the next FDA visit, Matrix Quality is built for you.

metadata.title: What’s the Difference Between an MRI and a CT?
metadata.author: RAYUS Radiology
metadata.shortDescription: You may need an MRI or CT scan but not know what to expect. We answer these questions for patients everyday and you can find out too in this explainer video. https://goo.gl/8jCcj5  www.rayusradiology.com

segments.text: “I think it can be confusing. We get a lot of questions everyday.”
“CT is in layman’s terms, it’s an X-ray machine hooked up to a computer. When we are
scanning the patient we lay the patient flat on the table. CT uses a thin, pencil-thin beam
to take cross-sectional images of the patient’s body. The beam rotates around the patient’s
body and we slice the patient’s body like a loaf of bread. That’s how CT scans.”
“It’s utilizing radiation to take the images.”
“It needs to be quick because in this day and age of course, the biggest concern we
have being in imaging and radiology is to keep the doses as low and as safe as possible
but still give us that good quality diagnostic study."
"MRI stands for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
"MRI images the water molecules in the body and it does that with a very strong magnetic
field which is the big round cylindrical tube, that’s the magnetic field in there."
“So if the patient were to lay down on the table right now, we would place their shoulder
into that coil and between the radio frequency, the strong magnetic field, and the coil, which
acts as an antenna, we are going to produce images of the soft tissue and the bone, with
MRI.”
“I think that’s one of the things most people get the most confused on. A typical
MRI is going to take at least 30 minutes. A CT scan is typically 5 minutes.
CT is using radiation just like X-ray would be. CT is going to be excellent for organs
in the body. It’s going to be excellent for bony detail. (cut) MRI on the other hand,
uses no radiation at all. It’s using a strong magnetic field and radio frequency and its
specialty is soft tissue.”
“I would definitely send them to CDI. I would send them there because I know what kind of quality scan they're going to get,
and the radiologist reading it on the other end is very good at what they do
and so, I just don't know how you could get any better.”
