segments.text: Imagine for a second a 58-year-old
hypothetical character, Ramesh Uncle,
who experiences chest pain. He undergoes
angioplasty at the hospital, and a small
metal mesh is inserted into his heart
artery. This is called a stent. Now,
listen carefully. Before February 2017,
the maximum retail price of such stents
in India ranged from approximately ₹
25,000 to ₹ 1.98 lakh. Then, in 2017,
the government imposed a price cap, and
the price of stents dropped by up to 85
With one order, the price of something
that goes inside the human body dropped
so much in about a week, and citing NPPA
data, PTI reported that the trade margin
on some stents was as high as 654%.
A simple question: if the price of a
stent could fall this much, what was the
real cost in the original price, and
where did the rest of the money go?
And the second big question: if
manufacturers were getting such high
margins, why were some major companies
pulling their stents out of India after
the price cap?
In this video, we won't just understand
medical devices; we will decode the
economic engine of this industry. Where
the money comes from, where it goes, who
earns, and who loses out. Let's start
from the beginning. What does "medical
device" mean? Look, anything that isn't
a drug but is used for treatment or
diagnosis is a medical device.
From bandages and syringes to BP
machines, glucometers, pacemakers, hip
implants, ventilators, ultrasound
machines, MRI, and CT scans—everything
is within one industry, including a ₹ 5
syringe and a multi-crore MRI machine.
That is why this industry feels
difficult to understand. It is not one
industry, but a cluster of many small
industries, each with different
economics. Who is the customer? Here is
the first twist. Often, the person who
uses the product is the patient. The
person who chooses it is the doctor, and
the one who pays for it is the hospital
, insurance company, the government, or
sometimes the patient themselves. This
means the buyer, the user, and the
decision-maker can all be different.
This makes pricing very strange. Just
like at a wedding, the one who eats the
food doesn't pay the bill, and the one
who pays the bill doesn't decide the
menu. Now, look at the scale. According
to an industry report by Rubix Industry
Insights, India's medical devices market
was worth approximately $ 15.2 billion
in 2025. The same report provides a
projection of $ 50.1 billion by 2030.
But take note here, because this is a
projection, not a guarantee. Global Data
has a different estimate, suggesting
only about 6%annual growth from 2025 to
2035, while various research firms place
the 2025 market size between $ 15 and $
18 billion. Meaning the industry is
large-scale, but there is no complete
consensus on the exact numbers. It is
certain that India is considered the
fourth-largest medical devices market in
Asia and ranks among the top 20 in the
world.
>> But this is where the real game begins.
A very large portion of the devices sold
in the Indian market is imported.
Estimates suggest an import dependence
of approximately 70 to 80%. According to
a compiled report, the import bill for
medical devices in FY 2025-26 was
approximately ₹ 89,000 crore, and
government data shows medical device
exports in FY 25 were about $ 4.1
billion. This means we import
significantly more than we export. The
items being manufactured in India are
mostly low-end. Gloves, syringes,
bandages, and consumables.
High-end items like imaging machines,
advanced implants, and robotic surgery
equipment mostly come from abroad.
Keep this in mind because the rest of
the video is connected to this. An
imported device is not just a machine;
it is the final, small piece of an
entire supply chain. Now, let’s follow
that supply chain as if a shipment were
moving through it. Let’s create a
fictional company named Neo Care Devices
in Hyderabad, founded by Rohan, a
biomedical engineer. Neo Care makes two
things.
A patient monitor placed near an ICU bed
and the disposable sensors used for
every patient.
This company is hypothetical, but its
economics are built on real-world
patterns. Rohan’s journey begins with
raw materials: plastic, silicon,
electronic chips, sensors, displays,
batteries, and metal housing. This is
where the first shock hits. Chips and
many precision components are not even
being manufactured in India.
This means that for Rohan’s device,
which is called "Made in India," a
significant portion of what is inside is
imported. Therefore, if the dollar gets
expensive, Rohan's costs increase, but
the selling price to hospitals is
already fixed in contracts. Then comes
manufacturing. Rohan needs a factory
with clean-room standards, quality
testing machines, and trained engineers
Then comes the most boring but most
expensive step: regulation. In India,
before 2017, medical devices were
legally viewed just like medicines.
Under the same old Drugs and Cosmetics
Act, 1940. Then the Medical Devices
Rules 2017 were introduced, implemented
from 2018, and devices were categorized
from Class A to Class D based on risk.
For Class C and D devices, such as
implants and high-risk equipment,
licensing became mandatory by October
2023. Meaning, now a startup doesn't
just have to build a product, but also
documentation, testing, audits, and
quality systems. All this costs money
without earning a single rupee. Now the
product is ready, who should they sell
it to? There are two paths here:
directly to the hospital or through a
distributor.
Large hospitals have purchase committees
, and for small nursing homes and
clinics, distributors are the biggest
route.
Distributors hold inventory, provide
services, and offer credit. After that
comes the hospital, and finally, a
hidden part: the secondary market,
refurbished machines.
Regarding these second-hand machines, a
Parliamentary Standing Committee report
stated that the Medical Device Rules
2017 do not directly regulate
refurbished devices.
They come under separate rules. This
means there is an entire market where
money flows, but oversight is weak. Now
, look at the journey of ₹ 100. This is
a hypothetical example. It is not data
from any real company. It is just for
understanding. Suppose a patient or
their insurance spends ₹ 100 on a
disposable implant. First, about ₹ 5
goes into taxes. GST rates vary by
device, so consider this just an
approximation. The hospital keeps its
margin. Let's assume ₹ 25, and the
distributor gets ₹ 15. Now the
manufacturer is left with ₹ 55. Out of
these ₹ 55, ₹ 15 goes into raw materials
and manufacturing.
₹ 17 goes into the sales team, doctor
training, clinical support, and reaching
the hospital. ₹ 7 goes into R&D,
clinical studies, regulatory, and
quality. ₹ 5 goes into general overheads
, and the company is left with an
operating profit of about ₹ 11. Now
think, even in this imaginary breakdown
, the manufacturer is left with perhaps
₹ 11 out of the ₹ 100 paid by the
customer.
The hospital and distributor together
took ₹ 40, and this is the very thing
the government looked at in 2017. In the
case of coronary stents, the NPPA fixed
a maximum trade margin of 8%on February
20, 2017, which applies to the entire
supply chain. From the manufacturer or
importer to the end customer, including
hospital handling charges, this 8%was
already included in the stent's ceiling
price.
For orthopedic implants too, the NPPA's
analysis found total trade margins for
importers and distributors on devices
like femoral, tibial, plates, inserts,
and patella to be an average of 211%to
This means it wasn't just the story of
stents; wherever the patient has no idea
of the price and the doctor makes the
decision, room for margins is created.
But a new question arises here. If so
much margin is circulating in the chain
, is everything easy for the
manufacturer? Absolutely not. Let's look
at Neo Care's unit economics. All these
numbers are hypothetical. Rohan's
patient monitor sells to hospitals for ₹
1 lakh. The manufacturing cost is ₹
Meaning, the gross profit per monitor is
₹ 40,000, but this machine is just a
doorway. The real earnings are in the
disposable sensors. One sensor sells to
the hospital for ₹ 400. It costs ₹ 150
to manufacture. Gross profit is ₹ 250
per sensor. Now, assume one sensor is
used daily on an ICU bed for 300 days a
year. Meaning, one monitor brings in ₹
75,000 in gross profit every year just
from sensors. Over 7 years, that's ₹
5.25 lakh. ₹ 40,000 from the machine and
₹ 5.25 lakh from the sensors. This is
called the razor and blade model. Sell
the razor cheap and earn from the blades
, or think of it like printers being
cheap while cartridges are expensive;
and yes, there is another part, the
Annual Maintenance Contract. Assume the
annual AMC is 8%of the machine's cost—
this is hypothetical—but note that this
is recurring revenue.
A company that enters a hospital once
keeps getting repeat business, and there
is also a switching cost for the
hospital.
The staff gets used to one brand's
monitors, the same software, and the
same sensors.
Switching to a new brand means
re-training, compatibility issues, and
risk. Now let's look at costs in two
parts. Fixed costs and variable costs.
Fixed costs are those you have to pay
whether you sell or not. Factory rent,
clean room maintenance, salaries,
quality team, regulatory team.
Understand this like the rent for a tea
shop, which must be paid even if not a
single cup of tea is sold. Variable
costs are those that increase with every
unit. Plastic, chips, packaging,
sterilization. Rohan's fixed cost is ₹ 6
crore per year. This is also
hypothetical. Contribution per sensor is
₹ 250, so at how many sensors is the
break-even? 6 crore divided by ₹ 250,
which is 2.4 lakh sensors. If the
factory capacity is 6 lakh sensors, then
break-even comes at 40%utilization. Here
, one number changes the entire
calculation.
If utilization drops below 40%, Rohan
has no profit even on paper—it's a loss
. If it goes to 70%, that's 4.2 lakh
sensors, meaning an extra contribution
from 1.8 lakh sensors, or a profit of ₹
4.5 crore. Same factory, same rent, same
salaries. Just more sensors sold. This
is called operating leverage.
An idle factory isn't just empty; it
burns money every month, like a
half-empty train that consumes full
diesel. Now, understand another major
difference: operating expense and
capital expenditure. Opex is your
day-to-day spending: salaries,
electricity, and marketing.
Capex is a large, one-time investment
that serves you for years, such as new
cleanroom lines, molds, and testing
equipment.
In medical devices, besides capex, R&D
is a major component, and this R&D often
shows no revenue for four to five years
. Now, let’s see what the engine of one
of the world's biggest companies really
looks like. According to Medtronic's FY
2026 results, the company's annual
revenue was approximately 36.4 billion
dollars. The adjusted gross margin in Q4
was 65.4%, meaning for every 100 dollars
in sales, about 65 dollars remain after
production costs. Sounds like a lot,
right? But let’s look further down.
Taking one quarter as an example: R&D
was about 722 million dollars, and SG&A
—that is, selling and general expenses—
was about 2.96 billion dollars.
This means spending on sales, marketing
, doctor relationships, training, and
admin was four times higher than R&D,
and the adjusted operating margin for
that quarter was around 23%.
There is a lesson to be learned here.
Gross margins in medical devices look
high, but the cost of reaching the
doctor eats into that significantly, and
free cash flow in FY 2026 was
approximately 5.4 billion dollars.
This is real, coming from the company's
own results, but the most interesting
part is yet to come. The difference
between profit and cash. When Rohan gave
his monitor to a hospital, an invoice of
1 lakh rupees was generated, revenue was
booked, and profit appeared on paper,
but the hospital paid 120 days later.
This is also a hypothetical number, and
often in private or government hospitals
, this duration is even longer.
During this time, Rohan still has to pay
his suppliers, pay salaries, and buy new
inventory. This is called a working
capital problem. Profit can exist on
paper, but it doesn't necessarily mean
there is cash in the bank account, and
which one matters?
Revenue is what was sold; gross profit
is sales minus the direct cost of
production; EBITDA is operating profit
before interest, taxes, and depreciation
Operating profit is what remains after
depreciation. Net profit is what is left
after interest and taxes. Cash flow is
what actually entered or left the bank,
and free cash flow is what you truly
have left after capex.
Medtronic has FCF, which is why it can
pay dividends and make acquisitions.
A startup like Rohan’s can have negative
FCF even after being profitable because
it is building inventory and waiting for
payments.
The biggest money in this industry isn't
what meets the eye. So, what is that
industry money which the customer
doesn't even see?
First is consumables, which we've seen;
second, service contracts and spare
parts; third, training and software
upgrades; and fourth, financing.
Often, machines are given to hospitals
on lease or a reagent rental model,
where the machine is cheap or free, but
hospitals must buy tests or sensors from
those companies all year; and fifth,
data.
Today's connected devices generate
patient data, and in the long term, that
can create revenue from software and
analytics.
This last point is still emerging, but
that is the direction.
Now, imagine companies like Rohan’s have
to do all this, and yet, many still fail
. Why? Listen to a story. Let's imagine
a hypothetical failure with NeoCare.
Suppose Rohan set up a second factory
line based on a large export order,
taking a 40 million rupee loan.
The order got cancelled. Now, the loan
EMIs are due, but the factory is
operating at 30%utilization. Meaning, it
is below break-even. On top of that,
hospital payments are taking 150 days.
Furthermore, the dollar became expensive
and the cost of imported chips rose, but
prices in hospital contracts are fixed.
These three things—debt, low utilization
, and delayed payments—together wipe out
the cash keeping the company alive. In
medical devices, companies often fall
not due to bad products, but due to poor
cash management. Now, let’s look at a
real case study where government policy
shook up the entire economics. Stent
price caps.
The facts: The NPPA used the
extraordinary powers of Paragraph 19 of
the Drug Price Control Order 2013 and
fixed the ceiling price for coronary
stents in February 2017.
According to Business Standard, after
the price cap, MNCs like Abbott,
Medtronic, and Boston Scientific pulled
some stents from the market, and a
Chinese company, MicroPort, launched its
stent in India after the cap.
The NPPA claimed that after the cap, the
share of domestic manufacturers
increased—an initial shift of about 4%.
Domestic companies said the new price
was unviable for them too, and a
company's offer document, citing NPPA
data, stated that DES usage increased by

videos.full_text: Imagine for a second a 58-year-old hypothetical character, Ramesh Uncle, who experiences chest pain. He undergoes angioplasty at the hospital, and a small metal mesh is inserted into his heart artery. This is called a stent. Now, listen carefully. Before February 2017, the maximum retail price of such stents in India ranged from approximately ₹ 25,000 to ₹ 1.98 lakh. Then, in 2017, the government imposed a price cap, and the price of stents dropped by up to 85 %. With one order, the price of something that goes inside the human body dropped so much in about a week, and citing NPPA data, PTI reported that the trade margin on some stents was as high as 654%. A simple question: if the price of a stent could fall this much, what was the real cost in the original price, and where did the rest of the money go? And the second big question: if manufacturers were getting such high margins, why were some major companies pulling their stents out of India after the price cap? In this video, we won't just understand medical devices; we will decode the economic engine of this industry. Where the money comes from, where it goes, who earns, and who loses out. Let's start from the beginning. What does "medical device" mean? Look, anything that isn't a drug but is used for treatment or diagnosis is a medical device. From bandages and syringes to BP machines, glucometers, pacemakers, hip implants, ventilators, ultrasound machines, MRI, and CT scans—everything is within one industry, including a ₹ 5 syringe and a multi-crore MRI machine. That is why this industry feels difficult to understand. It is not one industry, but a cluster of many small industries, each with different economics. Who is the customer? Here is the first twist. Often, the person who uses the product is the patient. The person who chooses it is the doctor, and the one who pays for it is the hospital , insurance company, the government, or sometimes the patient themselves. This means the buyer, the user, and the decision-maker can all be different. This makes pricing very strange. Just like at a wedding, the one who eats the food doesn't pay the bill, and the one who pays the bill doesn't decide the menu. Now, look at the scale. According to an industry report by Rubix Industry Insights, India's medical devices market was worth approximately $ 15.2 billion in 2025. The same report provides a projection of $ 50.1 billion by 2030. But take note here, because this is a projection, not a guarantee. Global Data has a different estimate, suggesting only about 6%annual growth from 2025 to 2035, while various research firms place the 2025 market size between $ 15 and $ 18 billion. Meaning the industry is large-scale, but there is no complete consensus on the exact numbers. It is certain that India is considered the fourth-largest medical devices market in Asia and ranks among the top 20 in the world. >> But this is where the real game begins. A very large portion of the devices sold in the Indian market is imported. Estimates suggest an import dependence of approximately 70 to 80%. According to a compiled report, the import bill for medical devices in FY 2025-26 was approximately ₹ 89,000 crore, and government data shows medical device exports in FY 25 were about $ 4.1 billion. This means we import significantly more than we export. The items being manufactured in India are mostly low-end. Gloves, syringes, bandages, and consumables. High-end items like imaging machines, advanced implants, and robotic surgery equipment mostly come from abroad. Keep this in mind because the rest of the video is connected to this. An imported device is not just a machine; it is the final, small piece of an entire supply chain. Now, let’s follow that supply chain as if a shipment were moving through it. Let’s create a fictional company named Neo Care Devices in Hyderabad, founded by Rohan, a biomedical engineer. Neo Care makes two things. A patient monitor placed near an ICU bed and the disposable sensors used for every patient. This company is hypothetical, but its economics are built on real-world patterns. Rohan’s journey begins with raw materials: plastic, silicon, electronic chips, sensors, displays, batteries, and metal housing. This is where the first shock hits. Chips and many precision components are not even being manufactured in India. This means that for Rohan’s device, which is called "Made in India," a significant portion of what is inside is imported. Therefore, if the dollar gets expensive, Rohan's costs increase, but the selling price to hospitals is already fixed in contracts. Then comes manufacturing. Rohan needs a factory with clean-room standards, quality testing machines, and trained engineers . Then comes the most boring but most expensive step: regulation. In India, before 2017, medical devices were legally viewed just like medicines. Under the same old Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Then the Medical Devices Rules 2017 were introduced, implemented from 2018, and devices were categorized from Class A to Class D based on risk. For Class C and D devices, such as implants and high-risk equipment, licensing became mandatory by October 2023. Meaning, now a startup doesn't just have to build a product, but also documentation, testing, audits, and quality systems. All this costs money without earning a single rupee. Now the product is ready, who should they sell it to? There are two paths here: directly to the hospital or through a distributor. Large hospitals have purchase committees , and for small nursing homes and clinics, distributors are the biggest route. Distributors hold inventory, provide services, and offer credit. After that comes the hospital, and finally, a hidden part: the secondary market, refurbished machines. Regarding these second-hand machines, a Parliamentary Standing Committee report stated that the Medical Device Rules 2017 do not directly regulate refurbished devices. They come under separate rules. This means there is an entire market where money flows, but oversight is weak. Now , look at the journey of ₹ 100. This is a hypothetical example. It is not data from any real company. It is just for understanding. Suppose a patient or their insurance spends ₹ 100 on a disposable implant. First, about ₹ 5 goes into taxes. GST rates vary by device, so consider this just an approximation. The hospital keeps its margin. Let's assume ₹ 25, and the distributor gets ₹ 15. Now the manufacturer is left with ₹ 55. Out of these ₹ 55, ₹ 15 goes into raw materials and manufacturing. ₹ 17 goes into the sales team, doctor training, clinical support, and reaching the hospital. ₹ 7 goes into R&D, clinical studies, regulatory, and quality. ₹ 5 goes into general overheads , and the company is left with an operating profit of about ₹ 11. Now think, even in this imaginary breakdown , the manufacturer is left with perhaps ₹ 11 out of the ₹ 100 paid by the customer. The hospital and distributor together took ₹ 40, and this is the very thing the government looked at in 2017. In the case of coronary stents, the NPPA fixed a maximum trade margin of 8%on February 20, 2017, which applies to the entire supply chain. From the manufacturer or importer to the end customer, including hospital handling charges, this 8%was already included in the stent's ceiling price. For orthopedic implants too, the NPPA's analysis found total trade margins for importers and distributors on devices like femoral, tibial, plates, inserts, and patella to be an average of 211%to 449%. This means it wasn't just the story of stents; wherever the patient has no idea of the price and the doctor makes the decision, room for margins is created. But a new question arises here. If so much margin is circulating in the chain , is everything easy for the manufacturer? Absolutely not. Let's look at Neo Care's unit economics. All these numbers are hypothetical. Rohan's patient monitor sells to hospitals for ₹ 1 lakh. The manufacturing cost is ₹ 60,000. Meaning, the gross profit per monitor is ₹ 40,000, but this machine is just a doorway. The real earnings are in the disposable sensors. One sensor sells to the hospital for ₹ 400. It costs ₹ 150 to manufacture. Gross profit is ₹ 250 per sensor. Now, assume one sensor is used daily on an ICU bed for 300 days a year. Meaning, one monitor brings in ₹ 75,000 in gross profit every year just from sensors. Over 7 years, that's ₹ 5.25 lakh. ₹ 40,000 from the machine and ₹ 5.25 lakh from the sensors. This is called the razor and blade model. Sell the razor cheap and earn from the blades , or think of it like printers being cheap while cartridges are expensive; and yes, there is another part, the Annual Maintenance Contract. Assume the annual AMC is 8%of the machine's cost— this is hypothetical—but note that this is recurring revenue. A company that enters a hospital once keeps getting repeat business, and there is also a switching cost for the hospital. The staff gets used to one brand's monitors, the same software, and the same sensors. Switching to a new brand means re-training, compatibility issues, and risk. Now let's look at costs in two parts. Fixed costs and variable costs. Fixed costs are those you have to pay whether you sell or not. Factory rent, clean room maintenance, salaries, quality team, regulatory team. Understand this like the rent for a tea shop, which must be paid even if not a single cup of tea is sold. Variable costs are those that increase with every unit. Plastic, chips, packaging, sterilization. Rohan's fixed cost is ₹ 6 crore per year. This is also hypothetical. Contribution per sensor is ₹ 250, so at how many sensors is the break-even? 6 crore divided by ₹ 250, which is 2.4 lakh sensors. If the factory capacity is 6 lakh sensors, then break-even comes at 40%utilization. Here , one number changes the entire calculation. If utilization drops below 40%, Rohan has no profit even on paper—it's a loss . If it goes to 70%, that's 4.2 lakh sensors, meaning an extra contribution from 1.8 lakh sensors, or a profit of ₹ 4.5 crore. Same factory, same rent, same salaries. Just more sensors sold. This is called operating leverage. An idle factory isn't just empty; it burns money every month, like a half-empty train that consumes full diesel. Now, understand another major difference: operating expense and capital expenditure. Opex is your day-to-day spending: salaries, electricity, and marketing. Capex is a large, one-time investment that serves you for years, such as new cleanroom lines, molds, and testing equipment. In medical devices, besides capex, R&D is a major component, and this R&D often shows no revenue for four to five years . Now, let’s see what the engine of one of the world's biggest companies really looks like. According to Medtronic's FY 2026 results, the company's annual revenue was approximately 36.4 billion dollars. The adjusted gross margin in Q4 was 65.4%, meaning for every 100 dollars in sales, about 65 dollars remain after production costs. Sounds like a lot, right? But let’s look further down. Taking one quarter as an example: R&D was about 722 million dollars, and SG&A —that is, selling and general expenses— was about 2.96 billion dollars. This means spending on sales, marketing , doctor relationships, training, and admin was four times higher than R&D, and the adjusted operating margin for that quarter was around 23%. There is a lesson to be learned here. Gross margins in medical devices look high, but the cost of reaching the doctor eats into that significantly, and free cash flow in FY 2026 was approximately 5.4 billion dollars. This is real, coming from the company's own results, but the most interesting part is yet to come. The difference between profit and cash. When Rohan gave his monitor to a hospital, an invoice of 1 lakh rupees was generated, revenue was booked, and profit appeared on paper, but the hospital paid 120 days later. This is also a hypothetical number, and often in private or government hospitals , this duration is even longer. During this time, Rohan still has to pay his suppliers, pay salaries, and buy new inventory. This is called a working capital problem. Profit can exist on paper, but it doesn't necessarily mean there is cash in the bank account, and which one matters? Revenue is what was sold; gross profit is sales minus the direct cost of production; EBITDA is operating profit before interest, taxes, and depreciation . Operating profit is what remains after depreciation. Net profit is what is left after interest and taxes. Cash flow is what actually entered or left the bank, and free cash flow is what you truly have left after capex. Medtronic has FCF, which is why it can pay dividends and make acquisitions. A startup like Rohan’s can have negative FCF even after being profitable because it is building inventory and waiting for payments. The biggest money in this industry isn't what meets the eye. So, what is that industry money which the customer doesn't even see? First is consumables, which we've seen; second, service contracts and spare parts; third, training and software upgrades; and fourth, financing. Often, machines are given to hospitals on lease or a reagent rental model, where the machine is cheap or free, but hospitals must buy tests or sensors from those companies all year; and fifth, data. Today's connected devices generate patient data, and in the long term, that can create revenue from software and analytics. This last point is still emerging, but that is the direction. Now, imagine companies like Rohan’s have to do all this, and yet, many still fail . Why? Listen to a story. Let's imagine a hypothetical failure with NeoCare. Suppose Rohan set up a second factory line based on a large export order, taking a 40 million rupee loan. The order got cancelled. Now, the loan EMIs are due, but the factory is operating at 30%utilization. Meaning, it is below break-even. On top of that, hospital payments are taking 150 days. Furthermore, the dollar became expensive and the cost of imported chips rose, but prices in hospital contracts are fixed. These three things—debt, low utilization , and delayed payments—together wipe out the cash keeping the company alive. In medical devices, companies often fall not due to bad products, but due to poor cash management. Now, let’s look at a real case study where government policy shook up the entire economics. Stent price caps. The facts: The NPPA used the extraordinary powers of Paragraph 19 of the Drug Price Control Order 2013 and fixed the ceiling price for coronary stents in February 2017. According to Business Standard, after the price cap, MNCs like Abbott, Medtronic, and Boston Scientific pulled some stents from the market, and a Chinese company, MicroPort, launched its stent in India after the cap. The NPPA claimed that after the cap, the share of domestic manufacturers increased—an initial shift of about 4%. Domestic companies said the new price was unviable for them too, and a company's offer document, citing NPPA data, stated that DES usage increased by about 40%after the cap. This is the company’s claim, and analysts might have a different opinion on it. Now for the interpretation, which is my take, as different people read it differently. On one hand, they say patients benefited from the cap and access increased because stents became affordable for the common man. On the other hand, industry associations said that such a strict cap could limit innovation and options. As Advamed stated in their release. There are arguments on both sides, and the real economic lesson here is that when prices are controlled from one end , the entire chain must be redesigned. What to sell, at what margin, and what to discontinue. Now, let's look at the risks. Currency risk, because of imported components. Regulatory risk, because price caps can be imposed at any time. Changes in taxes and import duties. Demand risk, when hospitals halt capex as interest rates rise, and competition , where Chinese and global companies have the advantage of scale; a recent example is Medtronic, which stated that their FY 2027 guidance assumes a $ 250 million impact from tariffs on their cost of goods sold. This means global trade policy is now part of device economics, and it is also cyclical, but in a different way. However, capital equipment like MRIs or new cath labs depends on hospital budgets and loan costs, while elective procedures like knee replacements or cosmetic surgeries depend on income and insurance. That is why disposable devices are more stable and large equipment is more cyclical. Now, regarding the government , India’s Production Linked Incentive scheme for medical devices is running from FY21 to FY28 with an outlay of ₹ 3,420 crore. According to a July 2026 government update, the PLI scheme has seen an investment of approximately ₹ 1,153 crore, and FDI in the sector is reported at ₹ 17,201 crore. Keep in mind that the outlay is the government's incentive budget while the investment is the company's own capital ; these are two different things, and in June 2026, the Health Ministry also proposed draft amendments to the Medical Devices Rules to shorten the timeline for manufacturing licenses. This means the government is focused on two things: incentivizing local manufacturing and reducing the burden of compliance. But this raises a question: if the economics are so difficult, regulations are heavy, payments are delayed, and there is the fear of price caps, then why do companies even enter this industry? And the simple answer is because once you are in, the moat is very deep. The first reason is the nature of demand; as long as humans have heartbeats, vision, or knee pain, there will be a need for treatment. Second is recurring revenue, consumables, and service upgrades. Third is switching costs. A surgeon trained on an implant system does not want to change it without a reason. Fourth, trust and regulatory approval are barriers in themselves; it is not easy to replace someone who has spent years building approvals, clinical data, and hospital relationships. And fifth, strategic importance. During COVID, the world saw what supply chains for ventilators and testing kits actually mean. That is why governments now view this not just as business, but also as a matter of national and health security. Second, connected and monitoring devices , wearable glucose monitors, and remote patient monitoring. According to reports , monitoring devices could be a fast-growing category. So, uh I lost my train of thought for a second there, but I hope that answers the question. >> Um yeah, we have um Let me find it. I lost it myself. Hold on. >> It's okay. >> Um How long is the average sales cycle in capital equipment in hospitals versus outpatient centers? >> How long is the It depends on the product. So, I mean again, it's Some capital products literally could be sold within a month. You know, but when you get above the department uh max that they can approve. So, for instance in a cardio A lot of cardiology departments in New York used to be 150,000 or 100,000 in some of them where the the chief could approve anything 100,000 or less. So, once you get above that, now they need multiple departments because again, they're going to be pulling from another department to help pay for this product. That's going to increase the timeline. So, real the I mean, the quick answer, it could be anywhere from a month to three or four years. And I'd say that average for the average capital equipment product, which again, it's a hard answer, I'd say about a year to 18 months. >> Okay. Um There, I Let's see. What Where is it? I just Here we go. Uh how many deals should uh be in the pipeline at each stage? >> How many deals? The more the better. The more the better. Just be The key is to be realistic what what a potential deal is. So, if you're again, your funnel's going to dwindle from stage to stage. If you We'll make it simple. If there's five stages and you have 30 accounts in stage one, by time you get to stage five, you hope you have one or two. You know, so the more that you can have in that funnel, the better because it's going to increase your chances of each stage of having accounts in that stage. But, if you're lying to yourself because you want to make the company happy and showing you're doing all this you know, making all this progress with things that aren't real, it's it's a bad bad path to go down, guys. You don't want that. So, if you only have a couple that are real, I'd rather see that because you're going to see more come out the end. You're going to see more real deals come through because you were up-front with yourself of what is a real potential prospect. So, you Knowing that at the beginning is going to increase your success. Lying to yourself is only going to hurt you. >> Uh I'm sure this is product specific, but is there any data that is considered must-have before a hospital move forward on an expensive purchase? >> It's typically the data that they want they want to see proof from other hospitals. You know, and and this is a tricky game, too, because when you deal in this space, especially with teaching centers and centers of excellence I mean, those are basically centers where people fly around the country to come see certain cases done because they're the best in cardiology, you know, in electrophysiology or or ortho, whatever it is, you know, so you you want to make sure that it sometimes hospitals don't respect other hospitals. So, they're not going to respect the data or the physicians from another hospital. I've seen this firsthand. When I was trying to do site visits and get physicians from some of the key centers in New York, they wouldn't just come to any hospital in New Jersey. They just wouldn't. You know, they some there a lot of doctors that they didn't want to go to those programs. They wanted to fly across the country, you know, because those specific physicians, they had good relationships and they really respected their program. So, you it's always going to be another proof of concept you know, not in every case cuz there's a lot of early adopters that they want to be the first to have it, but a lot of times hospitals want to see proof of concept. They want to see the data. Not, you know, not uh suggestive or small studies. They like to see larger uh sample sizes, but they like to see that it's actually being used elsewhere. The flip side of that which can get hospitals motivated, too when they are the first to get say a robotic system in New Jersey because that's a marketing move that now they can use where they are the only ones like when the intuitive robot first came out excuse me when the da Vinci robot came out from intuitive a lot of hospitals jumped on that because it was you know it's an amazing device but for them to say we have this new robot that provides all this the safety features and accuracy and everything else that they they used to sell that product and they were the center of excellence so you had to go from they would attract patients if it wasn't you know from a 30 or 50 mile radius now they're attracting from a 300 mile radius cuz people want to come and get a procedure done with this new device that's a huge motivator too so it's either the clinical data on one end where they see the the proof of concept or it could be we want to be the first as a marketing tool to drive revenue and increase patients coming in >> Okay we have a YouTube comment uh what about algorithms sales cycle could you walk through that how do you how do you do the initial outreach >> What about algorithms sales cycle I don't even know what that means to be honest with you but uh could you walk through that and >> How do you do the initial outreach is the last part >> The the initial outreach is is finding out doing your research and finding out if who the players are in that hospital you know you're going to start with a product that is in a initial it's going to be in for a certain uh therapeutic area so if it's cardiology you're going to the cardiology departments first within the hospital and then it's it's fact-finding, guys. There's There is no like when you first walk in, you go see Dr. Jones, and then from Dr. Jones, you're going to see Dr. Smith, and then you're going to see the nurse practitioner Susan, and then you're going to see the office manager or the the vice president of the department. No, you go in there first and set up an in-service. If you have a million-dollar cardiology product, go to the car- cardiology department, set up an in-service, and find out the process. You have this million-dollar product, what does that look like? Who's the chief? The chief is going to be involved in this. So, whoever the chief of cardiology is, you want to speak to him or her. You know, you you and then you they will help guide you in the process. You're not going to get everything in one conversation. It's going to be multiple meetings. It's going to be constant fact-finding. But, set up that initial outreach with the department and the department heads first, because they're going to give you the information. When you do a lunch, you know, in a hospital, it's going to cost you a pretty penny because some of those departments can feed up to 60, 70 people. You know, you're going to have to spend money on that, but that's part of it. But, get as much information from that lunch as possible. I mean, I've had lunches that were 4 hours. I won't leave until they kick me out because I'm utilizing my company just spent a lot of money on that. I'm going to fact-find and get as much information that day that I can possibly get because that's going to help set you up for success moving forward. But, that's my quick answer. You know, I apologize about the algorithm and all that. I mean, there's there's no algorithm that I know of for the sales cycle. It's just going out there, starting with the department that your product is going to be useful for, and then continuing to expand and and build relationships. >> Okay, uh Aman followed up and said, "Algorithms-based medical devices." >> Yeah, it still doesn't make sense to me. I apologize, Aman. >> Okay, um what strategies work for reopening cold accounts or resurrecting stalled deals? >> Well, you got to find out I mean, the first thing I would do, I'd find out who stalled that deal. Who closed it? I mean, there's another rep or manager or someone that was involved in that. Find out what the real story is. Cuz when you take over a capital sales role and it's an established product, guys, this is another, you know, like teaching moment that through experience, find out if you could speak to the previous rep that was in that position, that's key. Now, you got to take it with a grain of salt to find out why that person's not in that role anymore cuz they could be pissed off, disgruntled, they hate the company cuz they fired them, and all those things could come with the play, but you want the person that was involved hands-on in that role because they're going to be able to tell you why it was stalled. So, companies sometimes will just have you go out there and be like, "Just go run through walls. They they they did a bad job there. You get out there and do it. You They screwed up, that previous person." And it's always the other person's fault. And sometimes they they have you go out there to dead-end streets, you know, because they really believe that there's something there. Meanwhile, when you speak to the other rep, they're like, "Yo, there's there's the project's done." You know, for instance, when we had rooms that there was no construction projects going on for the next 3 years, there's no project that could possibly happen for us. So, that would be a closed account. So, I would first and foremost, if I can get a conversation with whoever covered those accounts last, that is huge. You know, so just understand they might be disgruntled, but I more often than not, a lot of these guys are good guys out there. They're not They They moved on. They started a new job. You could get some really good information and save time, but don't think that you're going to be Superman trying to revive a lot of stalled accounts. It You have to know the reasons why. If it's a dead deal that's not happening, or if someone may have just left cuz sometimes a champion could leave the hospital or retire. Now you're starting from from square one again. You need to know the facts. So, the best thing to do is find out from that previous rep what happened, or speak to someone at the company to really get a good understanding cuz you don't want to just run down dead end streets. You need to know what's really going on before you close it yourself. >> Okay. Um What are the most common contract terms or clauses that slow down capital deals? >> Um I mean, it's just That's on the legal end a lot of times, you know, just sometimes the lawyers involved on the legal team of the hospital, they you know, they're always It deals are always going to get slowed down once legal's involved. Um but a lot of times on the sometimes a service agreement that could slow things down. I've had that cost me a couple deals where I worked on one deal for almost 3 years. Literally almost 3 years. And I did a presentation. I'm obviously not going to mention names of the hospital, but I did a big presentation for the cardiology department. And we were this close to to getting everything approved. They had a broom. They had the funding. I had the champion. I had the support. I had the support from the C-suite. You know, everything was was great. And one individual jumped up during my meeting and said in front of everyone, "Yeah, why don't why don't you wait till he tells you how much the service agreements are?" You know, and it really wasn't important to the people in the room, but it just started a negative flow into the conversation. I I mean, I was sick to my stomach because it was a price that was too high for them, and it just was a negative spiral with it through within the room that people now that didn't need to know that, you know, because that's more of the uh more for the admin and getting budget, you know, to to get that annual budget that clinically wasn't really relevant, but it created a negative spiral that that essentially cost me the deal. So, it's one comment, literally one comment destroyed 3 years of work. Yeah, I was sick for a while after that. So, it's it that time it was a service agreement, um but it typically it's it's it could be something that you never know. It's like it's almost like selling a house where if you're a realtor, you don't want to count your your chickens until they hatch because until that deal is done, you anything can happen that can derail it. So, just don't celebrate too soon, don't take the pedal off the gas, keep going until you get that purchase order and you're you're set up for whatever construction or, you know, once you get that PO, that's that should be the time to celebrate, but don't celebrate any sooner because small factors like that can derail it. >> Okay, we got How do reps handle situations where the decision maker wants the equipment, but finance doesn't? >> I mean, that's that's just part of it. So, you you have to You're going to get a lot of clinicians that want your product. If you have a good product, you're going to get You're going to get the buying from clinicians. Again, it's another tool that they can use. Why would they say no? You know, it's same as kids wanting different toys in their house. Most kids are going to say yes to every toy that someone brings them, but their parents are essentially the finance department. And they're going to say, "Okay, yeah, I think it's cool, too. We don't have the money for that." So, I can't buy you a new, you know, uh motorcycle, dirt bike. We don't have the money. So, you you have to understand that, but you have to make the the finance team see the value. So, a lot of people are going to They're always going to say we don't have the money. But, you got to You have to be able to find out is it Do they not have the money or they're not sold on what you're selling them? And that typically is getting back to that ROI conversation. Cuz again, different hat. They're not going to care so much about talking about specific arrhythmias or or ailments. They want to see dollars and cents. So, you have to have put that different hat on and talk, you know, financially on why that makes sense to convince them. So, go in with those different hats, have different conversations, because you're going to get brought up That's going to come up every deal. It's never smooth where everyone loves this product and they want it purchased. They get hit up with hundreds of products every month that they constantly have to say no to because they don't have the budget. So, make them realize and see the value financially on why they should approve it. >> Uh and last question I got, Joe, is uh what should reps do in the first 30 to 90 days after a capital deal closes? >> What should reps do after it closes? >> Yeah. >> Go celebrate. I mean, it's It's uh I mean, I mean, obviously I'm kidding, but what you want to do I mean, you definitely want to celebrate. That's not a joke. But, you want to You want to partner with whoever your clinical team is that's going to drive adoption, drive utilization. Cuz most capital reps, they make their deal and that's it. But you can't have that attitude as a capital rep because that utilization and that success is now going to to snowball into more success in the future cuz you're going to have to sell it to future accounts. So if if an account the worst case scenario is they buy it and they don't use your product. Now you made your money on your commission on that one deal, but how likely are you to sell more if they're not even using it? Because trust me, doctors will talk. They'll say, "Yeah, I know NYU has it. They don't even use it." You know, I saw it sitting there collecting dust. And we actually had equipment around the country where certain hospitals didn't use it and then they got upgraded to to better platforms and then started using it, you know, like crazy. But sometimes with an old platform, you know, that or or whatever the product is, they could stop using it and as a good capital rep, you want to uh work with your clinical team to drive utilization and adoption and that'll help you become more successful. >> Uh yeah, that's all I got for you today, Joe. >> Awesome. Well, guys, uh James, first off, thank you again for fielding all those. Uh always appreciate it, man. >> And uh thank you all again for joining. Thank you for providing all the questions. Uh I know this one was a little bit more of a you know, an advanced topic and that's what we're going to continue to do on Mondays. Remember to join us every Monday for more advanced topics at 3:00 p.m. Eastern and every Wednesday for more broader topics that anyone from entry-level up to, you know, seasoned professionals can find value in. Uh you know, to move forward uh for all my lobby members, please, if you're looking to book any one-on-one coaching with me, please send in your promo code. The promo code is Lacata, l i c h a so that will enable you to get more discounts. And also for I'm excited to announce that we are launching the Rep Path Academy. So for any of you individuals that are looking for coaching to break into the industry or also to advance in your career, I'm very excited about this guys. Feel free to reach out and message me about that. And if if that's it, I hope to see you guys on Wednesday at 3:00 p.m. for for more of our latest podcast and I hope to see you guys soon. Take care.

Welcome to the Medical Equipment Industry. All States M.E.D. is now offering franchise opportunities for individual franchisees and territory development opportunities for investors. 

All States M.E.D. has a proven business model and has reached one of the highest level of achievements, being nominated INC 5000 as one of the fastest growing private companies in The United States. In 2021 All States M.E.D. was nominated the 616th Fastest growing and in 2022 the 631st fastest growing private company in ALL INDUSTRIES! 

If you are interested in entering the prestigious medical equipment industry and would like to join a reputable company, this is your chance. We are offering only 1 franchise per territory so don't miss the opportunity to own an All States MED franchise in your location of choice! 

Reach out to us today to learn more.

All States MED Franchising
877-ALL-1MED (877-255-1633)
franchising@allstatesmed.com
www.allstatesmed.com 

* Any offer of a franchise from us can only be made directly by us (or our representatives) outside of this website and with delivery of a franchise disclosure document as required by federal and some state laws. Certain states in the United States regulate the offer and sell of franchises within their respective states. Registration states include California, Hawaii, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New York, North Dakota, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Virginia, Washington, and Wisconsin (“Registration States”). We will not offer or sell any franchises to any residents of any Registration State until we have filed and received approval of our franchise disclosure document from that specific Registration State. If you are a resident of any Registration State or any state that requires approval of our franchise disclosure document, then you will not be offered a franchise until we can deliver to you a franchise disclosure document that has been registered and approved according to the laws of your state.

metadata.title: Beginners Troubleshooting Medical Device Power
metadata.author: Better Biomed Channel
metadata.shortDescription:
Medical device won't turn on? A beginner's guide to how a medical device receives power and what it does with it internally, with a flow diagram that covers most no-power problems.

----------------------------------------
Biomed jobs (W2 & 1099): https://bmetwork.com
Events, news & test equipment education: https://betterbiomed.com
Playlists: Biomed Basics, Equipment Repair, HTM Theory, Tours!, Vlog
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/justin-barbour-8602b886/
Support the channel: http://betterbiomedchannel.betterworld.org/campaigns/world-wide-biomed
More teardowns: @TakeItApartChannel

Subscribe for weekly biomed repair, troubleshooting and HTM career videos.

#Troubleshooting #MedicalDevice #BMET

metadata.title: FT10 Functional Tests | Safety Checks and Output Verification (Part 6)
metadata.author: MedDeviceEngineerX  | Isiah
metadata.shortDescription:
Ever wondered how medical engineers verify that electrosurgical generators deliver precise, safe energy during surgery? In this video, we break down the Safety Checks & Output Verification process for the Valleylab FT10 generator — one of the industry’s most advanced energy platforms. You’ll see how engineers ensure these systems meet IEC 60601 safety standards, perform within output limits, and stay reliable throughout their service life.

We’ll walk through the full procedure — from visual inspection and power testing to high-frequency leakage verification and grounding checks. You’ll also learn how preventive maintenance protects both clinicians and patients while keeping medical equipment compliant and ready for critical use. Whether you’re a biomedical technician, engineering student, or healthcare professional, this guide will help you understand the science and responsibility behind device safety verification.

If you find this breakdown useful, subscribe to the channel, like the video, and share it with others who are passionate about medical technology. Got a question or insight? Drop it in the comments — your input helps others learn.

Follow me on LinkedIn: www.linkedin.com/in/iperez22

#MedicalDevices #BiomedicalEngineering #FT10Generator #SafetyChecks #OutputVerification #Electrosurgery #MedTech #Biomed #PreventiveMaintenance #MedicalDeviceEducation #MedDeviceEngineerX

Tags: Valleylab FT10, electrosurgical generator, IEC 60601, power output verification, biomedical engineer, biomed service test, Medtronic FT10, medical equipment safety, preventive maintenance, device calibration, service mode test, high-frequency leakage, REM system test, medical device training, hospital engineering.

Educating and empowering the next generation of engineers through clear, practical insights into medical technology — that’s what MedDeviceEngineerX stands for.

segments.text: In this session, we'll review how to
verify that the Valab FT10 generator
performs safely and accurately after
service or during routine maintenance.
The goal is simple. Confirm that every
output, alarm, and circuit behaves as
designed. will follow the procedures
from chapter six of the service manual
focusing on inspection, power
verification, and leakage checks. By the
end, you should understand how to
confirm electrical safety to IEC
standards and ensure the generator
delivers precise power for clinical
reliability.
Periodic safety checks are part of every
preventive maintenance cycle. The goal
is to ver verify that the generator
remains both electrically safe and fully
functional.
Technicians confirm visual condition,
grounding, and leakage limits. This
process aligns with IC 60601 standards
and manufacturer guidance. Each test
protects patients and staff from
possible hazards like insulation failure
or poor grounding.
Think of it as a structured routine to
catch small issues before they become
performance problems.
Testing begins with proper setup. Place
the FT10 on a grounded static safe
bench. Attach a calibrated 100 ohm lead
to the output port. This stimulates
simulates surgical conditions.
Connect a highfrequency analyzer to
measure output power and a leakage
tester to assess electrical safety.
Confirm all instruments are within
calibration date. Setup accuracy is
critical because the data you gather
depends entirely on stable connections
and reliable reference equipment.
Start with a detailed inspection.
Examine every cable and port for wear or
discoloration.
Look for cracks, corrosion, or liquid
residue that could signal signal fluid
intrusion.
Test the activation switch and foot
switch for smooth, responsive operation.
Visual checks may seem simple, but they
often reveal early signs of wear or
overheating.
Document all findings before moving on
to electrical testing. This baseline
helps track long-term reliability.
When the FT10 powers on, it
automatically runs internal diagnostics.
Watch the progress bar and ensure the
boot sequence completes without error
codes. The screen and audio should
respond immediately. These checks
confirm the microcontroller, sensors,
and user interface are functioning
properly.
If you see any persistent alarms, the
test sequence stops here until resolve.
A clean start up indicates that internal
systems are stable and ready for
calibration level verification.
This test confirms that the generator's
actual output matches its displayed
setting. In service mode, open the RF
output test screen. Apply the 100 ohm
lead and record power at several output
levels, typically 30, 100, and 300
watts. The measured values should remain
within 10% of the set point. Deviations
may indicate calibration drift or
internal board faults.
Accurate power output is essential for
predictable surgical performance.
The return electrode monitoring system
or REM ensures proper patient contact.
Using your analyzer, simulate both
normal and disconnected conditions. The
FD10 should immediately detect the
change, displaying a warning and
blocking activation.
Then test each output channel to confirm
isolation known as crossoupling
prevention.
These steps validate patient safety and
confirm the generator can detect
electrode faults accurately.
Leakage
and grounding are the foundation of
electrical safety. Use a safety analyzer
to measure both ground resistance. It
should be below 0.2 ohms. Next, check
both low frequency and high frequency
leakage. The high frequency leakage must
stay within 150 milliamps while chassis
and patient leakage follow 60601 limits.
These results prove that insulation,
shielding, and grounding paths remain
intact, preventing any current from
reaching the patient or operator.
After all tests pass, complete the
service record. Include serial numbers,
technician signatures, calibration
references, and measured values. A
proper record demonstrates compliance
and accountability. Once verified,
attach a service verified label with
inspection date.
This documentation is more than
formality. It ensures traceability and
provides confidence that the FD10 meets
operational standards for clinical use.
Every maintenance session ends with
confirmation. The FD10 must perform
safely, deliver accurate energy, and
meet all electrical standards. Regular
testing identifies small faults before
they affect patient care. If a reading
falls outside tolerance, recalibration
or service intervention is required.
Consistent testing isn't just
regulatory. It ensures reliability,
accuracy, and the continued trust place
in the surgical system.

metadata.author: MFI Medical
metadata.shortDescription:
To read more about Setting Up a Veterinary Office: Essential Equipment and Supplies click here: https://mfimedical.com/blogs/news/setting-up-a-veterinary-office-essential-equipment-and-supplies

Setting up a veterinary office requires careful selection of essential equipment to ensure effective and compassionate animal care. Investing in quality examination tables, diagnostic tools, surgical instruments, imaging equipment, and sterilization machines will provide a solid foundation for a successful practice. For more information and to purchase these items, visit MFI Medical here: https://mfimedical.com/collections/veterinary

metadata.title: How Low Quality Remanufactured Parts Inside Medical Devices Increase Total Cost Of Ownership
metadata.author: TechNation TV
metadata.shortDescription:
This 60-minute webinar will feature Larry Nguyen, CEO and CTO at Summit Imaging, and Kyle Grozelle, Manager of Global Education and Training at Summit Imaging.

During this presentation, healthcare facilities will learn how to protect themselves from counterfeit ultrasound transducers that risk patient safety and lower quality of care. Ultrasound transducers are one of the most common imaging devices found in healthcare institutions, and their integrity is critical to providing excellent patient care.

The healthcare industry is being deceived, as unvalidated ultrasound remanufactured components are being hidden inside transducers under the illusion of “repair”. These compromised transducers are exposing healthcare facilities to severe increases in total cost of ownership and unnecessary liabilities, all while hiding in OEM marked bodies.

A thorough understanding of FDA regulations and requirements of remanufactured components will prepare healthcare facilities to select the best medical device support option for their organization.

# FDA's 2026 CSA Guidance — Risk Assessment and Assurance Activities | Video 18 of 35

💻 **Computer System Validation in Pharmaceuticals — US FDA Regulations and Guidance**

Welcome to **Video 18 of 35** in the Pharma Best Practices educational series on *Computer System Validation in Pharmaceuticals*.

This is the second video examining FDA's **February 2026 Computer Software Assurance (CSA) guidance** for medical-device production and quality management system software.

The video explains how FDA recommends evaluating software intended use, identifying foreseeable failures, determining process risk and selecting appropriate assurance activities.

🔍 **WHAT DOES THIS VIDEO COVER?**

✅ **Identifying Software Intended Use**

• Understanding the functions performed by computerized systems.  
• System-level and function-level evaluation.  
• Relationship between intended use and assurance activities.

✅ **Risk-Based Software Assurance**

• Identifying reasonably foreseeable software failures.  
• Evaluating the consequences of failures.  
• Considering existing process controls.

✅ **High Process Risk**

• Software failures that may result in quality problems foreseeably compromising medical-device safety.  
• Examples involving automated process control.

✅ **Not-High Process Risk**

• Software failures that do not foreseeably compromise device safety.  
• Understanding that not-high risk does not mean no assurance is necessary.  
• FDA's recognition of a spectrum of risk.

✅ **FDA's Material-Restocking Example**

• Software-supported material ordering and delivery.  
• Risk assessment with an independent material check.  
• Risk assessment without an independent check.  
• How existing controls influence process risk.

✅ **Selecting Assurance Activities**

• Assurance activities proportionate to intended use and risk.  
• Consideration of supplier information and existing controls.  
• Introduction to scripted and unscripted testing.

💡 **IMPORTANT REGULATORY DISTINCTIONS**

**Risk-based validation was already recognized in FDA's earlier software validation guidance.** CSA provides more explicit recommendations for evaluating process risk and selecting assurance activities.

FDA's February 2026 CSA guidance addresses **medical-device production and quality management system software** under the medical-device regulatory framework.

It is not a new pharmaceutical CGMP regulation under 21 CFR Part 211.

🎯 **WHO SHOULD WATCH?**

🔹 Quality Assurance and Quality Control professionals  
🔹 Computer System Validation personnel  
🔹 IT, Engineering and Automation specialists  
🔹 Manufacturing and Laboratory professionals  
🔹 Regulatory Affairs and Compliance professionals  
🔹 Students and young pharmaceutical professionals

This video may also be used for **professional education and training**.

📚 **ABOUT THE SERIES**

Our 35-video series examines US FDA regulations and guidance concerning computerized systems, software validation, electronic records, electronic signatures and data integrity.

▶️ **Previous Video — Video 17:**  
FDA's 2026 CSA Guidance — Evolution, Scope and What's New

▶️ **Next Video — Video 19:**  
FDA's 2026 CSA Guidance — Testing, Documentation and Practical Examples

📖 **OFFICIAL FDA REFERENCES**

FDA — Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality Management System Software (February 2026):  
https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/computer-software-assurance-production-and-quality-management-system-software

FDA — General Principles of Software Validation (January 2002):  
https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/general-principles-software-validation

21 CFR Part 820 — Quality Management System Regulation:  
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/part-820

🌐 **PHARMA BEST PRACTICES**

Pharma Best Practices is a **not-for-profit educational initiative** sharing pharmaceutical regulatory knowledge, scientific understanding and good practices.

We publish educational videos, articles and regulatory analyses to support professional learning and development.

🔔 Subscribe to follow the complete **35-video Computer System Validation in Pharmaceuticals series**.

**Pharma Best Practices — Sharing Knowledge, Promoting Better Practices.**

#ComputerSoftwareAssurance #CSA #ComputerSystemValidation #CSV #RiskBasedValidation #SoftwareAssurance #USFDA #QMSR #CGMP #PharmaBestPractices

To kick things off, we really need to ground ourselves in the regulatory context that we established in our previous explainer. It is absolutely crucial to remember that the 2026 CSA guidance didn't just invent risk based validation out of thin air. Not at all. It simply provided a more explicit structured framework for principles that the FDA had actually already established way back in their 2002 general principles of software validation guidance. The core idea that your assurance effort should be proportionate to your risk was already there. Identifying software intended use, where the risk assessment begins. What's really fascinating about the FDA's methodology here is that everything absolutely must start with identifying intended use. You know, a single computerized application rarely just does one thing, right? It might perform a whole bunch of distinct functions. We're talking from simply recording information or generating reports all the way to actively controlling manufacturing equipment or automatically determining product acceptability. And naturally the consequences of a simple report generation failure are vastly different from say an equipment control failure. That's exactly why the FDA recommends examining the intended uses of individual software features or functions rather than just looking at the software as one giant monolithic block. Because of this functional variety you actually have choices in how you evaluate it. You might evaluate the software as an entire system which by the way is completely appropriate if an application really only has a single intended use or if all of its functions share the exact same risk profile. The FDA doesn't want you unnecessarily slicing and dicing software just for the sake of it. But if your application has a bunch of diverse features that have very different relationships to product quality, well breaking it down and doing a function level evaluation becomes incredibly useful and efficient. A really practical example helps illustrate this perfectly. The FDA uses commercial off-the-shelf spreadsheet software as a reference point. Let's say you use a basic spreadsheet just to document time and temperature readings during a curing process. For that standard vendor evaluation and installation might totally be enough. But what if you take that exact same spreadsheet software and add a complex custom formula that calculates statistics to actively monitor and control the process. Your assurance needs just changed completely. The software product itself is identical but the intended use has shifted. So your assurance activities have to shift right along with it to verify that custom formula actually works. The risk assessment process, the FDA's sequential approach. Okay, so once we clearly know the intended use we can step right into the actual risk assessment process itself. The FDA lays out this really logical four-step funnel for determining your risk-based approach. It guides us sequentially. We start by identifying reasonably foreseeable failures. Then we could those failures lead to a quality problem? Next, we consider if that specific quality problem foreseeably compromises medical device safety. And then finally, based on that exact chain of events, we select our appropriate assurance activities. Let's zoom in on that first step for a second. When identifying failures, the FDA expects you to consider reasonably foreseeable issues. Notice I didn't say events you think will occur frequently. For example, a power outage might be super rare, but it is reasonably foreseeable over the lifespan of a system. You also need to think about incorrect configurations, calculation errors, data corruption, or even just plain old operator error. It's not meant to be a universal checklist, but rather a really targeted look at what could actually go wrong based on how you're using the software. Now here is a crucial distinction. You really need to separate your software risk analysis under CSA from your broader medical device risk analysis like ISO 14971. They are absolutely related, but they're distinct. The CSA analysis focuses strictly on whether the software performs its intended production or quality functions and what happens if it fails. Determining process risk levels, high process risk versus not high process risk. This brings us right to the core categorization of the CSA framework, classifying the specific process risk level of your software functions. Listen closely to this definition because high process risk hinges on an exact chain of consequences. It's a situation where a software failure results in a quality problem, and that specific quality problem foreseeably compromises medical device safety. Both of those elements have to be present. So if a piece of software automatically controls a process parameter that is essential to safety and its failure throws that parameter off, boom, that is high process risk. You can use your own classifications like low, intermediate, or moderate risk, just as long as they fall logically within that broader not high criteria. To make this all a bit more concrete, let's look at a highly practical example pulled directly from the FDA guidance involving material restocking. Picture this. Scenario one. The software automates ordering, but before any of that material is actually used in production, a qualified human independently checks it. If the software messes up and orders the wrong thing, the human catches it. That makes the software failure risk not high. Now look at scenario two. The software performs automated material checking with absolutely no independent human backup. Now, while high-risk functions naturally lean toward rigorous scripted testing and not high-risk opens the door beautifully for unscripted methods like scenario testing or error guessing, the FDA deliberately doesn't impose rigid one-size-fits-all rules here. For instance, you might find that automated scripted testing is actually incredibly efficient for a not high-risk function. The point is you have the flexibility to combine these methods efficiently based on your specific circumstances. We're going to dive much deeper into testing methods in our next video. metadata.title: FDA QMSR Compliance Calls for a New Mindset | FDA 21 CFR Part 820 Evolution PART 2
metadata.author: QT9 Software
metadata.shortDescription:
As of February 2, 2026, the FDA has officially begun enforcing the Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR)—a structural shift aligning 21 CFR Part 820 with ISO 13485 and redefining how medical device manufacturers will be inspected.

In this QT9 Q-Cast episode, host Christian Reyes speaks with Michelle Keane, QA/RA Director at ComplyGuru, to unpack what enforcement looks like now that QMSR is active. The discussion moves beyond theory and into inspection reality—how FDA investigators will follow risk threads across complaints, CAPA, management review, and design controls rather than auditing procedures in isolation.

Michelle explains why QMSR is not a documentation rewrite exercise, why ISO 13485 certification alone does not equal compliance, and how leadership decision-making under risk becomes central to inspection outcomes. The episode explores the retirement of QSIT, the shift toward faster, data-driven inspections, and why siloed spreadsheets and disconnected systems will create exposure.

The core message is clear: QMSR rewards organizations with integrated, validated systems, executive accountability, and real-time visibility across quality processes—while exposing fragmented workflows and performative compliance.

For quality leaders, regulatory professionals, and executives in medical devices and life sciences, this episode outlines what “inspection-ready” truly means under QMSR enforcement.

Guest Information:
Michelle Keane 
- QA/RA Director, ComplyGuru 
-  Lead Auditor & MDR Assessor

🌐 Learn more about QT9 Software:
https://qt9software.com/go/youtube

Links & Resources
• FDA Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR): https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/postmarket-requirements-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr/
• ComplyGuru: https://complyguru.com/ 
• ComplyGuru FDA QMSR Transition Training: https://complyguru.com/en-us/training/fda-qmsr-transition-course/

Chapters:
00:00 – QMSR Enforcement Begins
01:09 – Training Teams on Risk-Based Thinking
03:32 – Interconnected Processes & Plan-Do-Check-Act
05:10 – Where eQMS Systems Add the Most Value
07:33 – What Feels Different in FDA Inspections
08:00 – The New FDA Compliance Program Document
10:25 – Risk-Based Inspection Depth Explained
12:52 – Will Inspections Feel Like ISO Audits?
13:10 – Global Strategy & ISO 13485 Harmonization
15:34 – QMSR Myths: Lightning Round
16:54 – What “Good” Looks Like After Transition
18:27 – Recommended FDA & ISO Resources
21:44 – QMSR Training & Certification
24:49 – Final Takeaways for Manufacturers

metadata.title: CANDELA SKIN REJUVENATION Laser Skin Tightening All you need to know before procedure
metadata.author: Laser Queen MD | Candela Laser & Electrolysis
metadata.shortDescription:
✨ CANDELA SKIN REJUVENATION
Laser Skin Tightening | Hallandale Beach, FL

Want smoother, firmer, healthier-looking skin without aggressive treatments or lengthy downtime?

Candela Laser Skin Rejuvenation uses Nd:YAG 1064 nm laser technology to gently heat the skin, stimulate collagen remodeling, and gradually improve its appearance.

💜 WHAT CAN IT IMPROVE?

✔️ Skin texture and smoothness
✔️ Fine lines and early signs of aging
✔️ Mild skin laxity
✔️ Appearance of enlarged pores
✔️ Overall skin tone and radiance

✨ WHAT TO EXPECT

The treatment feels like gentle pulses of warmth and usually requires minimal downtime.

Results develop gradually as collagen remodels. A series of treatments may be recommended for optimal improvement.

🚫 WHAT IT DOES NOT DO

✖️ Remove pigmentation, sunspots, or melasma
✖️ Erase deep wrinkles or acne scars
✖️ Replace Botox, fillers, or a facelift
✖️ Deliver dramatic lifting after one session

💜 BEFORE YOUR APPOINTMENT

• Avoid tanning and excessive sun exposure.
• Arrive with clean skin, without makeup or lotions.
• Inform your provider about medications, recent Botox, fillers, or skin treatments.
• Avoid treatment on sunburned or irritated skin.

🌿 AFTERCARE

Avoid excessive heat and intense exercise for 24–48 hours. Use gentle skincare and daily SPF 30+.

Remember: Skin rejuvenation is about gradual improvement, not instant transformation.
