metadata.title: QLD - Laser license Application Process Explained - For Doctors
metadata.author: K-Laser Australia
metadata.shortDescription:
Queensland Radiation Health regulates the possession and usage of medical lasers.
For cosmetic applications
For vascular, pigment and skin rejuvenation
For warts, seborrheic keratosis and moles
For onychomycosis and ingrown toenails
For wound healing and diabetic ulcers
For laser therapy and pain management of MSK injuries
For hair reduction

We explain the process, for medical practitioners with a skin interest, on how to apply for the laser license in QLD.

Step 1 Check your eligibility and laser applications 
Webinar " Medical laser application in a GP practice"

Step 2 Learn about Laser Safety
https://studylaser.com/courses/coslso4-cosmetic-laser-safety-officer-lso-course-class-4-vascular-laser-skin-rejuvenation-australia/

Step 3 Prepare the laser room

Step 4 Laser license & Laser training

Step 5 Possession license to purchase a laser

To download the Possession license application form
https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0015/150135/ata-ra.pdf

To download the User license application form
https://www.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0029/149195/app-use.pdf

segments.text: Understand the process of laser
licensing in Queensland.
The process can be very confusing and
raise many questions.
Who is eligible for a laser license?
What training and safety course are
required?
How long does it take?
How much does it cost?
For doctors willing to acquire a laser
license in Queensland,
we have put in place a step-by-step
explanation.
First step, eligibility and clinical
applications of the laser.
Queensland Radiation Health has a list
of possible laser usage.
As a doctor, you are eligible for many
of them.
Skin rejuvenation,
age spots, and vascular lesions are the
most common in cosmetic procedures,
but also ablation of warts,
seborrheic keratosis,
skin tags, and other benign superficial
skin lesions.
You can also treat onychomycosis with
lasers.
Not to mention all the applications of
healing light therapy,
active acne,
chronic ulcers,
vasculitis,
wounds,
hematoma and edema post surgery,
and pain management of musculoskeletal
injuries.
As part of your license application, you
will need to select and describe the
clinical applications you wish to use
the laser for.
Second step,
laser safety.
As part of your application, Queensland
Radiation Health requires proof of laser
safety training.
You will find many online laser safety
courses.
Select one that matches your profession
and the clinical applications you wish
to treat with your laser.
Once you have passed the quiz,
make sure to print your laser safety
certificate and add it to the
application form.
For a faster licensing process, K-Laser
Australia offers a free laser safety
course to medical practitioners.
This course is already known to the
Queensland radiation health department.
At this stage, you can now apply for a
user license.
Don't forget to certify all the required
documents by a justice of the peace
and send your application.
The average waiting time to receive an
answer is 5 to 8 weeks.
Meanwhile, you can prepare the next
steps.
Third step,
the laser room.
If your clinic already has lasers, the
laser room should already have a
certificate of compliance.
If not, you can find a list of laser
consultants on the public register of
Queensland Health.
Click on the public register.
Select the tab accredited persons.
Then, select the aim of the
certification and the source of
radiation.
For a laser room, look for the keyword
premises.
The source of radiation being a laser,
look for the keyword non-ionizing.
Here it is, premises within the scope of
the standard for premises of
non-ionizing radiation apparatus.
Then, click on search to visualize the
list.
For a faster licensing process, K Laser
Australia offers free guidance to help
you prepare your laser room.
Remove any reflective areas. Install
specific signage and ventilation when
required.
Fourth step,
the user license.
When you receive your user license, each
clinical application of the laser will
be listed. For each of them, Queensland
Health grants you a full or a trainee
license.
They decide it on a case-by-case. It is
based on your qualifications,
experience, and extra certificates and
diploma in dermatology, skin cancer,
aesthetics medicine, and others.
With a full license, you can use a laser
for this application without a
supervisor.
With a trainee license, you will be
required to log a number of practice
hours for this specific application and
in the presence of a supervisor.
The supervisor can be anyone with a full
laser license.
To ease the process, K Laser Australia
organizes practical laser training in
Queensland.
To learn more, click on the link below
or contact us.
Once you have completed the practical
training, you are ready to use a laser
in Queensland.
However, if your clinic does not have a
laser already, the clinic will need to
apply for a possession license.
This extra step takes about 2 to 3
months.
The application form is easy,
but you must include an RSPP,
radiation safety protection plan.
It is a long legal document specific to
your clinic, the clinical application
that you will treat,
and the specificity of the laser
apparatus that you wish to purchase.
Thankfully, to ease the process, K Laser
Australia guides you through the process
and writes the RSPP document with you.
So, if you are planning to purchase a K
laser, contact us to organize the
possession license.
Once you have received the possession
license number, you can then finalize
the purchase of your K laser
and apply for the approval to acquire a
laser apparatus.
This last document is required for us to
be allowed to deliver a laser in
Queensland.
It is very quick,
usually about 1 to 2 weeks.
Finally, once you have received your
laser unit, a laser consultant will
visit your clinic and deliver a
certificate of compliance for your laser
unit and for your laser room.
We know it sounds like a lot of
requirements,
But we are next to you for each step.

metadata.title: FDA UDI Regulation’s Impact on Medical Device Labelers Webinar
metadata.author: Medical Device Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
The FDA UDI Regulation Impact on Medical Device Labelers webinar presented by subject matter expert, Jonathan Bretz, provides specific recommendations and a 3-Step Plan of how to plan for, implement and follow through to meet the requirements of this new regulation, its global impact, benefits, definitions, key compliance timelines (September 24, 2014 for Class III/PHS Act devices) and why this is a “publish or perish” regulation.

Blog Excerpt from “What is UDI and Why It Matters.” 

“In this blog, “What is UDI and Why It Matters” the author reviews the fundamentals of UDI, FDA’s Final Rule applications and its global significance. 

FDA’s Final Rule (Federal Register – UDI Definition) states a Unique Device Identifier (UDI) is a code that sufficiently identifies a medical device throughout its distribution and use. The UDI is comprised of a static component, “Device Identifier” (DI) and a dynamic component, “Production Identifier” (PI). 

The DI itself is made up of your Labeler Identification Code and a code that pinpoints the specific version or model of that device. PI, on the other hand, includes manufacturing information for that specific device, such as lot or batch number, serial number, expiration date or manufacturing date (both in YYYY-MM-DD format).” 

For more Digital and Remotely Delivered Training please visit the Webinars Section of our website at-

http://medicaldeviceacademy.com/webinars/

metadata.title: A Step-by-Step Guide to the Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) Database
metadata.author: Dr. Hashem Abu Serhan
metadata.shortDescription:
We were honored to host Dr. Ibraheem M. Alkhawaldeh, MD, who delivered a distinguished and highly practical lecture on the Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database.

In this comprehensive session, we provided a step-by-step guide on how to effectively use the MAUDE database, including:
1. How to navigate and search the database
2. Real-world examples of adverse event analysis
3. Practical tips on transforming MAUDE data into publishable research

This lecture is designed to serve as a foundational resource for clinicians, researchers, and trainees interested in device-related research and post-marketing surveillance.

For any queries or further discussion, feel free to reach out to Dr. Ibraheem directly: ibraheemfamous096@gmail.com

We would also like to thank Health Sciences Professional Association (HSPA) — more information about MAUDE and related educational resources can be found at: https://myhspa.org/

To simplify data extraction and analysis, you may also utilize tools and guidance shared by Dr. Mohamed Marouf from University of South Florida: https://share.google/5se5jX5dh8w7Ed7ai

We hope this lecture becomes a cornerstone reference for anyone aiming to publish high-quality research using the MAUDE database.

Don’t forget to like, share, and subscribe for more academic and research-focused content.

metadata.title: Critical FDA Recall: A Usability Issue… or a Software Bug? #fdarecall #usability #software
metadata.author: Human Factors Engineering
metadata.shortDescription:
A new FDA Class I recall perfectly highlights the intersection between software design and human factors engineering in medical devices. And yes — I found it at almost 2 AM, right after recording training content — but it’s such a perfect real-world example that I had to break it down immediately.

In this short video, we look at how a completely normal user action — tapping on-screen buttons quickly — can trigger a software interruption, cause the device to shut down or restart, and lead to serious patient risks, including therapy interruption and desaturation.

So is this a human factors issue?
Is it a software defect?
Is it a “use error” under FDA definitions?
Or is it a combination of all three?

This recall is a case study in why usability engineering and software validation cannot be treated as separate worlds. If you design, develop, or audit medical devices — especially software-driven systems — follow the channel for more real-world regulatory examples, late-night insights, and human factors engineering breakdowns.

#HumanFactors #MedicalDevices #FDA #UsabilityEngineering #SoftwareValidation #Cybersecurity #RegulatoryAffairs #RiskManagement #ClassIRecall #MedicalDeviceAcademy

And then I checked my email and I found the perfect realworld example of why the FDA cares so much about the overlap between software and human factors engineering. Because a device, and I'm not going to say which one, just received a class one recall. And that's the FDA's most serious level of recall. And why did they receive the recall? And why is this both a human factors and a software problem? Simply because if the user taps the onscreen buttons too fast, it can accidentally force the entire system to shut down and restart. And the effects of that include therapy interruption. The patient can experience desaturation, increased arterial pressure and that has its own risks for serious injury and yeah even death. But is this related to human factors engineer? I think absolutely. This is this failure is triggered by a user interaction with the device user interface. And is this also a software issue? I would say also yes. This problem occurs because rapid user inputs break the devices processing logic. It triggers a sudden and unexpected shutdown and restart. But the good news is if this error occurs, it can be diagnosed specifically through a system diagnostic notification. And the correction of this recall involves simply just a software update. But what I find perhaps the most fascinating about all of this is I'm not even sure this meets the strict definition from the FDA of a use error. It's usability related because this stems from user interactions through the user interface. The underlying [clears throat] issue, on the other hand, is a software design flaw that can't properly accommodate real world user behavior. So, I think what I'm going to have to do is make an entirely separate video when it's not 2:30 in the morning and I am not this exhausted so that we can figure out like, yes, this is a usability problem, but I'm not so sure it's actually a use error. I'm gonna have to trace out an actual decision tree to to confirm. So, if software, cyber security, human factors engineering, are those are the kinds of device problems you like breaking down, make sure you give this page a like and a follow because apparently I make these videos at around 2:30 a.m. Whenever I think the FDA sends an interesting email,

metadata.title: MRI Accidents - Learning from the MAUDE Database
metadata.author: Metrasens
metadata.shortDescription: We take a close look at projectile accidents, using three recent incidents including reports to the FDA MAUDE (Manufacturer And User Facility Device Experience) database.  For each, we review the report information and highlight best practice prevention and mitigation recommendations which could potentially have prevented the accident.

metadata.title: QSR to QMSR: The Rewrite of 21 CFR Part 820 & Key Considerations for FDA Compliance
metadata.author: Greenlight Guru
metadata.shortDescription:
This on-demand webinar hosted by Greenlight Guru addresses the major transition from FDA’s Quality System Regulation (QSR) to a Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), which will align with ISO 13485:2016, and a revision of relevant sections of 21 CFR Part 4 (Combination Products). 

Watch this session to learn about the QMSR proposed rule, next steps in the rulemaking and implementation process, and important considerations for medical device manufacturers. 

Main points covered:
1. Overview of the QMSR proposed rule and the transition from QSR.
2. Explanation of how ISO 13485 fits into the regulatory landscape.
3. Discussion of "incorporate by reference" in the context of these regulations.
4. Important concepts from the proposed rule.
5. The impact of QMSR on the industry and FDA.

Target Audience:
• Regulatory Affairs Professionals and Management
• Quality Professionals and Management
• Medical Device Executives

Access the printable slides for this presentation here:
https://www.greenlight.guru/webinar/qsr-to-qmsr-the-rewrite-of-21-cfr-part-820

segments.text: Hello, my name is Tanya Wilbon,
assistant director for the postmarket
industry education team and the consumer
education team of the division of
industry and consumer education in the
center for devices and radiological
health at the US Food and Drug
Administration. Welcome to CDR learn
FDA's preeeminent catalog of multimedia
educational modules about medical
devices and radiological products. In
this module I will focus on the quality
management system regulation hereafter
referred to as QMSR
requirements for risk management
riskbased approach and riskbased
decisions.
This image illustrates the comprehensive
nature of risk management throughout the
product life cycle from initial design
through postmarket surveillance. Some of
you may think that the requirements
pertaining to risk may look similar to
this image sketchy, crowded, uncertain,
and even perhaps overwhelming.
Hopefully, this presentation will
provide you with knowledge, clarity, and
resources to understand and successfully
implement risk requirements of the QMR.
This presentation has four key learning
objectives. The learning objectives are
to define essential risk terms that form
the foundation of this presentation, to
explain the role of risk management
within the broader quality management
system, to identify the QMR requirements
for risk management, riskbased
approaches and riskbased decisions, and
to review a few examples of risk
documentation.
Let's begin by defining a few key terms
used in this presentation.
Understanding key risk terms is crucial
for implementing effective risk concepts
in your quality management system. Risk
is defined as the combination of the
probability of occurrence of harm and
the severity of that harm. This term
describes what could go wrong, how
likely it is to happen, and how serious
the consequences would be.
Risk management is defined as the
systematic application of management
policies, procedures, and practices to
the tasks of analyzing, evaluating,
controlling, and monitoring risk. The
term systematic used in the definition
clarifies that this is a structured and
documented approach to addressing risk.
These terms are defined in the American
National Standards Institute hereafter
referred to as ANIE,
the Association for the Advancement of
Medical Instrumentation, hereafter
referred to as Amy, and the
International Organization for
Standardization, hereafter referred to
as ISO. Thus, the ANIE Amy ISO 1345
standard titled medical devices quality
management systems requirements for
regulatory purposes and the ISO standard
2007 titled medical devices application
of risk management to medical devices
as indicated in FDA's response to
comment 9 FDA A does not in this
rulemaking incorporate ISO 14971
or any other standards referenced by or
listed as a source in ISO 1345,
but acknowledges that these other
standards may be helpful in
understanding application of ISO 13485.
FDA further clarified in their response
to comment 32 in the final rule that the
definition of the term risk used by ISO
1345 is appropriate.
Clause 0.2 two in ISO 13485 states that
when the term risk is used, the
application of the term within the scope
of this international standard pertains
to safety or performance requirements of
the medical device or meeting applicable
regulatory requirements.
FDA stated that it believes that a
definition of risk unique to QMSR is
thus not necessary.
Two additional key terms are riskbased
approach and risk based decision.
Risk-based approach is defined as
identifying risk and opportunities and
focusing on preventing or reducing
undesired effects. This is more of a
proactive approach. Risk-based decision
is defined as making a specific decision
based on risk assessment and other
criteria. The information obtained is
actively used to drive decisions
throughout the life of the device and
throughout the quality management
system.
Now let's explore the role that risk
management plays within your quality
management system.
Risk management serves several core
functions. It helps identify, assess,
control, communicate, and review device
risk to the quality management system
processes. It provides reasonable
assurance of safety and effectiveness
throughout the total product life cycle
from design and development through
postmarket surveillance and eventually
discontinuation.
Risk management provides a framework for
sound decisionmaking within your quality
management system. For example, it helps
you identify which design outputs are
essential for proper device functioning,
guides continuous updates based on
postmarket surveillance data, defines
the extent of verification activities

metadata.title: Medical Devices 101: An Entry Level Overview of the FDA
metadata.author: leanRAQA
metadata.shortDescription:
In this practical session, Michelle breaks down how the FDA actually looks at medical devices—so you can choose the right pathway, budget for testing, and avoid dead-ends. You’ll learn the three device classes, the five steps to market, what “substantial equivalence” really means, when De Novo fits, and why “approval” ≠ “clearance.” If you’re leading a MedTech program this year, this talk is a no-nonsense roadmap to reduce surprises. Follow this sequence and the surprises shrink.

02:41 FDA risk-based classification (Class I–III + unclassified)
05:01 The “bread & butter”: QSR (21 CFR 820) + labeling/MDR
07:00 What exemptions still require (registration, listings, complaints)
09:03 The 5 steps to market
09:33 Intended Use vs. Indications for Use (lock them early)
12:27 Is it even a medical device? (definition & software nuance)
13:24 Claims make devices (lamp & depression example)
16:15 The “diapers” test (why adult can be a device)
18:12 Finding the pathway (FDA databases & product codes)
19:15 Surgical mask case (FXX vs. alternatives, NIOSH wrinkle)
24:34 Recognized standards & (maybe) third-party review
26:02 General standards you’ll still need (sterilization, biocomp, etc.)
26:02 Wellness vs. regulated (bruxism app scenarios)
30:01 Valid scientific evidence (bench, animals, clinical, HF/UX)
31:25 510(k) types & the SE argument
33:17 Words to avoid (“novel” can push you to De Novo)
36:35 Primary & reference predicates (don’t build a Frankenstein)
38:04 De Novo: when, why, and afterlife for others
41:24 Strategy: stage features & submissions
42:23 Time & money: realistic clocks, fees, testing budgets
43:24 PMA: what “approved” actually means
45:59 Authorization vs. clearance vs. approval
46:13 After clearance: QMS, claims review, and ongoing work

Be sure to like and subscribe for even more insights on medical device regulations, compliance, and quality systems (it will be fun and not painful, I promise). 

Visit us at https://leanraqa.com/ for even more regulatory goodness and to learn more about our services.

We’re also on Substack! https://leanraqa.substack.com/

📩 Got a question or a topic for a future session? Drop it in the comments below!

#FDA #RegulatoryAffairs #MedicalDevices #MedTech #Compliance #PreSub #QualitySystems #submissions #commercialization #startups #productlaunches #businessdevelopment

metadata.title: QMSR Final Rule: Meeting FDA’s New Requirements
metadata.author: Greenlight Guru
metadata.shortDescription:
On 2 February 2024, FDA finalized revisions to the Quality System Regulation (QSR) harmonizing it to the international medical device standard ISO 13485:2016 under the new title Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR). The final rule becomes effective 2 February 2026.

This webinar provides background to the action taken by FDA, an overview of the final rule, how FDA responded to comments made to the proposed rule, and how it may impact both the MedTech industry and FDA. Particular emphasis will be placed on risk management, transition issues, and FDA inspections.

Specifically, this webinar will cover:
- Why ISO 13485 and why now?
- The meaning of "incorporation by reference"
- Step-by-step walk through of the new 21 CFR Part 820 (QMSR)
- Impacts of the final rule on combination products
- How risk management changes under the QMSR
- Considerations during the two-year transition period
- Clarification regarding FDA inspections under the final rule

Learn more: https://www.greenlight.guru/webinar/qmsr-final-rule

Perfect for newcomers and professionals seeking a refresher, this webinar provides a clear, practical introduction to the regulatory framework that governs medical devices in the United States. Learn how the FDA classifies devices, what pathways exist for market entry, and the compliance obligations every manufacturer must understand.

26:27 Small Business Application/Number
29:00 Additional Requirements For Certain Medical Devices
30:27 Registrar Corp’s Services

metadata.title: FDA Regulatory Education for Industry (REdI) Annual Conference 2023 – Devices Day 1
metadata.author: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
metadata.shortDescription:
The devices track will provide an overview and highlights of how to get a new medical device to market. It will also discuss some best practices for ensuring that medical devices maintain their quality and continue to be safe and effective once on the market; and offer technical topic updates on biocompatibility, artificial intelligence, and radiological health.

Chapters:

0:00  Intro

4:06 - Welcome to REdI 2022 Device Track, Part 1 - Elias Mallis

24:49 - Medical Device Regulatory Framework: Where to Start? - Kendra Holter

1:05:23 - Biocompatibility Basics - Jennifer Goode

2:03:08 - Appropriate Use of Voluntary Consensus Standards and the Conformity Assessment Program - Scott Colburn

2:43:00 - Detangling the 510(k) Process - Andrew Sprau

4:24:46 - CDRH Portal: Overview and Feature Walkthrough - Nelson Anderson

5:07:32 - Reduced Medical Device User Fees: Small Business Determination (SBD) Program - Jason Brookbank

6:05:15 - Welcome to REdI 2022 Device Track, Part 2 - Joseph Tartal

6:13:47 - Managing Medical Device Nonconforming Product with Quality - Ruth Bediakoh

6:53:39 - Handling Medical Device Complaint Files with Quality - Tonya Wilbon

7:33:30 - CDRH Day One Closing Remarks - Joseph Tartal

metadata.title: FDA QSR to QMSR Regulatory, Legal, and Risk Implications for Industry
metadata.author: Medmarc
metadata.shortDescription:
This webinar, recorded live on July 30, 2026 and presented by Denise Holliday with Capwell Consulting, focused on the FDA's transition from the Quality System Regulation (QSR) to the new Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR). Denise explained the reasons for the change, which include harmonization with the international standard ISO 13485-2016 to reduce duplication for manufacturers. She detailed the significant changes, such as the incorporation of risk-based thinking throughout the quality system and the FDA's expanded access to certain quality records. Denise also discussed the new risk-based inspection approach under the QMSR and shared insights from recent FDA inspection observations. The presentation emphasized that an effective QMS extends beyond compliance to manage organizational risk and improve inspection readiness.

44:44 - FAQs and Closing

metadata.title: What Happens to MRI Scanners When Hospitals Replace Them?
metadata.author: Reclaim Atlas
metadata.shortDescription:
Who buys a hospital’s old MRI scanner—and what happens before it can scan patients somewhere else?

Replacing an MRI machine does not automatically end its useful life. This documentary explores the market for used and refurbished MRI scanners, following the journey from a hospital’s replacement decision to specialist refurbishment and a potential new home.

We examine why another healthcare provider might consider a refurbished system, what refurbishment involves, and why buying the machine is only one part of the decision. Removal, installation and ongoing support also matter.

Manufacturer programmes such as Siemens Healthineers ecoline and GE HealthCare GoldSeal show how pre-owned imaging equipment can return to service. However, the condition and suitability of each system determine its next chapter.

Reclaim Atlas explores the second lives of machines, materials and products—and the businesses behind them.

What would you want to know before a hospital bought a refurbished MRI scanner?

#MRI #MedicalEquipment #CircularEconomy

its MRI scanner. The appointments have
stopped. Engineers are measuring the
exit route. Soon, the machine that
helped doctors look inside thousands of
people will leave the building. But
somewhere else, someone may be preparing
a room for its arrival. Who buys a
hospital's old MRI scanner and what
makes it worth trusting with another
patient? The next owner, the buyers can
be other hospitals, outpatient imaging
centers, and specialist healthcare
providers. But the person buying from
the original hospital may be an
equipment dealer or a manufacturer's
refurbishment business. They connect a
machine leaving one service with a
customer who can use it again. That
distinction matters. A hospital can sell
equipment without its next clinical
destination being ready. Between the two
owners, it's a business of inspection,
repair, logistics, installation, and
support. And this market is not limited
to places that cannot afford anything
else. In Finland, healthcare provider
Terveystalo describes choosing a
refurbished MRI system for its Tikkurila
location. In an article published in
December 2025, it explains that selected
components and software were modernized.
The provider presents the decision as
part of combining clinical needs,
cost-effectiveness, and sustainability.
That is a real buyer describing a real
installation. It does not tell us the
price, the machine's complete history,
or whether the same choice would suit
another clinic. But it answers the first
question. An older scanner can be a
deliberate investment rather than an
emergency compromise. The hard other
question is what has to happen before
that investment becomes useful. Why a
working scanner leaves a hospital
replacing a machine is not necessarily
declaring it broken. Its requirements
may have changed. It may want
capabilities its existing system cannot
deliver or a different workflow. An
equipment purchase can be driven by the
service a hospital wants to build next,
not simply by whether yesterday's
machine still operates. Think of two
hypothetical facilities. One needs to
expand a specialized imaging service,
the other needs dependable capacity for
examinations that an appropriately
configured older system can already
perform. The same scanner could be a
poor fit for the first facility and a
useful candidate for the second, but
nobody should decide that from the
machine's age or a photograph. Buyers
need to match its documented
capabilities to the examinations they
intend to provide. They also need to ask
what is actually being sold. A complete
system? A magnet with some accessories
missing? Equipment sold as it stands or
a package that includes refurbishment
and installation? Those descriptions can
refer to very different purchases, even
when the listing photographs look almost
identical. A second-hand listing also
captures just one moment. The buyer
needs to think ahead. If the service
grows, can the system still meet its
needs? If an essential component fails
later, is there a realistic repair path?
A machine that suits today's plan may
not suit the plan that justified buying
it. That is why remaining usefulness is
a better question than age alone. More
than the giant magnet. The recognizable
white tunnel is only the visible part of
the system. MRI uses magnetic fields and
radio frequency energy to obtain signals
from the body. Computers turn those
signals into images. Unlike a CT
scanner, MRI does not use ionizing
radiation to make those images. Inside
and around the scanner are components
with different jobs. The main magnet
provides a strong field. Gradient coils
vary that field in controlled ways,
helping locate where signals come from.
Radio frequency coils help transmit or
receive the signals used for imaging.
There are also electronics, software, a
patient table, and supporting equipment.
Imagine buying an expensive camera body
without checking its lenses, computer
connection, or available software. The
central object might be valuable, while
the complete setup cannot do your
particular job. With MRI, the
consequences of missing that distinction
are much greater. A buyer needs to know
which coils and software capabilities
are included, whether they are
compatible, and who will support the
system. A working magnet does not
establish that every examination the
buyer wants is possible. This is why
service records and a detailed equipment
inventory belong in the story alongside
the impressive machinery. The paperwork
helps reveal what the machine can become
and what it might still need. The room
becomes part of the purchase. Then comes
a problem that a normal second-hand
purchase rarely creates, the building
itself. A scanner needs a suitable route
out of its old location and into its new
one. Engineers must consider access and
structural support, including the weight
moving along that route. Equipment this
substantial cannot be treated like
office furniture. At the destination,
the project can involve electrical
supply, cooling, ventilation, and a room
designed for the particular system.
Radio frequency shielding helps keep
unwanted interference from affecting
imaging. Magnetic field considerations
also influence the layout and
surrounding space. The details vary by
scanner and site. A floor plan that
worked for one installation is not
automatically suitable for another. Nor
does disconnecting an ordinary power
cable establish that an MRI magnet is
safe to approach. Magnetic field hazards
require their own assessment, an
inactive screen is not proof of a safe
working area. Removal and transport
requires specialists following the
applicable procedures. For a buyer, all
of this becomes part of the cost and
schedule. Picture a clinic that has
found an attractive scanner, but has not
checked its building. The equipment
quote looks manageable. Then the
installation survey reveals additional
work. Nothing about the scanner's
advertised price has changed, yet the
actual project is now a different
proposition. What refurbishment has to
prove. Before an older system returns to
clinical work, someone has to establish
its condition and address the work it
requires. Siemens Healthineers describes
its refurbishment program in five
stages: selection, removal,
refurbishment, installation, and
services. Its selection criteria include
condition, service history, performance,
and technology level. That means a
professional refurbishment program
starts before the cleaning or
repainting. It begins by deciding
whether a particular machine belongs in
the program at all. The company
describes component checks, replacement
of worn parts, and suitable updates
within its process. These are the
suppliers' stated procedures, not a
promise that every seller follows the
same approach. The buyer still needs the
actual scope of work, configuration,
test results, and contract. A fresh
exterior cannot answer those questions.
Neither can the word refurbish on its
own. There is also a regulatory
distinction. In the United States, the
FDA distinguishes servicing from
remanufacturing that significantly
changes a device's performance or safety
specifications or its intended use. The
work performed matters, not simply the
label attached to the sale. Restoring a
system to specified performance is also
different from giving it every feature
of the latest model. Credible second
life depends on clear limits as much as
successful repairs. The cheap machine
and the expensive service. Now, imagine
two hypothetical offers for the same
clinic. The first has a lower equipment
price, the second costs more, but
includes a broader installation and
support package. Which is cheaper? You
cannot tell yet. The clinic needs
comparable totals, equipment, necessary
repairs, removal, transport, site
preparation, installation, and testing.
Then come the costs of operating and
maintaining the service. Even that
comparison is incomplete if the two
systems cannot perform the same required
examination. Here is the practical test.
Could this clinic use this configuration
in this building with the staff and
support it can actually obtain? A low
purchase price cannot compensate for a
missing capability essential to the
service. Nor does it solve a shortage of
trained staff or an unsuitable room. And
a service contract needs more than a
reassuring heading. What is covered?
Which parts are excluded? Who responds
when the system develops a fault, are
the promised services available at the
buyer's location? Philips, for example,
advertises warranty and service support
for its circular edition MRI systems.
That shows how support can be part of
the refurbished offering. It does not
mean every used scanner comes with
equivalent terms. For our hypothetical
clinic, downtime is another uncertainty.
A scanner awaiting repair occupies a
room while appointments may need to be
rearranged. An operating plan that
assumes uninterrupted service can make
an attractive purchase look better on
paper than it works in practice. So, the
buyer is evaluating more than a machine.
It is evaluating the ability to keep an
imaging service available. That is where
some apparent bargains disappear and
where a well-supported refurbished
system can make sense. Consider one more
detail in those two hypothetical offers,
the handover point. Does the seller's
responsibility finish when the equipment
is collected, when it reaches the
building, or after agreed installation
tests? The answer affects who must solve
an unexpected problem. A buyer comparing
only the headline prices could miss that
difference entirely. The contract
connects the promises in the sales
conversation to the work someone is
actually expected to complete. For
equipment that depends on a whole room
and a trained team, that connection can
shape the entire purchase. The first
scan is not the finish line. Once the
scanner arrives, producing an image is
only the beginning of proving that the
installation performs as intended. In
its MRI quality guidance, the American
College of Radiology calls for a
complete performance evaluation by a
qualified medical physicist or me a
scientist after installation and before
patient imaging. One tool used in MRI
quality assessment is a phantom, a
specially designed test object with
known features. Scanning something known
helps assess the system's performance
against expected results. A patient's
anatomy is not a convenient calibration
ruler. A test object gives specialists a
controlled reference. The ACR's
accreditation process includes both
phantom and clinical image quality
testing. These are elements of a
particular accreditation framework, not
a single worldwide permission slip. The
broader point is straightforward. A
machine has to be evaluated in the
service where it will operate. An
impressive photograph from its previous
location cannot establish its
performance after relocation, and checks
do not end when the opening day
photograph is taken. Ongoing quality
control is part of keeping the service
dependable. When another scanner needs
the parts, of course, not every retired
MRI system finds another clinical home.
Sometimes the work needed, available
support, or demand for that
configuration makes a complete resale
unattractive. Another potential buyer is
a business dealing in imaging equipment
parts. A compatible component with
documented condition in another system.
That does not mean every removed part is
reusable, or that a part from one model
will fit another. There is a difference
between recovering a useful component
and simply keeping a warehouse full of
unverified hardware. The rest of the
equipment still needs appropriate
handling. Its possible value as spare
parts does not make uncontrolled
dismantling sensible. There is another
outcome worth remembering, too. An older
scanner may stay where it is. Where an
appropriate upgrade exists, a provider
can retain valuable hardware and improve
the system around it. A second life does
not always require a second address. So,
who buys a hospital's old MRI scanner?
Sometimes a manufacturer or equipment
specialist buys it first. Sometimes
another health care provider becomes its
next operator. Sometimes a parts
business finds value in what can support
other machines. The deciding question is
not whether it once belonged to a
hospital. It is whether its remaining
capabilities, condition, support, and
total cost fit a real need. An MRI
scanner's second life succeeds when all
of those pieces come together, and the
next patient enters a service that is
ready for them.

Siemens Healthineers describes its refurbishment program in five stages: selection, removal, refurbishment, installation, and services. Its selection criteria include condition, service history, performance, and technology level. That means a professional refurbishment program starts before the cleaning or repainting. It begins by deciding whether a particular machine belongs in the program at all. The company describes component checks, replacement of worn parts, and suitable updates within its process. These are the suppliers' stated procedures, not a promise that every seller follows the same approach. The buyer still needs the actual scope of work, configuration, test results, and contract. A fresh exterior cannot answer those questions. Neither can the word refurbish on its own. There is also a regulatory distinction. In the United States, the FDA distinguishes servicing from remanufacturing that significantly changes a device's performance or safety specifications or its intended use. The work performed matters, not simply the label attached to the sale. Restoring a system to specified performance is also different from giving it every feature of the latest model. Credible second life depends on clear limits as much as successful repairs. The cheap machine and the expensive service. Now, imagine two hypothetical offers for the same clinic. The first has a lower equipment price, the second costs more, but includes a broader installation and support package. Which is cheaper? You cannot tell yet. The clinic needs comparable totals, equipment, necessary repairs, removal, transport, site preparation, installation, and testing. Then come the costs of operating and maintaining the service. Even that comparison is incomplete if the two systems cannot perform the same required examination. Here is the practical test. Could this clinic use this configuration in this building with the staff and support it can actually obtain? A low purchase price cannot compensate for a missing capability essential to the service. Nor does it solve a shortage of trained staff or an unsuitable room. And a service contract needs more than a reassuring heading. What is covered? Which parts are excluded? Who responds when the system develops a fault, are the promised services available at the buyer's location? Philips, for example, advertises warranty and service support for its circular edition MRI systems. That shows how support can be part of the refurbished offering. It does not mean every used scanner comes with equivalent terms. For our hypothetical clinic, downtime is another uncertainty. A scanner awaiting repair occupies a room while appointments may need to be rearranged. An operating plan that assumes uninterrupted service can make an attractive purchase look better on paper than it works in practice. So, the buyer is evaluating more than a machine. It is evaluating the ability to keep an imaging service available. That is where some apparent bargains disappear and where a well-supported refurbished system can make sense. Consider one more detail in those two hypothetical offers, the handover point. Does the seller's responsibility finish when the equipment is collected, when it reaches the building, or after agreed installation tests? The answer affects who must solve an unexpected problem. A buyer comparing only the headline prices could miss that difference entirely. The contract connects the promises in the sales conversation to the work someone is actually expected to complete. For equipment that depends on a whole room and a trained team, that connection can shape the entire purchase. The first scan is not the finish line. Once the scanner arrives, producing an image is only the beginning of proving that the installation performs as intended. In its MRI quality guidance, the American College of Radiology calls for a complete performance evaluation by a qualified medical physicist or me a scientist after installation and before patient imaging. One tool used in MRI quality assessment is a phantom, a specially designed test object with known features. Scanning something known helps assess the system's performance against expected results. A patient's anatomy is not a convenient calibration ruler. A test object gives specialists a controlled reference. The ACR's accreditation process includes both phantom and clinical image quality testing. These are elements of a particular accreditation framework, not a single worldwide permission slip. The broader point is straightforward. A machine has to be evaluated in the service where it will operate. An impressive photograph from its previous location cannot establish its performance after relocation, and checks do not end when the opening day photograph is taken. Ongoing quality control is part of keeping the service dependable. When another scanner needs the parts, of course, not every retired MRI system finds another clinical home. Sometimes the work needed, available support, or demand for that configuration makes a complete resale unattractive. Another potential buyer is a business dealing in imaging equipment parts. A compatible component with documented condition in another system. That does not mean every removed part is reusable, or that a part from one model will fit another. There is a difference between recovering a useful component and simply keeping a warehouse full of unverified hardware. The rest of the equipment still needs appropriate handling. Its possible value as spare parts does not make uncontrolled dismantling sensible. There is another outcome worth remembering, too. An older scanner may stay where it is. Where an appropriate upgrade exists, a provider can retain valuable hardware and improve the system around it. A second life does not always require a second address. So, who buys a hospital's old MRI scanner? Sometimes a manufacturer or equipment specialist buys it first. Sometimes another health care provider becomes its next operator. Sometimes a parts business finds value in what can support other machines. The deciding question is not whether it once belonged to a hospital. It is whether its remaining capabilities, condition, support, and total cost fit a real need. An MRI scanner's second life succeeds when all of those pieces come together, and the next patient enters a service that is ready for them.

metadata.title: What’s the Difference Between an X-ray, MRI and a CT? | Medical Advice With Doctor ER
metadata.author: Doctor ER
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn about the different types of medical imaging such as X-ray, CT scan, MRI, PET scan, and ultrasound. Real doctor, Jordan Wagner explains the different types of medical imagining technologies.

Do X-rays cause cancer? Did your doctor say you have to get a medical image but you’re really claustrophobic? Did you break a bone and have to get an X-ray? Maybe you're pregnant and want to schedule an ultrasound? With so many different medical imaging technologies out there, it’s hard to keep track of which “x ray” is which? It is one of the most common questions that Doctor ER gets asked: Which scan or medical image is right for me? Make sure you watch and learn the difference between different types of medical images out there!
